News.title: Russia is ‘secretly helping Iran develop supersonic cruise missiles’ that can take out US aircraft carriers
News.content:
SECRET ALLIANCE Russia is ‘secretly helping Iran develop supersonic cruise missiles’ that can take out US aircraft carriers

RUSSIA has reportedly been secretly helping Iran develop supersonic cruise missiles built to take out US aircraft carriers.

A bombshell report has revealed how some of the Kremlin’s most experienced missile specialists were enlisted for the top secret programme, codenamed C430L.



The multi-year covert partnership was uncovered by the Financial Times, who pieced together leaked Russian correspondence with travel records and military patents.

Mad Vlad’s scientists are working with the Iranian regime to develop a ramjet propulsion system – an engine that can send a missile flying at several times the speed of sound.



Such an engine would allow Iran‘s Supreme Tyrant to threaten US aircraft carriers and other warships in the Middle East.

Iranian missiles expert Fabian Hinz said the regime has wanted to get their hands on this kind of tech for decades, adding that Putin himself will have approved the plot.

He told the FT: “This is the transfer of a highly strategically sensitive military technology from Russia that the Iranians have wanted to acquire for decades.

“A programme like this would require political clearance from the very top in Russia.”



And Iran has reportedly already built and flight-tested the terrifying ramjet propulsion system.

But there is no evidence it has yet deployed a Russian-assisted supersonic cruise missile.

It comes as the US ramps up attacks on Iran after weeks of relative calm in the region.



Mojtaba Khamenei and Russia’s deranged dictator enjoy an increasingly close relationship, with Iran supplying Shahed drones to Putin.

Ukraine has also accused Russia of sharing battlefield intel with Iran to help the regime target US bases.

And Putin has supplied Iran with information about the whereabouts of US warships and aircraft, sources told the Washington Post at the start of the US-Israeli war in Iran.

One source said the intel-sharing “appears to be a fairly comprehensive effort”.

Sources said that Russia‘s intel comes as the battered Iranian regime’s ability to locate US targets for itself “has been degraded”.



Professor Nicole Grajewski said the top secret ramjet project “shows Russia is trying to broaden the Ukraine war and draw the US into different theatres”.

She added: “Russia doesn’t care as much about the red lines in the region.”

In July, Trump warned China and Russia that interfering in the Iran war “would be very bad for them”.

The US president posted on Truth Social: “President Putin, despite the horrible War going on in Ukraine (The relationship remains, as it does with President Zelenskyy), told me that he would not sell Weapons to Iran.

“He understands that I do not sell Weapons to Ukraine, but to NATO Countries.”



RECOMMENDED STORIES

The US president insisted that the two countries were “not participating”.

But he warned: “If they did, it would be very bad for them — Certainly not in their best interests.”

News.title: Manhunt launched after two men shot dead and several injured as armed cops swarm factory site in Germany
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

GUN RAMPAGE Manhunt launched after two men shot dead and several injured as armed cops swarm factory site in Germany

AT LEAST two men have been killed and several injured in a horror shooting spree at a factory in Germany.

Cops have launched a major manhunt after a gun-wielding suspect rampaged through a complex in Hamburg.



Huge numbers of police armed with submachine guns have swarmed to the complex on Lagerstrasse early on Tuesday evening.

The building houses a meat wholesaler and a boxing gym – both of which are being searched by cops.



One man was gunned down and killed at the scene while another was shot in the stomach and died in the ambulance, reported German newspaper Bild.

Paramedics had been unable to save him after the bullet reportedly ripped through a major artery.

Drones have been deployed to locate any potentially fleeing suspects from the sky.

Hamburg Police have not yet released any theories about the motive for the heinous shooting.

Rescue workers could not enter the building initially for fears that the perpetrator was still inside, reported News5.

On Wednesday, tens of thousands of visitors are expected at a neighbouring exhibition hall for a large shipbuilding trade fair.



More than ten police cars and sevral ambulances are on site and officers have cordonned off the surrounding area.

Elsewhere in Germany two men reprtedly exchanged fire on a high street on Tuesday evening.

More than ten bullets richocheted across Duisburg – an industrial town 40 miles north of Cologne – according to Bild.



One man was injured as bullets smashed through windows, cars and building facades.

It comes just weeks after a gunman stormed a youth centre in Germany and killed six.

The deadly rampage unfolded at a mother-and-baby centre in Stade, near Hamburg.

Four women and one man died at the scene of the horror shooting and a sixth person died later in hospital.

Mass shootings are relatively rare in Germany, especially when compared to the United States, but the nation has seen a recent spike in killings.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

In 2023, a gunman in Hamburg shot six people dead before killing himself at a Jehovah’s Witness worship hall.

In 2016, a German-Iranian teen who was obsessed with mass killings murdered at least nine people in Munich.

News.title: Cops didn’t tell grieving family of Nottingham victims they were being stalked as parents blast ‘staggering’ failure
News.content:
LEFT IN THE DARK Cops didn’t tell grieving family of Nottingham victims they were being stalked as parents blast ‘staggering’ failure

THE GRIEVING families of the Nottingham rampage victims have blasted the police’s failure to not tell them they were being stalked as “staggering”.

Students Grace O’Malley-Kumar and Barnaby Webber, both 19, and school caretaker Ian Coates, 65, were stabbed to death by paranoid schizophrenic Valdo Calocane, 34, on June 13, 2023.



Now, it has been revealed that cops failed to notify their families they were being followed by another man with a history of mental illness, reports The Times.

The individual had a past record of threatening behaviour, had been referred to the Prevent programme and had absconded from a mental health facility after he was sectioned.



Obsessed with the Nottingham attack and believing there had been a “cover up”, the man subsequently attempted to seek out the parents of two of Calocane’s victims.

But it took 18 months for officers to tell Barnaby Webber’s family the man had travelled to Somerset to find them.

And when the man fled a mental health hospital – after he was sectioned for threatening London ambulance staff – it took cops one week to let the families know he was on the loose.

Emma Webber, who’s son Charlie attends school in the area, said it was “profoundly upsetting”.



“To discover that we were left completely in the dark, without any safeguarding advice or guidance for our family, workplaces or Charlie’s school, while police officials were quietly circulating internal subject profiles and consulting legal teams, is both terrifying and deeply unacceptable,” she said.

She blasted Nottinghamshire Police for a “systemic lack of transparency, inadequate risk assessment and a severe breach of duty”.

The man had also tried to reach Dr Sanjoy Kumar – father of murdered Grace O’Malley-Kumar – at his GP surgery.

Dr Kumar said he was left “horrified” to discover he had “not been given an official warning”.

“We as victims do not even get a fair warning at the time that this man was missing from being sectioned and trying to find us,” he fumed.



“This is how the country treats victims, we are second-class citizens.”

He also highlighted the difference in treatment between his family and Calocane’s, who were provided with police protection following his rampage.

Cops played down the threat the man posed to the victims’ families, saying he was trying to “offer his help” while failing to mention his background.

Ian Coates’ son James simply said he was “just not surprised anymore” when he was told of the latest blunder.

The police force has reportedly referred itself to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC), who have also apologised to the families.



The Sun has contacted Nottinghamshire Police and IOPC for comment.

Calocane is serving an indefinite hospital order after prosecutors accepted his guilty pleas to manslaughter on the grounds of diminished responsibility.

Earlier this year, damning evidence revealed how signs that Valdo Calocane was a danger to the public were ignored by two police forces, mental health workers and university staff from as early as May 2020.

He was known to police for violence and stalking and had been sectioned four times.

In July, The Sun reported how the NHS trust that discharged the twisted killer is now facing a manslaughter probe.



The victims’ families said the “fear of stigma and bias” from authorities had left Calocane free to kill and previously slammed doctors for their “failure” to treat the killer appropriately.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Earlier this year they blamed “decades of entirely predictable failures” for their loved ones’ deaths.

The inquiry into the Nottingham attacks, which lasted more than three months and heard from 164 witnesses, finished in June.

News.title: Andy Burnham’s vow to deliver ‘hope’ will be utterly meaningless if a lurch to the Left plunges us all into recession
News.content:
PM’s gilt trip

ANDY Burnham’s first proper day as Prime Minister brought less-than-fond memories of Labour U-turns past, a worrying grasp of the present — and a nightmare vision for the future.

Before the new PM even got a chance to address MPs for the first time since seizing power, the victim of his leadership coup had delivered one more signature reverse ferret.



Sir Keir Starmer, who pledged only weeks ago to stay on as an MP, announced he was quitting for good.

His unwelcome parting gift leaves Burnham facing a by-election headache against Zack Polanski’s Greens.



But far worse for voters was the markets’ reaction to Burnham’s economic fantasy of wielding more Socialist state control to bring down the cost of living.

A global debt sell-off had already sparked a frenzy among bond traders.



But spooked by Britain’s unsustainable debt — fuelled by ballooning welfare payments — they delivered a uniquely bad punishment beating to us.

It sent the cost of Government borrowing to 5.89 per cent, the highest since 1998 and way beyond the rates which led Liz Truss to resign after her 2022 mini-Budget shambles.

That blows a hole in Chancellor John Healey’s Budget plans — including urgent demands for more defence cash.

It is madness — as the threat of a debt-fuelled global financial crisis grows by the day — for Burnham’s only answer to be MORE borrowing to fund MORE out-of-control spending.



His words yesterday about delivering “hope” will be rendered utterly meaningless if a lurch to the Left plunges us all into recession.

Chagos chaos

IN a staggering decision slipped out, the Government confirmed the PM plans to resurrect Keir Starmer’s insane plan to give away the Chagos Islands.

Billions will be paid to Mauritius for the privilege of losing a key strategic territory — and all the cash will come from the already hopelessly inadequate defence budget.

Donald Trump’s ire over Starmer’s craven surrender of the islands led to the plans being halted earlier this year.

But it is crazy for Burnham to once again infuriate our US allies and wantonly damage UK security in the process.



Cry Freeview

FREE to air TV is a vital lifeline for the elderly and poorer households who cannot afford costly broadband and subscriptions.

It also remains a key security tool for Government information in the event of a catastrophic internet outage.

That’s why ministers must listen to MPs from all sides demanding a planned switch-off in 2034 is delayed.

News.title: Andy Burnham’s holiday romance is over and he’s already dumping entire ice baths on his promises
News.content:
SO, it seems Britain’s new boyfriend now just wants to be friends.

Suited and booted in a tie so hideous it could only have been a gift, there was a whiff of screeching rubber in the air as Andy Burnham finally made it to the House of Commons.



And what a difference six weeks makes.

Free from the constraints of any proper scrutiny, Burnham’s summer lovin’ tour was all things to all people.



That charming lad with the pretty eyelashes promised us all the world if we just trusted him.

Those baddies Thames Water? They “should be” nationalised.

The evil tax trap that drags millions more into income tax? That should be raised.

Defence spending? Hike it! Social Care: Fix it first! Crippling energy bills? Slash ’em!

We were promised a new era of hope, optimism and, above all, a government that could speak to ordinary people.

Yet suddenly, the fluffy TikToks about crisps, singalongs to The Smiths and all those sweet nothings felt like distant memories.



As autumn approaches, that nice boy Andy, who was so chatty when trying to get into our knickers, now says “it’s complicated”.

He says he was going to “do politics differently”, yet suddenly the new guy sounded a lot like the old guy.

“Britain is not where any of us would wish it to be,” said our newly po-faced PM. “Things are not working as they should.”

Apparently, “life is too expensive and too hard for too many” after Brexit ruined the country, and everything is seemingly, well . . . just a bit too tricky.



Holiday romance Andy said if we let him in, he would slip us “the most significant change moment in our politics for 40 years”.

Instead, at Tuesday’s back to school reality check, he wasn’t so much pouring cold water on his promises, but dumping an entire ice bath on them.

Defence hikes? They will have to wait for not just November’s Budget, but the multi-year public spending review next year.

Let’s just hope the Russians aren’t banging on the doors of the Baltics by then.



Thames Water nationalisation? That’s just an option now after a beancounter with a big red pen must have explained the notoriously complex and dangerous idea of taking billions of debt on to the public books to him very slowly.

Flashy promises of electoral reform? Kicked into the next Parliament.

Social care fixed? Well, far from being top of the list, that’s now relegated to something Burnham “won’t leave office” without looking at.

It seems that the revolution will have to wait until stakeholders have been engaged, pens have been pushed and Labour MPs have clucked a little more.

Instead, we were treated to his big new solution to Britain’s woes: “A triple helix approach to economic development”.



So much for the straight-talking, brilliant new communicator.

What is it about this job that means politicians enter the black door of No10 and re-emerge regenerated, Stars In Their Eyes-style, spouting meaningless drivel and incomprehensible buzzwords?

Burnham had the cheek to say his Commons statement yesterday set out a “clear, coherent and credible path to growth”.



I must have blinked and missed that bit of the speech.

Of course, this was always going to be much harder than simply a change of tone and frontman. But frankly, Britain does not have time for Burnham to be learning on the job.

He was in a hurry to seal the deal and get into office, despite having watched what had happened to his predecessor who seized power without a proper plan.

But the summer is over now Prime Minister, and the storm clouds are gathering.

On Burnham’s first proper day in the job, UK borrowing costs saw their biggest one day jump in months, pushing ten-year loans to their highest price since the crash.



Liz Truss got decked when those costs hit 4.5 per cent for a few weeks in 2022.

When Labour came to power they were bumping around four per cent. Yesterday they hit 5.23.

Yes, there is global bond market carnage but once again, Britain is in the worst possible position to weather instability.

Decisions on spending and borrowing are having a direct impact on confidence in our country.

When it comes to 25-year UK government bond rates, they’re at their highest rate in nearly 30 years.



Interest rate hikes can only be a matter of time, and any headroom Burnham may have hoped for in the Budget has evaporated.

It’s hardly surprising that he was looking and sounding downbeat yesterday . . . winter is coming.

Starmer steals the thunder

FOR Sir Keir Starmer, revenge was a dish served GREEN.

Word is the ex-PM did not even bother tipping off No10 he was resigning his seat in the Commons – on the day the man who knifed him had his first big day at the office.



You could see what Burnham’s big electoral strategy was going to be . . .

Bash Brexit, hype up climate change, keep away from Trump and go hard after our ally Israel – all in a desperate bid to unite the Left and lure back some LibDem voters.

Bleeding voters to the Greens, his paint-by-numbers approach to foreign policy, so far, has been far from subtle.

And it was showing signs of life, as Zack Polanski’s party slumped and Burnham got a moderate bounce in the polls.

All while the Right remains hopelessly divided as Reform and the Tories battle for supremacy.



Inevitably, the early election chatter has simply refused to die: Burnham would be mad not take advantage of this electorally lucrative battle ground.

But now Sir Keir has thrown a mega spanner in the works.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Triggering a by-election in his lefty North London seat, dominated by graduates and ethnic minorities, he’s handed Wacko Zacko a major shot at entering Parliament and upending Burnham’s entire strategy with a Green resurgence.

You’d have to have a heart of stone not to laugh . . .

News.title: Sweating PM blames Brexit and Mrs Thatcher for Britain’s woes before failing to rule out even more tax hikes
News.content:
ANDY Burnham yesterday tried to blame Brexit and Margaret Thatcher for Britain’s woes — as he failed to rule out soaking the country with more tax hikes.

The new PM used his first Commons speech in the job to warn that “Britain is not where any of us would wish it to be”.



He singled out “a series of wrong turns in the 1980s” as well as the decision to leave the European Union as the reason for a lack of UK growth — rather than the record taxes Labour has imposed.

Mr Burnham faced MPs for the first time since entering No 10 six weeks ago and embarking on a summer tour announcing relatively small cost-of-living giveaways.



Ahead of his marathon three-hour grilling by MPs yesterday, the Labour leader was seen working up a sweat during his morning run.

The PM will feel the heat even more, as long-term government borrowing costs rose to their highest level since 1998.



At the dispatch box for the first time in 16 years, Mr Burnham said: “Britain is not where any of us would wish it to be. Things are not working as they should. Life is too expensive and too hard for too many.”

The ex-Manchester Mayor said his decade away from Westminster had given him a “clear diagnosis” of the source of the UK’s troubles.

The Prime Minister took aim at the legacy of former PM Mrs Thatcher and her programme of privatisation, as well as pulling out of the EU.

He said: “Political power was centralised, economic power privatised, the country deindustrialised, austerity followed, hollowing out councils and depriving them of the agency to act to reverse any of this.”



He added: “Then Brexit compounded the damage, ushering in a decade of low growth and stalled regeneration. Far from taking back control, the combination of these policies took control out of the hands of communities up and down Britain.

“For 40 years, too many places have been drifting.”

Tory leader Kemi Badenoch attacked Mr Burnham for living in the past when he should be focused on the future.



She hit back: “The year is 2026, yet the Prime Minister said in his statement that everything has gone wrong since the 1980s, still complaining about Margaret Thatcher. I may not look it, but I’m 46 years old. He is talking about a woman who became Prime Minister before I was born. He is living in the past and he wants to take us back to the 1970s.

“On this side of the House, we are for the future, not the past. That is the difference between them and us. His ideas are all about more government control, more spending, more tax, more politicians.”

She blamed the £70billion of tax rises under this Labour Government for failing to propel Britain out of the economic doldrums.

Mr Burnham is facing harsh economic realities as PM. Yesterday saw the yield on 30-year gilts — a loan to the Government — rise to 5.89 per cent, the highest since 1998.

And the yield on benchmark ten-year gilts rose to 5.223 per cent — the highest since the 2008 financial crash, eclipsing even Liz Truss’s mini-Budget.



Debt is already on the brink of hitting £3trillion and taxpayers are on the hook for £100billion every year, just to pay off the interest on that pile.

The PM yesterday repeatedly refused to rule out tax rises in the October 28 Budget to pay for increased spending.

Ms Badenoch instead challenged him to cut Britain’s ballooning welfare bill, asking whether he would “stand up to his backbenchers in a way that his predecessor (Sir Keir Starmer) never could”.

Mr Burnham insisted he was committed to bringing the welfare bill down, but said it would not be done through “crude cuts”.



He said the answer was better support, particularly for young people who had been “let down” by the education system.

The Prime Minister was also pressed on defence, after refusing to commit to spending three per cent of GDP on it by 2030.

Mr Burnham said Chancellor John Healey would set out the path at the Spending Review.

He said: “This is a changing and challenging world in which we live.



“But can I say very directly, I appointed this Chancellor precisely because of his commitment to the defence of our realm and the arguments he has made.

“He will set out at the Spending Review the path to honouring our international commitments in full, as I said we would when I was before the steps of Downing Street.”

Mr Burnham put his programme for public control of industries at the heart of his address, taking aim at the water industry specifically as a “leaking monument” to a failed economic approach.

On migration, the PM confirmed he and Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood would continue looking at return hubs and insisted that co-operation with France was making “significant progress”.

Mr Burnham is due to welcome French President Emmanuel Macron in Downing Street today, with tackling small boat Channel crossings on the agenda.



He also vowed to bring in new laws over the coming months to overhaul the “unfair” leasehold system, including plans to ban leasehold on most new flats and give homeowners more control over their buildings.

He also opened the door to including a change to a proportional representation voting system in Labour’s next manifesto.

Mr Burnham gathered his Cabinet, including Housing Secretary Angela Rayner, for just the second time yesterday as MPs returned from their summer breaks.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The PM last night pledged to save Jodrell Bank observatory after a backlash over it being defunded.

He told MPs that there “must be a way to save” the Cheshire site, which includes radio telescopes which helped to track the first moon landing.

News.title: British Airways cabin boss guilty of sexually assaulting sleeping air hostess who called him her ‘work husband’
News.content:
CABIN CREEP British Airways cabin boss guilty of sexually assaulting sleeping air hostess who called him her ‘work husband’

A BRITISH Airways cabin boss has been found guilty of preying on a sleeping air hostess after downing beer and wine at his home.

Amardip “Amo” Dhariwal, 55, assaulted the female colleague after boozing with her over dinner.



The ex-lead flight manager was on trial for a single attack on one woman in 2022 — but a jury also heard from two other stewardesses who alleged he raped them on foreign trips.

Dhariwal earlier denied but was convicted of one count of sexual assault by penetration on Tuesday after a two-week trial.



He could face years in jail according to sentencing guidelines.

One British Airways stewardess told The Sun that “dozens of BA crew have been praying for this outcome”.

“This guy was a brute of a boss. The worst kind of manager bully. A proper old school sex pest. Amo was a disgusting creep,” she said.

Reading Crown Court heard he invited the woman to his then-home in Bracknell, Berkshire, for dinner, where they drank beer and wine.



The woman, then engaged and now married, said she dozed off as they watched a film and woke to find Dhariwal touching her intimately.

Prosecutor James Partridge had told jurors: “They met three months prior to the incident on a flight to Cape Town.

“They got on so well that they met for coffee a few times. She went to his house for taco and movie nights.”

She even referred to Dhariwal as her “work husband”.

Mr Partridge added: “They started watching a film. As they watched it, the victim said she had her legs up.



“She awoke to the defendant touching her.”

He said the woman “felt bewildered” and escaped by finding a key while he was upstairs and called a friend “crying and whispering” on the phone.

Dhariwal, now of Southall, West London, told cops: “Anything that happened was consensual.”

The jury was told Dhariwal allegedly raped a colleague in a Singapore hotel room in 2020.

She woke naked in his bed, confused by how she got there, she said.



Local police investigated but took no further action and would not help British cops, it was said.

The other stewardess claimed she was assaulted while asleep and drunk in a hotel room in Malaysian capital Kuala Lumpur in 2018.

Dhariwal denied those allegations.

He was handed conditional bail and will be sentenced at the same court on October 19 this year.

The BA air stewardess added: “The brave BA women who came forward and helped get Amo convicted deserve a medal.



“They have saved many other women from being attacked by this depraved individual.”

She claimed he would “target inexperienced BA woman” younger than his daughter and that he “turned into a predator” after splitting with his wife years earlier.

She said “his disgusting behaviour would start on the plane itself”, adding: “Down-route, his tactic was to ply girls with drinks during wild nights out betwen flights, so he could later try and take them back to his room.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“At the end of the boozy night, he would target individual women and say, ‘I’ve got Baileys in my room, come and have a night-cap with me’. And then inside his room he’d claim everything was consensual.

“He was notorious. He had a reputation and women would warn each other about him. You never wanted to be alone with him, even in a public space.”

News.title: Female British tourist, 34, ‘stabbed to death in hotel corridor’ at Portugal holiday hotspot as man, also 34, arrested
News.content:
HOTEL HORROR Female British tourist, 34, ‘stabbed to death in hotel corridor’ at Portugal holiday hotspot as man, also 34, arrested

A BRITISH woman has been stabbed to death in a luxury Portuguese hotel as cops arrest a fellow Brit on suspicion of murder.

The man allegedly knifed the tourist, 34, multiple times in the coastal city of Albufeira – with one local report saying she was killed in front of her child.



Emergency services raced to the Alfagar Alto Da Colina hotel after the alarm was raised at 6:45pm on Tuesday.

The luxury resort is described online as having “striking sea views” and being “within walking distance to the beach”.



Local reports say the woman had been staying there with her partner and her child.

Paramedics said the woman was already dead when they arrived at the scene.

They said she had “multiple knife wounds” after being attacked in a hotel corridor, adding that there was nothing they could do to save her.

The suspected killer, 34, has been arrested and is being held in custody, cops confirmed.

Portugal national police force and the separate Policia Judiciaria have launched a probe into the horror killing.

News.title: Charlie Kirk murder suspect pleads not guilty as judge clears way for death penalty trial
News.content:
The defendant, wearing a grey suit and occasionally consulting with his lawyers, appeared in court in the city of Provo on Tuesday.

Kirk's widow, Erika, the mother of their two children, and his parents, â Robert and Kathryn, were also at the hearing.

Closing arguments followed a five-day preliminary hearing in July, during which prosecutors outlined their evidence to show probable cause for trial.

That included DNA allegedly tying Robinson to the murder weapon and other items recovered at the scene; confessions he allegedly made to loved ones; and a taped video statement from his roommate and romantic partner, Lance Twiggs.

"There is a mountain of evidence that proves that he is the shooter," prosecutor Ryan McBride told the court on Tuesday, outlining video that he said showed Robinson "dressed to kill" on campus on the day of the shooting.

"We know that the defendant is the shooterâ¦ first, because of the video evidence; second, because of the DNA; third, because of his admissions; and fourth, because of circumstantial evidence," McBride said.

Prosecutors said the accused, a former apprentice electrician, was in a relationship with his roommate and regarded Kirk's conservative views, particularly on transgender issues, as "repugnant" - which they argued was the motive.

News.title: Burnham promises more devolution and public control of essential services
News.content:
Andy Burnham has promised to set out plans for "stronger public control" of essential services as he addressed the House of Commons for the first time since taking power.

The prime minister said "a series of wrong turns" since the 1980s had seen economic power in the UK privatised and pointed to the water industry as "a leaking monument to that approach - a country run in the private rather than public interest".

He reiterated his belief that political power had been centralised and announced he would be making devolution powers available to more areas in England.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused Burnham of offering "more government control, more taxes and more politicians".

"His diagnosis is completely wrong, his theory of growth is completely wrong, he thinks that if government spends more money, we will all get richer - that is not how this works," she said.

Badenoch also warned the prime minister that his new job would be "very different" to his previous Greater Manchester mayoral role where he "did not have to make difficult trade-offs".

Burnham became prime minister on 20 July shortly after Parliament closed for the summer recess.

Tuesday marked the first day of the new parliamentary session and provided his first opportunity to address MPs and take questions.

He told the House of Commons that "Britain is not where we would wish it to be", but promised to "build a new sense of optimism around the country".

Following his 10 years away from Parliament, Burnham said he was returning with a "clear diagnosis" of what had gone wrong in the country.

"From the 1980s, this country took a series of wrong turns," he said.

"Political power was centralised, economic power privatised, the country deindustrialised, austerity followed, hollowing out councils and depriving them of the agency to act to reverse any of this.

"And then Brexit compounded the damage, ushering in a decade of low growth and stalled regeneration."

In the months before becoming prime minister, Burnham stopped short of calling for full nationalisation but said he wanted to see greater public control of water and energy.

On Tuesday, he promised that a plan to achieve this would be produced "later in the year".

Pressed on his plans for the water sector by Conservative MP Alison Griffiths, Burnham said it was important to "look at all possible solutions".

"It's a very regrettable situation that the privatisation of water has left us in a position where we're going to find it very difficult to reverse," he added.

News.title: UK long-term borrowing costs highest since 1998 ahead of October Budget
News.content:
Long-term government borrowing costs have risen to a 28-year high, putting further pressure on Prime Minister Andy Burnham ahead of his first Budget next month.

The yield on a 30-year gilt â a loan to the British government â rose to 5.89% on Tuesday, the highest since 1998.

Borrowing costs in the US, Japan and Europe have hit similar highs in recent days, reflecting investors' concerns about inflation, state borrowing levels and spending levels by large tech companies on AI.

Burnham told the House of Commons his government's "bedrock", as it seeks to tackle the cost-of-living crisis, would be "fiscal responsibility".

All of those factors will make the Budget process trickier for Burnham, who on Tuesday addressed MPs for the first time as prime minister, and his Chancellor, John Healey.

Burnham told the House of Commons the economy and the cost of living were "the biggest issues facing the country".

Higher borrowing costs will reduce the amount of headroom the government has against its self-imposed fiscal rules, limiting the amount Healey can spend on consumer-friendly measures to ease the cost of living.

Despite the squeezed public finances, Burnham said he would bring about "more substantial change" to ease living costs.

"Britain is not where any of us would wish it to be," he added.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused Burnham of "living in the past".

"His diagnosis is completely wrong," she told the House of Commons. "His theory of growth is completely wrong. He thinks that if Government spends more money, we will all get richer.

"That is not how this works."

The chancellor has previously said he will stick to a set of fiscal rules imposed by his predecessor, Rachel Reeves, that restrict borrowing. These rules are designed to help markets have clarity about the path of borrowing.

The more that is forecast to be spent on interest payments, the more likely that there will be a squeeze on spending or some form of tax rise to meet these rules.

On top of that, higher government rates can feed through to higher business and household borrowing costs, and so weigh on the economy.

Burnham was already facing a tough balancing act with taxing and spending, due to pressures on defence and the cost of living.

Burnham's ex-economic adviser Lord Jim O'Neill told BBC News that high government borrowing costs would force Labour to "get real" about "dealing with the triple lock" on the state pension, and "excessive" welfare spending.

Lord O'Neill, who recently turned down the offer of a formal position in the prime minister's team, said that current market pressure would force changes over "some of the things that no political figures ever seem to want to deal with".

As well as the rise to 30-year gilt yields, the yield on the benchmark 10-year gilt rose to 5.22% on Tuesday. This is its highest rate since June 2008, at the height of the global financial crisis.

Gilt yields move counter to the value of the bonds, meaning their prices fall when yields rise.

News.title: Rising numbers of children in mental health crisis ending up in A&E
News.content:
There has been a sharp rise in children and young people attending A&E units in England in a mental health crisis, NHS doctors are warning.

The number of six to 17-year-olds turning up in significant distress for things like self-harm and eating disorders, or in emotional crisis, rose by 36% between 2019 and 2025, according to the Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health analysis.

Some faced waits of more than 12 hours once there. The college said A&Es were not the best place for them, but a lack of support in the community meant they often had nowhere else to turn.

The government said it was looking to improve services and would be setting out plans soon.

The analysis â based on figures provided under the Freedom of Information Act by NHS England â found there were 75,491 attendances at A&E by children and young people for a mental health concern in 2025.

That is up from 55,525 in 2019 with some of the biggest rises seen in very young children aged six to nine. The increases far outstrip the overall jump in attendances, which has risen by just over 8% over the period.

Doctors said the cases included children and young people brought in by families, carers and police â some of those in emotional crisis become aggressive or have challenging behaviour.

In total, more than 6,200, around 8%, waited over 12 hours in A&E.

News.title: Tiger Woods to change plea after crash arrest
News.content:
No one was injured in the crash, though Woods had to crawl out through the passenger door to free himself.

Police released body camera footage in April that captured the aftermath of the incident, showing the golfing legend after his vehicle clipped a truck and rolled over.

In the video, Woods appears calm, kneeling on one knee as he tells officers: "I looked down at my phone, and all of a sudden, boom".

He passed a breathalyser test but declined to take a urinalysis screening for other drugs, Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said at the time.

Woods told officers he had not consumed alcohol that day. When asked about any prescription medication, he responded, "I take a few", adding he had done so earlier that morning.

He then listed the medication, though that portion of the footage was redacted.

Officers told Woods they suspected his "normal faculties" were impaired by an "unknown substance".

Authorities later reported finding two white pills in his pocket, identified as hydrocodone, an opioid commonly prescribed to treat pain.

Woods wrote on social media following the incident, "I know and understand the seriousness of the situation I find myself in today.

"I am stepping away for a period of time to seek treatment and focus on my health. This is necessary in order for me to prioritise my wellbeing and work toward lasting recovery."

The incident marked Woods' second arrest on suspicion of driving under the influence.

News.title: Urine test can spot more than nine in 10 bladder cancers
News.content:
More than 300,000 cystoscopies are performed in the UK each year and there are significant waiting lists in some areas.

While the urine test is not a replacement for cystoscopies, it could help doctors identify patients at greater risk who should be prioritised for urgent ones rather than wait.

This NHS trial found that the Galeas urine test identified 92% of bladder cancer cases.

A negative result meant there was more than a 99% chance that the patient did not have bladder cancer.

It checks for any genetic material shed into the urine by bladder cancer and was originally developed by the University of Birmingham with funding from Cancer Research UK (CRUK).

It looks for more than 450 DNA mutations associated with bladder cancer across 23 genes.

Prof Richard Bryan, co-author of the study and from Birmingham University, said after spending years developing and evaluating the science, it was exciting to see "very promising early performance" in a large real-world patient population.

Under a licensing agreement, the test has been commercialised by Nonacus, which pays back part of the revenue to the University and CRUK.

Michelle Mitchell from CRUK said: "Too many people are waiting longer than they should for a bladder cancer diagnosis, and it's essential that we find ways to tackle this problem.

"It's early days for this test and further research is needed, but it's vital that we continue to find faster and less invasive ways to help diagnose or rule out cancer."

Bladder cancer is more common in men over the age of 60 and the main symptom is blood in your urine.

How serious bladder cancer is depends on how big the cancer is and whether it has spread elsewhere in the body.

Early detection and treatment of cancer saves lives.

News.title: Apple Maps changes Lake Ontario to Lake America, joining Google
News.content:
Apple has renamed Lake Ontario as Lake America on its maps service app, after an order from US President Donald Trump as part of Washington's trade spat with Canada.

The change was made for US-based users, while those in Canada will continue to see Lake Ontario displayed. The BBC has contacted Apple for comment.

The iPhone maker's move follows Trump's executive order to change the lake's name after trade talks between the neighbouring countries collapsed late last month, with Washington imposing new 50% tariffs on $20bn (Â£14.8bn; C$28bn) worth of Canadian goods.

Rival technology giant Google made a similar switch for its users in the US in recent days, leading to backlash on social media.

Canada has responded to Washington's levies, saying it will implement "dollar for dollar" counter-tariffs.

Prime Minister Mark Carney's administration had walked away from the trade negotiations, due to what his office has called unacceptable demands.

Carney told the Trump administration to "start being serious" and stop trying to be tough before discussions between the sides can restart.

Trump's executive order gives the US Department of the Interior 30 days to update the change with the Geographic Names Information Service - the official database of what places are called in the country.

Apple was specifically urged by Trump to rename Lake Ontario on its Maps platform to comply with the executive order signed, according to US Interior Secretary Doug Burgum

The president has also posted several AI-generated videos on social media, including a clip of him kicking over a Lake Ontario sign and replacing it with another that says "Welcome to Lake America".

At the lake itself, Canada has installed a new sign with the words "Lake Ontario. Now and Always".

"Just in case President Trump or anyone else forgets, we've set up this sign to remind them, it's Lake Ontario, now and forever," Ontario Premier Doug Ford said.

News.title: US aircraft carrier to dock near Thai beach resort Pattaya after record 250 days at sea
News.content:
After a record 250 days at sea without a port stop, the nuclear-powered aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln is preparing to dock in Thailand, giving its nearly 5,000 crew members a much-needed break.

The ship is docking close to the beach resort of Pattaya, known for its raucous nightlife and for sex tourism. For the US it also carries strong historical echoes.

When the weary sailors walk into the city's bars and restaurants, they will literally be treading in the footsteps of the hundreds of thousands of US troops who came here for R&R â rest and relaxation - during the Vietnam War.

They transformed it from a sleepy fishing village to one of the world's most famous and frenetic party towns.

Today the neon-lit alleys running down to the beach are much quieter than usual. The bars in the city's famous Walking Street still screen videos on their walls of pole-dancing women, trying to lure customers inside.

But there are not many of those customers, and most seem to be family groups from the Middle East more interested in the Turkish ice-cream vendor than the go-go bars.

The Iran War, which has affected tourism and consumer spending, has hit businesses hard here. The prospect of thousands of American sailors, with nine months of salary unspent while at sea, offers a rare opportunity to local businesses.

News.title: Israel warns it will retaliate if UK imposes sanctions
News.content:
Israel's Foreign Minister Gideon Saar has warned his country will retaliate if the UK imposes sanctions against it over the potential expansion of settlements in the West Bank.

Addressing Parliament for the first time as foreign secretary, Ed Miliband said he would introduce a "comprehensive reset" of policy on Israel "in the coming weeks".

He said the government would examine how to stop UK companies "financing, constructing or advertising new settlements" in the occupied West Bank.

Responding, Gideon Saar told Hebrew-language news website Ynet: "If Britain acts against Israel, Israel will act against Britain."

"If they act, I think they will be making a big mistake," he said.

Last month, Israel opened up tenders for the construction of some 1,200 settlement homes in the so-called E1 area - a strategically important area east of Jerusalem. The plans have drawn widespread international condemnation.

The development would in effect divide the West Bank in two and isolate East Jerusalem.

Miliband said the plans are "illegal under international law" and called them "the crossing of a red line, as it cuts through the heart of the West Bank and risks making a Palestinian state unviable".

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham also warned that Israel's statement about the E1 area could "imperil or end" the two-state solution in the Middle East.

All settlements are illegal under international law and, under global pressure, Israel held off for decades on plans to build in the area.

News.title: Women pose as men to buy testosterone online after prescription difficulties
News.content:
Tomlinson said: "It's a postcode lottery and very dependent on the practice and the clinician, but you can hit barriers along the way.

"It's really difficult when you might know somebody else who's going through exactly the same thing and has sailed through the process and might not have gone into secondary care.

"There is no consistency across the board unfortunately."

Olver runs the menopause clinic at Aneurin Bevan's health board and said "we have definitely seen a very sharp increase in testosterone referrals from primary care - for women wanting to access it".

"It is difficult to meet demand and we have a testosterone clinic set up now for women who want to trial it."

She said each of the seven health boards in Wales used a traffic light system - some are red, meaning only specialists can prescribe the drug.

There are two amber options - one involves a GP requesting the support or agreement from a hospital specialist that testosterone is appropriate for a patient.

The second requires the hospital specialist to start and monitor the prescription with a "shared care agreement", with GP's continuing to prescribe it.

"One of the main reasons for this disparity is because we don't have a licenced product for woman on the NHS," Olver said.

A female testosterone product has been available in other countries for many years, and is available from private clinics across the UK.

Olver said it had now achieved a licence in the UK but still needed to be appraised by NICE, external to determine if it was cost-effective to use in the NHS, at which point discussions would also be required with the pharmaceutical industry about the cost to the NHS.

Currently the female product, Androfeme, costs the NHS around Â£100, but the male product, Testogel, is Â£30.

"Studies show about 60% of women will find benefit in improving their libido," said Olver.

"It's really important to manage expectations, because it's not this wonder drug that sometimes it's made out to be on social media.

"There's lots of reasons why women don't want to be intimate - some of those will be external factors, some will be anatomical.

"So it's really important to be fully counselled on what to expect when using testosterone, but also the limitations of its use."

The Welsh government said: "All health boards are expected to adhere to the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence's (NICE) guidelines on identification and management of menopause including providing individualised care when prescribing HRT.

"We are aware that this may include some practitioners prescribing testosterone for some women.

"We expect all health boards to conform to any recommendation made by NICE in relation to prescribing testosterone when its guidance is published."

News.title: Fake 10 Downing Street listing exposes 'unfit' Booking.com, says consumer group
News.content:
Consumer group Which? says it was able to create a fake listing for 10 Downing Street on travel giant Booking.com.

The UK watchdog said its researchers were able to book a bogus stay at the prime minister's address - as well as leave a fake review noting "hanging out" with resident mouser Larry the cat as a highlight.

It said despite clear signs it was fake, Booking.com did not remove the listing until two months after it was uploaded.

"This limited test is not a true reflection of the experience of millions of listings or reviews published on our platform," a Booking.com spokesperson told the BBC.

They said because Which?'s listing was not "live" on its site across the two months it was present, "some of our automatic fraud controls were not triggered to completely remove the closed listing".

People could only see the listing and request to book the property during a 20-minute window opened by Which? so its researchers could try to book it.

Booking.com's spokesperson added "a range of checks and verification measures" help secure the site, and technologies such as AI "help us detect and remove the majority of fraudulent listings within 24 hours".

But Which? Travel editor Rory Boland said its checks had been shown to be "unfit for purpose".

"If Booking.com's so-called sophisticated AI systems can't spot that 10 Downing Street is not a holiday rental, then it's no wonder scammers can exploit the platform so easily," he said.

"It would be laughable that we were able to list the UK's most famous address for rent, if the consequences weren't so devastating for holidaymakers, who risk losing thousands of pounds to bogus listings and phishing links."

It is not the first time the site has faced criticism over its security efforts and customer service.

News.title: Range Rover launches first fully electric model
News.content:
Range Rover has unveiled its first fully electric model, after a yearâlong delay to its planned launch.

The Range Rover Electric, to be built in Solihull, marks a major shift in its electrification programme, backed by largeâscale upgrades across its West Midlands sites.

Parent company JLR said it had up-skilled 10,500 workers for electric production as it pushes ahead with modernisation despite recent financial pressures and planned job cuts.

The launch comes as the Coventryâbased carmaker faces falling profits, supply chain disruption and restructuring following a cyber attack last year.

The company said the launch was being supported by new battery and electric drive unit production lines as well as training around 9,000 employees in Solihull for electrification and a further 1,500 trained across the region.

JLR's Electric Propulsion Manufacturing Centre in Wolverhampton is now producing battery packs and electric drive units alongside internal combustion engines.

Martin Limpert, managing director of Range Rover, called the new model the result of a decade of "considered engineering".

JLR's electric roll-out comes after a turbulent year with profits dropping to Â£66m in the first quarter after a fire at a key Norwegian supplier.

The business is also undergoing restructuring, confirming that fewer than 300 roles will go less than a year after a cyber attack halted production for more than a month.

At the time of the results, the firm said new product launches would leave "JLR in good shape whilst acknowledging the continuing geopolitical, inflationary and regulatory challenges the industry faces".

News.title: More than 110 rescued a week after Nepal deadly floods, army says
News.content:
One hundred and nineteen people have been rescued using air resources in Nepal following deadly floods, a spokesperson for the country's army said.

It comes nearly a week after the disaster that hit both Nepal and neighbouring Tibet, killing more than 1,000 people, with more than 3,900 still missing.

A Nepali army spokesperson earlier said a British male was among those rescued, along with 118 Nepalese people, of whom 44 were female and 74 male.

Later on Tuesday, the British man, Alastair Chambers, told the Telegraph and PA Media he was not rescued and had travelled to the region to help with aid efforts.

The BBC has contacted the UK Foreign Office for comment.

On Tuesday, Foreign Office minister Lord Wood of Anfield confirmed 36 British people remain unaccounted for - an increase from the 33 previously reported.

More than 600 are workers believed to be trapped in a vast network of mud-filled tunnels at hydropower sites along Trishuli River are among the thousands who are still missing.

Nepalese Prime Minister Balendra Shah said on Monday that 279 people had been rescued from the sites.

The rescue operation is being spearheaded by an international team made up of Chinese and Nepalese military personnel, while experts from India, Korea and Australia are also involved.

On Tuesday, the Nepalese Tourist Board said it had rescued 330 foreign nationals in total.

Saturday saw a rapid development team from the UK arrive in Nepal to provide support for Britons and their families.

News.title: Family mourn 'deeply loved' girl killed in Middlesbrough fire
News.content:
The family of a seven-year-old girl killed in a house fire said their lives had been changed forever by her "devastating loss".

Valentina Foster died alongside her aunt Natalie McDonald, 34, in the blaze at Grangetown, near Middlesbrough, in the early hours of 26 August. A man has been charged with their murders.

In a tribute, the youngster's parents said their daughter would "always be in our hearts, and her memory will live with us forever".

"She was deeply loved and will be missed beyond words by her family, friends, and everyone whose life she touched," they said.

"Our lives have changed forever, and we are struggling to come to terms with this devastating loss."

They added she would be "forever missed" by her brothers and sisters.

News.title: Keir Starmer announces he is standing down as MP
News.content:
Former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer has announced he is to stand down as an MP to focus on a role in international affairs.

The move will trigger a by-election in the London seat of Holborn and St Pancras, long a Labour stronghold, which he has represented since 2015.

Sir Keir, who left Downing Street in July, had previously said he would stay on as an MP until the next UK general election, which is not due until 2029.

But in a surprise statement hours before his successor Andy Burnham made his debut in the House of Commons, he said he was resigning to work on issues such as international affairs and violence against women and girls.

Paying tribute to his predecessor, Burnham highlighted Sir Keir's work with Ukraine and the Hillsborough Law drawn up under his government to improve the accountability of public officials, which is going through Parliament.

"He has given this country a lifetime of public service, particularly for those fighting for justice," he added.

"His leadership took our party from one of its worst defeats to its best victories and created a platform to change this country for the better. We will use it well, and we wish his family the very best for the future."

Announcing his resignation, Sir Keir told the Camden New Journal, external it had been a "huge honour and privilege" to represent the London constituency for 11 years, ending weeks of speculation about whether he would remain an MP.

He added he was ready to "pass the baton to a successor", telling the newspaper it was the "right time" for him to leave Parliament.

He said: "I will now focus on other things and that will be international affairs including defence, security, trade and technology in a fast-changing world.

"I will also continue, as I have done for a long time now with others, to work on combating violence against women and girls; that is an issue that matters to me hugely.

"It's work I started before I became an MP and it's work I'm keen to continue after I'm an MP. So international affairs on the one hand, and continuing my work on violence against women and girls on the other."

Sir Keir became prime minister after winning a landslide majority at the 2024 election, but quit No 10 after pressure from Labour MPs to stand aside.

News.title: Baby girl found at house was stabbed, say police
News.content:
A newborn baby girl who was discovered fatally injured at a house in Sheffield died as a result of stab wounds, police have said.

The baby was found at a house on Holywell Heights in the Wincobank area on Sunday morning, after police were called to reports of concern for her safety.

South Yorkshire Police said despite the best efforts of police and paramedics, the baby died at the scene.

Seven people aged between 15 and 37 were arrested on suspicion of her murder. Two of them, aged 26 and 37, were later bailed, but police confirmed on Tuesday a warrant had been obtained to extend time in custody for the remaining five as inquiries continued.

Det Ch Insp Tom Woodward, leading the investigation, said: "We recognise this is deeply distressing for those who would have loved to have a chance to love this baby girl, for the emergency services who responded and for the community who will inevitably be shocked by this incident.

"Everyone involved in responding to this tragedy - from the first officers and paramedics on the scene to the detectives now leading the investigation - has felt the profound impact of this investigation."

He added: "Our commitment to this little girl is unwavering. We will confront every difficult and distressing challenge and pursue every line of inquiry with determination and care to secure justice for her.

"We know the local community will hold her in their thoughts and support us as we work through this complex investigation."

A South Yorkshire Police spokesperson said officers were continuing their investigations in the Holywell Heights area and asked anyone with information that might be useful to contact them.

News.title: India’s power demand is surging, but some solar energy is going to waste
News.content:

When India’s power demand surged at the height of summer, the country struggled to meet evening needs as air conditioners ran longer amid hotter nights. Despite this demand, some renewable energy providers were told to limit their output because the country had more clean electricity available than its grid could safely handle.

In the last 15 months, India curtailed nearly 11 terawatt-hours of solar generation — enough electricity to power about 10 million homes, according to government data and research by energy think tank Ember. That solar power went unused even as extreme heat and poor monsoon rains drove up demand for power in India for cooling and pumping groundwater for agriculture.

India, the world’s most populous country and one of the largest emitters of climate-polluting gases, is rapidly adding clean energy, especially solar, to its power mix. However, it can't use all the clean power it could generate because of insufficient transmission and storage capacity and the technical difficulty of shifting between fossil power and renewables.

Energy experts say that contradiction points to the next big challenge for India’s energy transition. Building solar and wind farms is no longer enough. India also needs more transmission lines to move electricity across the country, batteries to store renewable power until it is needed and a more flexible power system that can quickly adjust as wind and solar output rises or falls.

“We’re in a stage where some of the biggest hurdles in renewables are starting to hit us,” said Neshwin Rodrigues, an energy analyst at Ember.

Clean power gets switched off despite record demand

India has more than 300 gigawatts of clean power capacity, more than half its total installed electricity capacity. But coal still produces most of the country’s electricity.

Experts said the main reason for this is curtailment — when a wind or solar plant could produce electricity but is ordered to reduce or stop generation as the grid cannot take the power.

Rodrigues said that when solar generation surges in the afternoon, it's difficult for coal units to reduce their output because they are relatively inflexible and cannot ramp down quickly without compromising efficiency, increasing costs or risking operational problems.

Trying to make thermal power plants flexible and adapt to increasing supply from clean energy sources “is like asking an elephant to dance,” said Vinay Pabba, CEO of Hyderabad-based renewable energy company Vibrant Energy.

Pabba said curtailment results in losses for clean power developers. “We get paid only for what we put on the grid,” he said.

The high concentration of renewable generation in western India has also meant that transmission lines in that part of the country get congested quickly. The western states of Gujarat and Rajasthan account for nearly 50% of India’s solar power capacity.

“When solar peaks, usually in the afternoon, there is a limited pipe to evacuate it,” said Pabba.

Another risk of not building storage quickly is that dirty fuels get used more. “Without enough storage, India risks keeping coal plants running even when cheap renewable power is available,” said Vibhuti Garg, South Asia director at the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis.

While a solar or wind farm can sometimes be completed within two years, building new power lines can take a minimum of three years, according to energy experts.

India has achieved only about 80% of its annual transmission construction targets over the past five years, research by Ember has found.

Spreading more renewable development across other parts of the country, while adding more wind and smaller local solar projects, could reduce pressure on crowded transmission corridors and make the electricity supply more balanced throughout the day, said Disha Agarwal, an energy analyst at the New Delhi-based Council on Energy, Environment and Water.

Agarwal said the challenge is likely to become more difficult as renewable capacity keeps rising.

India is aiming for 500 gigawatts of clean electricity capacity by 2030. Also, Indian policymakers expect nearly 70% of India’s installed power capacity to come from nonfossil sources by 2036.

Batteries could help save power for when it is needed

A study released earlier this month by the India Energy and Climate Center at the University of California, Berkeley, found that renewable power backed by batteries can provide electricity with reliability approaching that of conventional power plants at a price researchers said is lower than the price of power from new coal-fired plants.

Batteries make it possible to store solar electricity when it is abundant in the afternoon and discharge it after sunset, when demand remains high.

But India’s storage sector remains far smaller than what planners said will eventually be required.

“If we try to increase the solar installations without solving for energy storage, it is only going to lead to curtailment,” said Ankit Mittal, CEO of battery storage company Ingro Energy.

Mittal said India is trying to transform several parts of its electricity system simultaneously as power demand rises. “Things that were supposed to happen over decades” are now happening at once, he said.

The government said in July that it had about 3 gigawatts of battery storage and 7.4 gigawatts of operational pumped-storage capacity. It expects India's storage needs to reach about 74 gigawatts by 2032.

“If high quality energy storage projects are not built, we could be adding an additional layer of risk to grid operations while also decelerating our nation’s ability to achieve our energy transition targets,” said Avinash Rao, CEO of Mahindra Susten, a leading renewable energy company in India.

Rodrigues, the energy analyst, said batteries can be built much more quickly than major transmission infrastructure, making them one of the fastest options for easing some immediate constraints.

Industry stakeholders said that few, if any, foresaw the incredible increase in demand happening as the country’s transportation and other major sectors electrify and data centers are built.

“None of us saw it coming. If we had seen it coming, we would have probably planned our way around it,” said Pabba of Vibrant Energy.

News.content:

Dozens of young people gathered recently on a beach in Peru’s capital to dance, pose and show off their most creative moves — all in pursuit of one thing: aura.

They were taking part in a so-called “aura battle," a real-world spin on the Internet trend known as “aura farming” that is sweeping across Latin America.

Dressed up as characters from comic books or animated films, competitors engaged in dance battles of sorts, vying for the crowd’s applause. Those with the loudest cheers and the most creative moves advanced to the next round. One competitor dressed up as Spider-Man performed forward rolls and push ups, as techno music played in the background. Another hopped on one leg while kicking the other forward, in a move that looked straight from a video game.

“Aura farming is about letting your essence flow in a place where people are watching you, but where there is no shame,” said Liam González, a 20-year-old film student who attended dressed up as the movie character Shrek.

Gonzalo Cornelio, 19, came dressed as former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, wearing a grey tracksuit like the one worn by the deposed leader the night he was captured by the U.S. military.

Rooted in video games and boosted by social media

Aura farming competitions first emerged in Brazil and spread through social media. Now, teenagers and adults are holding aura battles across Latin America.

“It’s not about being popular,” said María Paula Martínez, a professor in the arts faculty at Colombia’s Los Andes University. “It’s about showing off good vibes, and having others recognize that.”

Like video game characters who farm for points, people who go aura farming are trying to earn a reward. In this case, it's about generating good vibes, and thus improving their “aura,” a term that, according to some spiritual traditions, refers to an energy field that surrounds people.

Fernando Lícito, a Peruvian content creator, said that in aura battles participants do not touch each other or trade insults. “They are simply farming their aura," said Lícito, 25. “And whoever gets the crowd to make more noise wins.”

Lícito said he saw a video in June of an aura farming contest in Brazil, and decided to bring the idea to Peru. So far, he has organized three aura battles there.

During the contests, some participants imitate soccer star Cristiano Ronaldo’s goal celebration, extending their arms downwards and making a sound that sounds like “siuu."

Aura farmers also draw on other online trends, with some repeating the words “six, seven” as they move their hands.

Aura battles have spread to cities across Latin America, including Mexico City, Quito and Buenos Aires, where dozens of people staged a battle in front of the Obelisk, one of the most iconic monuments in the Argentine capital. The contests have also reached Spain, with events taking place in Madrid, Burgos and Zaragoza.

Martínez, the Colombian arts professor, said that the concept of aura farming has moved beyond the digital world into physical spaces, enabling teenagers to socialize.

Supporters and detractors

But some aura battles have met some resistance.

In Lima’s Miraflores district, officials recently cancelled an aura farming event, saying organizers had not obtained the permits required to hold it in a public space.

In July, the mayor of Cuiaba, a city in southwestern Brazil, denied permits for an aura tournament, arguing it was not in the public’s interest. The event was transferred to a university campus. And in Costa Rica, the ministry of education banned aura battles in public schools arguing they could create conflicts between students or disrupt learning.

In Mexico, by contrast, the education minister embraced the trend, posting a video in which he smiles and says he is “farming good education” as the country prepares for the new school year.

González, the aura farmer who dresses up as Shrek, said that this hobby gives him a way to have fun and express himself, even if his grandmother doesn’t get what he’s doing and thinks it’s silly. “We were born in a different era,” he said.

___

Suárez reported from Bogota, Colombia. Associated Press journalists Mauricio Muñoz, Berenice Bautista and Gonzalo Solano contributed to this report from Lima, Mexico City and Quito, Ecuador.

Tiger Woods is set to appear in court on Wednesday for a change of plea hearing stemming from his car crash in Florida in March.

Woods, a 15-time major champion, was arrested and spent eight hours in jail before being bailed after the Land Rover he was driving rolled over in a collision with a pick-up truck towing a trailer.

He previously entered a written plea of not guilty via his lawyers to charges of driving under the influence, property damage and a refusal to submit to testing.

open image in gallery Tiger Woods is a 15-time major champion (Owen Humphreys/PA)

A court notice shows he is now slated to appear at Martin County Courthouse on Wednesday morning at 8.30am local time for a hearing, but it is unknown what Woods will change his plea to or if he has reached a plea deal with prosecutors.

Woods walked away unhurt from the crash, escaping out of his passenger door, and while he passed a breathalyser test for alcohol, the 50-year-old refused to submit to a urinary test for drugs.

According to a police affidavit, Woods was observed by the investigating officers to be “sweating profusely” while acting “lethargic and slow” with eyes that were “bloodshot and glassy”.

He admitted he “was looking down at his cell phone and changing the radio station” in the moments before the crash and “did not notice the vehicle in front of him had slowed down”.

Woods told the authorities he had not consumed any alcohol but admitted to taking “a few” prescription medications and had done so earlier in the morning while insisting he had not had any illegal drugs.

open image in gallery Woods was charged with driving under the influence, property damage and a refusal to submit to testing (Jane Barlow/PA)

Woods, who was also charged with property damage and refusal to submit to a lawful test, was observed to be “extremely alert and talkative” and had “hiccups during the entire investigation”.

Multiple sobriety exercises were conducted, where he struggled to follow instructions, leading a deputy to conclude: “How he performed on the exercises and based on my training, knowledge and experience, I believe Woods’ normal faculties were impaired and he was unable to safely operate the motor vehicle”.

During a search of his vehicle, investigators found two white pills, which were identified as hydrocodone, a prescription opioid used to treat severe, chronic pain.

Woods underwent emergency surgery after suffering multiple leg injuries following a serious car accident in California in February 2021. He has not competed on the PGA Tour since July 2024.

The affidavit stated Woods said he had 20 surgeries on his leg as a result of that crash, plus seven operations on his back, while the report also noted Woods was “limping and stumbling”.

Woods later wrote on X: “I know and understand the seriousness of the situation I find myself in.

“I am stepping away for a period of time to seek treatment and focus on my health. This is necessary in order for me to prioritise my wellbeing and work toward lasting recovery.”

Woods was also arrested on suspicion of DUI offences in 2017 after being found asleep at the wheel of his car in Jupiter, Florida.

He later pleaded guilty to reckless driving after it emerged he had had five prescription drugs in his system at the time.

In 2009, he crashed his car into a fire hydrant and tree outside his home in an incident that led to a spectacular unravelling of his private life.

News.content:

On the surface, Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to Egypt this week is a run-of-the-mill opportunity for two countries to strengthen economic and diplomatic ties.

But there is deep subtext to the meeting between Xi and Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sissi: China, the United States’ top global rival, is cultivating an extensive relationship with one of America's key allies in the Middle East as it moves to expand its influence in the rapidly changing region.

Xi aims to present China as a stabilizer in the region and contrast it with the United States, which for decades has been militarily entangled there – its six-month war with Iran being just the latest example.

“China continues to build up its soft power reserves while the United States self-sabotages its own stock,” Amr Hamzawy, director of the Washington-based Carnegie Middle East Program, wrote in a paper earlier this year along with Kathryn Selfe, a former fellow at the program.

Xi arrived Tuesday evening at the Cairo airport, which was adorned with Chinese and Egyptian flags. El-Sissi and military guards greeted him on the tarmac with a red-carpet ceremony. The leaders are scheduled to hold talks on Wednesday, and Xi plans to visit the Grand Egyptian Museum, near the pyramids of Giza.

It has been a while since Xi has visited the Mideast

Xi will be in Egypt for three days. It is his first visit there in a decade, and his first trip to the region since visiting Saudi Arabia in 2022. El-Sissi has visited China multiple times in recent years.

The leaders marked 70 years of diplomatic ties by publishing friendly opinion pieces Tuesday in Egypt’s state-run newspapers.

Xi wrote that Beijing and Cairo should “expand the scope of pragmatic collaboration" through development. El-Sissi lauded China's investments in Egypt and reiterated Cairo's support of China's claim that Taiwan is part of its territory.

Egypt views its growing relationship with China as a way to diversify its strategic partnerships.

In 2023, Egypt was invited to join the BRICS bloc of nations, a grouping of major emerging economies that includes Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa and is seen as a counterbalance to Western-led institutions such as the G7.

A year later, Egypt signed agreements with China to collaborate on its Belt and Road Initiative, a signature policy of Xi’s that seeks to build power and transportation infrastructure around the world.

China has invested more than $10 billion in Egypt, building a business hub east of the capital, Cairo, and an electric rail line for industry in the Nile Delta. Annual trade between the two countries is estimated at $20 billion, according to government figures.

Trade between the U.S. and Egypt was $15.7 billion in 2025. Egypt is a crucial partner in U.S. national security priorities in the region, and the countries' leaders enjoy close ties.

China has been trying to build bridges between Mideast nations

In 2023, Beijing brokered a deal to reestablish diplomatic ties between Iran — its most important regional ally and oil supplier — and Saudi Arabia, a longtime U.S. ally. The agreement showcased China’s aspirations to compete with the United States for influence in the Mideast.

Since then, ties between Riyadh and Tehran have frayed. Iran attacked Saudi Arabia and other Gulf countries as part of its retaliation against the U.S. and Israel, which launched the war on Feb. 28.

China has cast itself as a regional mediator in other ways. It has long advocated a two-state solution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, which is seen by the Arab world as a linchpin to regional stability.

Shortly before Hamas militants attacked Israel in 2023 and launched the war in Gaza, Xi had hosted Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas and announced a “strategic partnership” with the Palestinian Authority.

The Suez Canal is a vital alternative to the Strait of Hormuz

With oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz heavily disrupted by the Iran war, the Suez Canal — which is controlled by Egypt — has become an important alternative path for getting energy supplies out of the region.

“China has good reason to strengthen ties with the country that controls the route still open,” said Muhammad Zulfikar Rakhmat, a Middle East expert with Jakarta’s Center of Economic and Law Studies.

Xi views Egypt "as a base to reach the wider Arab and African world, at a time when the U.S. has less attention to spare there,” said Rakhmat.

In August, China and Egypt held a multiday air exercise at several bases across Egypt — the first-ever combat exercise for China’s J-16 fighter jets and Egypt’s French-made Rafale fighters.

Xi is visiting Cairo after attending a two-day conference of the 10-nation Shanghai Cooperation Organization, a political and security group billed as a counterweight to U.S. global influence. The leaders of Russia, India, Pakistan and Iran attended the conference in Kyrgyzstan’s capital, Bishkek.

The trip also comes on the heels of the Trump administration’s “economic onslaught” on Iran’s financial connections around the world. The sanctions aim to isolate the Islamic Republic from its remaining economic partners, including China, which buys more than 80% of Iranian oil shipments, usually through indirect channels.

Beijing says its trade with Iran has always abided by international law.

___________________

Associated Press writers Noha el-Hennawy in Cairo and Huizhong Wu in Bangkok contributed to this report.
