World.title: Trump says he reviews “every position” when asked about Falklands sovereignty
World.content:
Trump says he reviews “every position” when asked about Falklands sovereignty

1st Tuesday, September 2026 - 11:26 UTC Full article

“The UK's got some problems but they'll get solved,” Trump said

US President Donald Trump replied on Monday in the Oval Office, when asked whether his government was reviewing its position of neutrality on the Falklands: “I always review every position. That's just one of many.” It is the first time he has publicly addressed the sovereignty dispute between the United Kingdom and Argentina, though his answer committed to nothing.

Asked next whether he wanted the government of British Prime Minister Andy Burnham to raise its defence spending pledges, he replied: “The UK's got some problems but they'll get solved.”

The remarks follow a report in The Telegraph that senior Pentagon officials are considering a review of the US stance on the archipelago as leverage to press London to meet NATO's target of 5% of gross domestic product on defence. A senior official quoted by the paper said Britain's investment plan was “a step in the right direction”, but that “a step in the right direction is not enough”, adding that in the talks “nothing is ruled out”.

The same paper points to a second motive, unrelated to defence spending. Republican figures close to Israel have argued in Washington for months that the United States should reconsider its neutrality, viewing Britain as a less reliable ally, in connection with the sanctions and trade ban Burnham's government applied to Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank. On Friday, Yair Netanyahu, son of the Israeli prime minister and holder of no official position, posted in Spanish on X that the islands belong to Argentina.

The US position, held for decades, is to recognise de facto British administration without taking sides on sovereignty. It has tilted once before: in 1982 Washington initially adopted a neutral stance and, after peace talks collapsed, provided Britain with military and intelligence support during the conflict, which left 649 Argentines, 255 Britons and three islanders dead.

The US ambassador in Buenos Aires, Peter Lamelas, said in mid-August that “the United States has a position of neutrality on the islands” and that “this has not changed”. Javier Milei's government has opted for “caution and prudence” and reads the episode as a strategy aimed at NATO allies rather than a formal shift in US foreign policy.

The United Kingdom has administered the archipelago since 1833 and reaffirmed this year its status as a British overseas territory. Argentina maintains a sovereignty claim. In the 2013 referendum, residents voted overwhelmingly to retain their link with the United Kingdom.

World.title: Uruguay and Argentina seek to stop the green hydrogen plant repeating the pulp mill conflict
World.content:
Uruguay and Argentina seek to stop the green hydrogen plant repeating the pulp mill conflict

1st Tuesday, September 2026 - 10:32 UTC Full article

Orsi said on Friday in Paysandú that Argentina had withdrawn “the criminal complaint” filed against the project

The governments of Uruguay and Argentina are trying to contain tensions surrounding the green hydrogen and synthetic fuels plant that HIF Global plans to build in the Uruguayan department of Paysandú, on the Uruguay river, after a statement by President Yamandú Orsi drew three consecutive denials from the Argentine side.

The project, valued at some 5.4 billion dollars and presented as the largest foreign investment in Uruguay's history, would produce e-fuels from green hydrogen generated with renewable energy and carbon dioxide sourced from biomass chains. It envisages around 3,000 direct jobs and a first phase of about 1 billion dollars.

The original location, some three kilometres from the Entre Ríos city of Colón and facing its shoreline, drew objections in Argentina, led by Entre Ríos governor Rogelio Frigerio, over the potential visual impact on tourism and pollution of the waterway. After bilateral negotiations that included two meetings at Uruguay's foreign ministry, in November and April, the parties agreed to relocate the plant to a site belonging to the state oil company Ancap.

Orsi said on Friday in Paysandú that Argentina had withdrawn “the criminal complaint” filed against the project, describing it as good diplomatic news. Argentine federal prosecutor Josefina Minatta replied that she had not withdrawn hers and would maintain it while Uruguay fails to answer her requests for information on possible contamination. Deputy Guillermo Michel said his preventive civil action also remains under way. Uruguay's presidency secretary, Alejandro Sánchez, attributed the episode to a mix-up and said what had been dropped was a submission by Colón's deputy mayor to the support committee of the Escazú Agreement, the regional treaty on access to environmental information. The Colón municipality then countered that it had never filed any complaint and had only requested access to the Uruguayan case file, information it obtained before withdrawing from further consultation on August 25.

Sánchez argued that a bilateral treaty governs use of the Uruguay river, but that decisions on national territory are sovereign: “There is no Argentine judge who can impose sanctions on Uruguay or set the rules of the game for it.”

Both governments are seeking to avoid a repeat of the conflict over the Fray Bentos pulp mill, which between 2005 and 2010 led to prolonged blockades of the international bridges by Argentine residents and to a case brought by Argentina against Uruguay before the International Court of Justice.

The commercial agreement remains open. Still to be settled are ownership of the infrastructure, the division of investment and the price of the electricity to be supplied by the state utility UTE.

World.title: A Pentagon memo already floated in April using the Falklands as leverage over London
World.content:
A Pentagon memo already floated in April using the Falklands as leverage over London

1st Tuesday, September 2026 - 09:55 UTC Full article

An internal Pentagon memo leaked in April already raised the prospect of using a review of the stance on the archipelago as an instrument of diplomatic pressure on alliance partners

Senior US Defense Department officials are considering a review of Washington's position on the Falklands as one of several measures to press the United Kingdom to meet the 5% of gross domestic product military spending target agreed at NATO, the British newspaper The Telegraph reported, citing a senior US official.

The idea has surfaced before. An internal Pentagon memo leaked in April already raised the prospect of using a review of the stance on the archipelago as an instrument of diplomatic pressure on alliance partners. Secretary of State Marco Rubio described it at the time as a minor internal decision. According to Reuters reporting then, citing an internal email, the proposal formed part of a wider review of US diplomatic support for European “imperial possessions”, conceived as a way to penalise allied governments regarded as insufficiently supportive of the military campaign against Iran.

Washington's official position, held for decades, is neutrality on sovereignty over the islands while recognising British administration of the territory. What would be under review is that stance, not a recognition of sovereignty, which the United States has never issued. The United Kingdom has administered the archipelago since 1833 and Argentina maintains a sovereignty claim; in the 2013 referendum, residents voted overwhelmingly to retain their status as a British overseas territory.

A senior Pentagon official told the London newspaper last week that Britain would receive “special attention” in the US review of burden-sharing within the alliance, “because it has so much potential”, and that efforts would continue to “incentivise and enable the UK to step up in a major way”. The review examines whether member states have credible paths towards the spending target and includes a questionnaire sent to NATO ambassadors covering arms purchases and support for US foreign policy. Its conclusions will go to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

Allies agreed last year to devote 3.5% of GDP to defence and a further 1.5% to security-related infrastructure by 2035. The US administration is pushing what its officials describe as a new phase of the alliance, in which European countries and Canada would take primary responsibility for the conventional defence of the continent while Washington reorients its deployment towards the Indo-Pacific.

The British government has repeatedly said the islands' status as a British overseas territory is not open to discussion. Argentine President Javier Milei, whose government maintains a close relationship with the White House, reacted favourably to the prospect of a change in the US position.

World.title: Uruguay's central bank marks five years without intervening in the currency market
World.content:
Uruguay's central bank marks five years without intervening in the currency market

1st Tuesday, September 2026 - 09:49 UTC Full article

Against that backdrop, banks will have to warn clients of the exchange rate risk attached to dollar accounts

The Central Bank of Uruguay completed five years on Monday without intervening in the foreign exchange market. Its last operation was a purchase of 31.2 million dollars in 2021. Its president, Guillermo Tolosa, described the milestone as of “enormous” importance and said the country is going through a period of “absolutely free floating of the currency”.

“The exchange rate has behaved in a very harmonious way, at almost the same level we had back then,” he said in an interview with radio Universal. He attributed that stability to three factors: an economy exporting some 20 billion dollars a year, the legal prohibition on the central bank financing the government, and an inflation-targeting regime.

Tolosa linked the absence of intervention to price developments. “The fall in inflation today is sustainable. We have inflation close to our target and we did not depend on using our reserves to achieve it,” he said. Inflation stands at 4.3%, against a target of 4.5%. He recalled that for eighty years Uruguay assumed reducing inflation required intervening in the currency market using reserves, and said the tool would only be used in specific episodes of disruption or when the target is seriously at risk, with interest rate moves preferred first.

He warned of possible global downward pressure on the dollar stemming from the level of United States debt and deficit, after gross US debt passed 40 trillion dollars for the first time in August. He noted that recent weeks had seen selling of long-dated US bonds and of the currency itself, and acknowledged this could translate into a significant appreciation of the Uruguayan peso, as happened in January, though he specified it is not the bank's baseline scenario.

Against that backdrop, banks will have to warn clients of the exchange rate risk attached to dollar accounts. Tolosa set out the plausible range: the rate could move from 40 to 44 or 45 pesos over a matter of months, but not reach 60.

The measure has been questioned by the banking sector. The regulator replied that lenders “are comfortable with a status quo” in which they take dollar deposits, pay no interest on them and earn the US policy rate, close to 4%, with a wide intermediation margin. He added that fixed-term deposits of under six months yield below inflation with no valid justification. Banks have not publicly responded to those statements.

In August the dollar eased 0.07% in Uruguay and is up 3.08% for the year, trading at an average of around 40.24 pesos. Uruguay's country risk premium closed at 62 basis points.

World.title: The Venezuelan oil concession goes to Alejandro Betancourt's firm, under investigation in Europe
World.content:
The Venezuelan oil concession goes to Alejandro Betancourt's firm, under investigation in Europe

1st Tuesday, September 2026 - 09:23 UTC Full article

Betancourt said in a statement that Venezuela is “blessed with an abundance of natural resources, hardworking people and untapped potential,” and thanked Trump and Rodríguez

The White House on Monday identified the company that will operate seventeen Venezuelan oil fields for a century in partnership with the US government: North American Blue Energy Partners, owned by Venezuelan businessman Alejandro Betancourt, who is under investigation in Switzerland and Spain over his alleged involvement in a scheme to launder funds from the state oil company PDVSA. There is no conviction against him.

The announcement comes three days after President Donald Trump disclosed the agreement without identifying the private operator, a detail the administration had withheld. According to the document now released, Venezuela's acting president, Delcy Rodríguez, granted the company hundred-year rights over fields holding some 65 billion barrels of proven reserves, around a fifth of Venezuela's total.

Betancourt said in a statement that Venezuela is “blessed with an abundance of natural resources, hardworking people and untapped potential,” and thanked Trump and Rodríguez. He did not address the investigations open in Europe. His company is Venezuela's second-largest private producer after Chevron, pumping more than 200,000 barrels a day, with over 5,000 employees and 10,000 contractors, and aims to exceed a million barrels a day in the short term. The United States consumed around 20.6 million barrels a day last year.

The structure of the deal also became known on Monday. The Pentagon's Office of Strategic Capital will take a 35% stake in the company's parent, and the State Department will have a guaranteed purchase of 20% of output at production cost, plus right of first refusal over the remaining 80%. The US government will hold a veto over all board appointments, a majority of whom must be US nationals, and the agreement will be governed by US law and subject to the jurisdiction of US courts.

The company has committed to investing up to 100 billion dollars in oil infrastructure and, according to White House calculations, will pay some 200 billion in royalties and taxes over the first twenty-five years. Rodríguez had put that figure at 209 billion. “This deal secures our energy dominance for the next century, all at zero cost to the United States,” the statement says, adding that several of the fields were previously held by Russian and Chinese interests.

The US administration also maintains that the reconciliation process it is promoting in Venezuela has already produced judicial reforms and the release of hundreds of political prisoners. The agreement reached on August 12 between the interim government and a section of the opposition annulled and restarted the process for appointing Supreme Court justices, without mentioning political prisoners or the electoral authority. The deal has drawn criticism in Venezuela from both chavismo and opposition figures.

World.title: In second annual report to the nation, Sheinbaum hails a stronger, safer and more prosperous Mexico
World.content:
Listen to this article

One month shy of completing her second year in office, President Claudia Sheinbaum on Tuesday delivered her second annual report in a 67-minute speech, a wide-ranging and optimistic address that covered government achievements across areas including the economy, security, infrastructure and healthcare.

“I appear before the people of Mexico nearly two years after assuming the presidency of the republic. I do so with the certainty that we are transforming public life in this country,” Sheinbaum said at the beginning of her speech, delivered at the National Palace in the historic center of Mexico City to an audience that included high-ranking federal and state officials as well as Mexican business leaders.

Segundo Informe de Gobierno. Palacio Nacional https://t.co/uCe1PE8VkK — Claudia Sheinbaum Pardo (@Claudiashein) September 1, 2026

Early in her address, the president declared she was “convinced” that Mexico is on “the path to shared prosperity, with independence, freedom and a lot of dignity.”

“We have governed with integrity and republican austerity,” Sheinbaum said.

“We are fully aware that public resources belong to the people and must be used for their benefit. … The economic power was separated from the political power and we govern honestly,” she said.

Sheinbaum is approaching the completion of her second year in office with an approval rating of 68%, according to the newspaper El Financiero’s latest national poll, and an MND Sheinbaum Index™ score — to be published this Wednesday — of close to 70 out of 100.

However, her popularity as president doesn’t insulate her from a range of challenges and difficulties she faces as the leader of a nation of some 130 million people that, for better or for worse, neighbors the United States, the world’s largest economy — and the world’s largest consumer market for illicit drugs.

Sheinbaum faces ongoing security challenges — particularly in states such as Guanajuato and Sinaloa — and frequent pressure from the Trump administration to do more to combat Mexico’s notorious drug cartels. She faces economic challenges, such as low productivity and high labor informality, amid uncertainty about the future of the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA). She faces domestic and external pressure related to drug trafficking accusations against ruling Morena party officials. She faces ongoing claims that she is turning Mexico into a more authoritarian, less democratic nation. Meanwhile, the U.S. tourist visas of more than 50 Morena officials, including that of one of ex-president Andrés Manuel López Obrador’s sons, have been revoked. The list of challenges and difficulties faced by Mexico’s first female president goes on.

On Tuesday, however, Sheinbaum focused on the positives, and declared at the end of her address that “we” — i.e., Mexico and her administration — are “doing better” now than before, as she said would occur in her inaugural government report a year ago. She also said that Mexico has a clear path forward “set” by the Mexican people.

Below is a recap of Sheinbaum’s second annual report, or “segundo informe de gobierno,” as it is called in Spanish.

The economy

“Even in these difficult conditions, the Mexican economy remains stable and continues to grow.”

Sheinbaum said that in her almost two years in office, Mexico has faced “difficult international circumstances, marked by a change in the tariff policy of the U.S. government.”

“In particular, [U.S] tariffs on vehicles, steel, aluminum, and their derivatives, as well as the war in Iran, which drove up international oil prices, have created difficult circumstances for our country and for the entire world,” she said.

“Even in these difficult conditions, the Mexican economy remains stable and continues to grow,” Sheinbaum said.

She subsequently presented various data points to support her statement. They included that:

Sheinbaum also highlighted that the federal government’s revenue reached a record high of more than 6.4 trillion pesos (US $376.76 billion) last year. She said that tax income has continued to increase in 2026.

Sheinbaum also said that Mexico’s monthly minimum wage has increased “154% in real terms” since 2018 to reach 9,582 pesos (US $564) in 2026.

“On the northern border, the minimum wage stands at 13,409 pesos per month. The average wage in the formal economy reached an all-time high of 20,212 pesos per month, the highest on record,” she said.

“As a result, in-work poverty in 2026 is at its lowest level since 2005.”

Plan Mexico

“Twenty-five of the 100 industrial parks we announced are already in operation.”

Sheinbaum noted that early in her six-year term, she presented Plan Mexico, an ambitious economic initiative with 13 goals, including making Mexico the 10th largest economy in the world by 2030, increasing domestic manufacturing production and cutting red tape for investment projects.

“Two decrees with incentives for private investment were published,” the president said before highlighting that 10 of 25 “Economic Development Hubs for Well-Being” for which private investment was sought are now under development.

“Twenty-five of the 100 industrial parks we announced as a goal are now in operation,” Sheinbaum added.

“In addition, we established the Presidential Office for Investment Promotion, which operates a one-stop shop that approves [investment project] applications within a maximum of 60 days. Through this, 19 projects totaling US $3.76 billion have been approved in four months,” she said.

“In addition, 60% of the bureaucratic procedures [for new investments] have been simplified or eliminated, requirements have been reduced by 66%, and the average response time has been cut by 50%,” Sheinbaum said.

Welfare programs

“We have a duty to support those who for a long time were forgotten.”

The Sheinbaum administration has maintained all the welfare, social and employment programs launched by the government led by ex-president López Obrador, and added new ones, including educational scholarship schemes and cash transfers for women aged 60 and over.

The president said on Tuesday that the government’s welfare programs are “an expression of the conviction that nobody builds a nation alone.”

In a jab at pre-2018 governments, she also said that “we have a duty to support those who for a long were forgotten” — i.e., Mexico’s most disadvantaged people.

Mexico’s welfare programs are based on and draw from Mexican humanism, from a simple but powerful idea,” Sheinbaum said.

That idea, she said, is that “the wealth of Mexico must translate into well-being for its people.”

“A pension for a senior, a scholarship for a student or support for those who work the land aren’t concessions from power, but rather a way of recognizing the dignity and effort of millions of Mexicans,” Sheinbaum said.

She said that welfare programs will benefit almost 43 million Mexicans in 2026, “with a historic investment of one trillion pesos (US $58.85 billion).

Healthcare

“We are reversing the damage caused by decades of neglect in the area of health care.”

Sheinbaum said that when a “fourth transformation” (i.e., Morena) government first came to power in Mexico in 2018, a “profound deterioration in Mexico’s public health system” was evident.

She went on to claim that Morena governments are “reversing the damage caused by decades of neglect in the area of health care.”

Sheinbaum said that “in just two years” of her administration, 33 new public hospitals and 47 public healthcare centers have opened. She noted that her government is aiming to add 9,000 beds to the public health system by 2030.

“To ensure the timely supply of medications and medical supplies, we make consolidated purchases directly from suppliers. We also created the ‘Rutas de la Salud’ program for medical facilities and hospitals in the IMSS Bienestar system, through which 2 billion items have been distributed,” Sheinbaum said.

“No hospital that treats cancer lacks medications,” she asserted.

Infrastructure

“We’re recovering the passenger train network, hallmark of the fourth transformation.”

Sheinbaum enumerated infrastructure projects her government has completed, including highways and “70 bridges and interchanges.”

“… We doubled the budget for artisanal [hand-built] roads, and together with Indigenous communities we’ve built 135 roads measuring 368 kilometers,” she said.

Sheinbaum also highlighted that her government completed passenger train lines between Mexico City and Toluca and between Mexico City and the Felipe Ángeles International Airport. She noted that her administration is building various other railroads across Mexico. The president asserted that her government is “recovering the passenger train network” in Mexico, and said that doing so is a “hallmark of the fourth transformation” political movement she leads.

Sheinbaum also said that 2 million tonnes of freight have been transported on the Isthmus of Tehuantepec’s Interoceanic Railroad, on which two derailments — including a fatal one — have occurred during her government.

She said that her government is modernizing “hydro-agricultural infrastructure across more than 250,000 hectares, which will increase productivity on farms and at the same time release water for human consumption.”

Sheinbaum also spoke about various other water projects, including dams, aqueducts and the desalination plant set to be built in Rosarito, Baja California.

In addition, she said the government is “modernizing seven ports” and “11 international airports,” including those in Mexico City, Puerto Escondido and Tepic.

Security

“We’ve achieved a 51% reduction in homicides.”

Sheinbaum said that “the peace and tranquility of families” are a top priority for her government.

“Thousands of National Guard members, soldiers, marines, security agents, and public servants work every day on the four pillars of the National Security Strategy,” she said, highlighting that those pillars are attention to the root causes of crime; consolidation of the National Guard; strengthening of intelligence and investigative practices; and enhanced coordination between federal and state authorities.

“The results speak for themselves,” Sheinbaum asserted before declaring that “we’ve achieved a 51% reduction in homicides since we took office.”

She was referring to the reduction in homicides in July 2026 compared to September 2024, the final month of López Obrador’s presidency. The annual decline in murders in the first seven months of 2026 was a more modest, but still significant, 30.8%.

Sheinbaum also said that the incidence of high-impact crimes — such as murder, violent robbery, kidnapping and extortion — is down 54% so far this year compared to 2018. She highlighted that some 63,000 people were arrested for allegedly committing high-impact crimes between October 2024 and July 2026.

Sheinbaum said that 207 of those people were “priority targets from all the organized crime groups.”

In addition, Mexican security forces have killed high-profile criminal leaders, including Jalisco New Generation Cartel kingpin Rubén Nemesio “El Mencho” Oseguera Cervantes, who was fatally wounded in a military operation in Jalisco in February.

Sheinbaum noted that authorities have seized 32,824 firearms and 519 tonnes of drugs during her presidency, and dismantled 2,725 clandestine drug laboratories.

Mexico-US relations

“Our relationship with the U.S. government has had its challenges, but we’ve made the decision to always seek understanding.”

Toward the end of her address, Sheinbaum turned her attention to the relationship between Mexico and the United States, a relationship that has been strained by trade and security tensions.

After outlining Mexico’s constitutionally enshrined foreign policy principles, including that of non-intervention in the affairs of other countries, the president said:

“In this context, I would like to highlight our relationship with the U.S. government, which has had its challenges, but we’ve made the decision to always seek understanding.”

Sheinbaum didn’t mention the CIA’s alleged participation in a drug lab raid in April without the knowledge or authorization of her government. Nor did she refer to U.S. prosecutors’ drug trafficking accusations against Sinaloa Governor Ruben Rocha Moya and various other current and former officials. Sheinbaum has previously characterized those things as examples of U.S. interference in Mexican affairs. However, on Tuesday, she limited herself to reiterating her commitment to defending Mexican sovereignty.

“Mexico is a sovereign country and sovereignty isn’t negotiated, handed over or shared,” said Sheinbaum, who has maintained a respectful relationship with U.S. President Donald Trump despite the disparaging remarks he has made about her, including claims that she is “afraid” of Mexican cartels.

She said that “perhaps one of the most painful aspects” of the relationship with the United States “has been the treatment Mexicans have received” while under the custody of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). She noted that 17 Mexicans have died in ICE custody or during ICE operations since Trump returned to the White House in January 2025.

“In response, … we decided to file complaints … and we will follow up on them and demand that the human rights of our compatriots be fully respected,” she said.

Exactly two months after the U.S. government announced that it had declined to renew the USMCA “in its current form” for an additional 16 years, Sheinbaum said that dialogue with the Trump administration on trade issues is ongoing, “and we hope to reach an understanding.”

Despite the U.S. government’s decision to not renew the USMCA, the free trade pact remains in force. In 2026, Mexico has consolidated its position as the top exporter to, and top trade partner of, the United States.

10 more things

During her second government report speech, Sheinbaum also said that:

‘Mexico is strong, it has extraordinary people’

In her closing remarks, Sheinbaum said that “in these 23 months of great changes, we’ve shown that Mexico is strong and has extraordinary people.”

“… We are part of the project of the fourth transformation of public life,” she said.

“Let no one be mistaken — here there are no divisions, there are no ruptures,” Sheinbaum said, dismissing claims that there are rifts within the ruling Morena party.

“The only thing there is is the defense of the people of Mexico and their dignity,” she said.

Sheinbaum asserted that “the eyes of the world are on Mexico because here a great people has decided to write their own history.”

“We are strengthening a project that grew from the grassroots and which places equality, justice and well-being at its center,” she said.

“… Mexico is free and sovereign and is advancing with dignity, with the strength of its people and with our eyes set on a future that stems from our legacy of greatness,” Sheinbaum said.

World.title: An Archery Center of Excellence opens in Tijuana for Mexico’s world class archers
World.content:
Mexico has opened a new specialized archery training center in Tijuana as it builds its Olympic program toward Los Angeles 2028 and prepares to host the archery World Cup Final this month in Saltillo, Coahuila.

The Centro de Excelencia de Tiro con Arco, or Archery Center of Excellence, opened Saturday under the auspices of the federal sports commission Conade, the Baja California government, the state’s sports institute and World Archery Mexico.

The facility is part of a broader project to establish archery facilities in Tijuana and Mérida, Yucatán, at a cost of more than 40 million pesos, then worth about US $2.2 million, Conade said last year. Officials did not specify how much was allocated to each site.

Mexico has emerged as an international archery power, with four athletes currently ranked in the top six of their divisions, plus a bronze medal at the 2024 Paris Olympics and the country’s first World Archery Championships gold in Gwangju, South Korea, in 2025.

The current world rankings show Andrea Maya Becerra No. 1 in women’s compound, Matías Grande No. 3 in men’s recurve, Sebastián García Flores No. 4 in men’s compound and Ana Paula Vázquez Flores No. 6 in women’s recurve. Becerra is from Jalisco, while Grande, García and Vázquez are Coahuila natives.

At the 2026 Pan American Archery Championships held June 22-28 in Santa Úrsula Zimatepec, Tlaxcala, Mexico won seven medals, including two golds.

The new Tijuana center includes rehabilitated synthetic turf, an archery range with 20-22 shooting lanes, lighting, a gym and an equipment room. It is intended for national-team training and talent development.

World Archery Mexico President Gabriel Ramos attended the inauguration and said Mexico is working with 14 archers vying for spots on the national team: eight on Team A and six on Team B.

The approach is designed to deepen domestic competition ahead of the 2028 Olympics. Mexico’s compound-bow athletes recently spent seven weeks training in Switzerland before a camp in Tlaxcala, Ramos added.

The ceremony also drew Baja California Gov. Marina del Pilar Ávila Olmeda and Conade Director General Rommel Pacheco.

The next international test for Mexico’s archers will come Sept. 12-13 at the 2026 Hyundai Archery World Cup Final, following qualifying stages in Mexico (Puebla), China, Turkey and Spain.

The two-day competition will bring together 32 elite archers for knockout matches in Saltillo, Coahuila’s capital. The season-ending event is separate from the World Archery Championships.

With reports from Quadratin, ALMA Plus TV, Esto and Infobae

World.title: The Maya Train reports a ‘track-related incident.’ Was it another derailment?
World.content:
The Maya Train reported another mishap Monday afternoon in Campeche, described only vaguely as a “track-related incident” but serious enough to force the evacuation of passengers from a train traveling the Cancún–Palenque route.

The state-owned company reported no injuries and stated that protocols for passenger care and service continuity were activated.

#Entérate Se descarrila nuevamente el #TrenMaya #Campeche Una pasajera del Tren Maya compartió en redes sociales un video en el que, según su reporte, se observa un presunto descarrilamiento cerca de la estación San Francisco de Campeche. Debido al incidente, los pasajeros… pic.twitter.com/QT6RWW2qy5 — QuintanaRooNews (@quintanaroonews) September 1, 2026

According to a statement released by the train, the problem occurred around 3:30 p.m. as the train was departing the San Francisco de Campeche station. It involved the train’s last car, which had advanced a mere 50 meters from the railway terminal when it happened.

“In accordance with established technical procedures, the train driver brought the unit to a halt; no injuries were reported among the 123 passengers,” the Maya Train said.

It added that the passengers were evacuated as a precautionary measure and transported by road to the Edzná station, from where they would continue their journey on another train.

Although the official statement described the event only as a “track-related incident” (un percance de vía), various media reports indicated that the last car had partially derailed. So far, no technical report has been released confirming or ruling out any derailment or identifying the causes of the incident.

The Maya Train also announced that a Railway Accident Review Commission has initiated the necessary investigations to determine the cause of the incident.

This is the third incident of this type recorded on a Maya Train track. In August 2025, a derailment was reported near Mérida, also resulting in no injuries.

Earlier, in March 2024, another train derailed in Tixkokob, in Yucatán. Authorities later attributed the incident to a problem with a track-switching component.

The recurring problem occurs against a backdrop of questions regarding the project’s financial viability. Likewise, operational incidents increase pressure on the company to disclose the technical causes of the mishaps and the measures it will implement to strengthen safety, service continuity and financial sustainability.

An investigation published by the newspaper El Universal reported that the Maya Train recorded losses of 5.013 billion pesos (US $294.6 million) in the first half of 2026, compared to 4.810 billion pesos (US $282.7 million) recorded throughout 2025.

According to that report, from the service’s inauguration through last June, accumulated expenses and losses totaled 14.104 billion pesos (US $828.9 million), while revenue from sales and service provision amounted to 1.060 billion pesos (US $62.3 million).

With reports from La Jornada

World.title: Sheinbaum’s approval rating remains unshaken at 68%
World.content:
Ahead of her second annual report to the nation, President Claudia Sheinbaum had an approval rating of 68%, according to the most recent national poll conducted by the newspaper El Financiero, putting her ahead of her two predecessors at this point in the six-year presidential term.

The president’s August rating remains almost unchanged from December 2025, when Sheinbaum had a 69% approval rating, following her first full year as president. Thirty-two percent of respondents disapproved of Sheinbaum in August.

The government’s strongest area of performance continues to be social programs, of which 64% of respondents had favorable opinions, followed by economic management, with 50% approving.

Meanwhile, public opinions on security, organized crime and corruption have worsened since May, garnering just 13%, 11% and 14% approval, respectively. Negative opinions among respondents about public safety are also on the rise, increasing from 61% in July to 76% in August, marking the highest level in Sheinbaum’s presidency to date.

With negotiations of the Mexico-United States-Canada free trade agreement (USMCA) still underway, the share of respondents who held a positive view of Sheinbaum’s management of USMCA talks rose from 51% to 56% between July and August, while the percentage of people expressing optimistic attitudes towards Sheinbaum’s relationship with U.S. President Trump rose from 35% to 41%.

During the presentation of the new poll results, public opinion analyst Roy Campos stressed that Sheinbaum’s average approval rating is 14 percentage points higher than that of former President Andrés Manuel López Obrador, and 21 points higher than that of Enrique Peña Nieto as she approaches the start of her third year in office.

According to the results of El Financiero’s monthly poll, the president’s best approval rating so far this year was in February, at 72%, whereas her worst month was July, at 67%. Based on her current average, Sheinbaum is set to have the highest approval rating of the last six Mexican presidents.

Mexico News Daily offers its own MND Sheinbaum Index™ based on eight numerical pillars, such as inflation, the homicide rate and the unemployment rate, which has shown President Sheinbaum’s performance to be steadily improving month over month. For June, MND gave Sheinbaum a score of 67.5/100; check back tomorrow for the latest MND Sheinbaum Index™ analyzing the data for July.

With reports from El Financiero and Animal Político

World.title: Remittances increase for sixth straight month, but strong peso blunts the benefit
World.content:
Remittances to Mexico showed an annual increase for a sixth consecutive month, rising 3% in July compared to a year ago and remaining above US $5 billion for a third straight month, the Bank of Mexico reported.

The true gain, however, is offset by the strengthening Mexican currency, which results in fewer pesos pocketed in Mexico per dollar of remittance. In fact, in peso terms, remittances actually fell by 3.7% compared to July 2025, when the peso hit as high as 18.85 to the dollar as compared to a tick or two under 17 today.

Still, the US $5.57 billion that beneficiary households received in July was the second-highest monthly total of 2026, behind only the US $5.62 billion recorded in May.

Remittances to Mexico have now surpassed US $36.3 billion through the first seven months of the year, marking a 3.1% rebound compared to the same period in 2025. The increasing total is driven by a rise in the average amount of transactions, rather than an increase in the total number of transactions,

After an 11-year growth streak ended with a 4.6% decline in 2025, flows have stabilized and increased in 2026.

Unfortunately for those receiving remittances in dollars from abroad, while the peso’s remarkable recent appreciation improves purchasing power for the majority who receive income in pesos, it reduces the value of remittances when converted into pesos. It also makes Mexico more expensive for foreign tourists, and for residents whose income or pensions, including U.S. Social Security, are paid in dollars.

Analysis conducted by BBVA research produced an estimate that the purchasing power of remittances fell 8.3% year-on-year in June. That’s a key development, because family remittances represent roughly 4% of GDP, making Mexico the second-largest global recipient of cross-border transfers behind India.

The central bank also reported that remittance outflows — money sent abroad from within Mexico — through the first seven months of the year totaled US $731 million, an annual increase of 6.3% over the US $688 million reported in the same period of 2025.

Thus, in the first seven months of 2026, the remittance account surplus (cash in minus cash out) was US $35.62 billion, an amount greater than the US $34.56 billion observed from January through July 2025, an annual increase of 3.1%.

With reports from El Economista, El Financiero and Expansión

World.title: MND Local: Golf course, green spaces and industrial growth in San Miguel
World.content:
Plenty of San Miguel news has been circulating lately, including continuing talk of another golf course, additional trees for a beloved park, a possible new downtown parking garage and major industrial investments in the city and surrounding region. More details on these and related developments are below.

Potential golf course near El Charco sparks petition drive

Persistent rumors that a fourth golf course is being planned for an area north of the El Charco del Ingenio Botanical Garden on the northeastern edge of San Miguel recently prompted a petition drive opposing the proposal.

The petition had 19,050 verified signatures and 183 comments as of Aug. 31, the majority of which appear to oppose the project. Signers cite concerns about threats to the environment and water supply.

The golf course plan emerged nearly a year ago with the backing of Lorena Ochoa, a World Golf Hall of Famer who has been described as Mexico’s most accomplished golfer. However, no permits had been applied for or granted at that point, according to municipal officials.

El Charco has stated that the golf course’s placement would be in “the worst imaginable location” on a large rural tract of land directly bordering the botanical garden. Other issues include exotic grasses requiring intensive irrigation and the application of fertilizers and toxic pesticides, El Charco said.



“The municipal Urban Development Plan, which had previously designated the property as an area for ecological preservation, has been amended to allow a change in land use, paving the way for urbanization and the construction of the golf course,” El Charco’s August newsletter stated.

San Miguel currently has three golf courses: two 18-hole courses (Malanquin and Las Ventanas) and one nine-hole option (Zirandaro).

Municipal government planting more trees in Parque Juárez

A recently launched project is bringing 35 new ash trees to Parque Juárez as part of the city’s “active urban conservation and environmental maintenance initiative.” At roughly 15 feet tall, they are reportedly mature trees that will help renew the park’s canopy.

There are three ash species native to Mexico, all of which adapt well to mild, subtropical and tropical highland climates found across the country.

The project will replace trees that have reached the natural end of their lifecycle and assess existing trees for pruning, treatments and parasite removal – particularly mistletoe infestations.

Meanwhile, the city will also identify, manage and remove severely deteriorated or dry trees that may pose hazards to park visitors.

Nearby residents have expressed concern about dead trees and limbs falling into public pathways, seating areas and streets. They also say some of the ash trees show evidence of pests and woodpeckers.

Is a parking garage coming to Centro San Miguel?

A new parking garage may be planned for municipal property near the Templo de San Juan de Dios. The site was formerly a public hospital for low-income patients.

The idea, reportedly put forward by Mayor Mauricio Trejo Pureco, is meant to mitigate traffic on the narrow cobblestone streets in Centro’s historic district.

Municipal officials are looking to develop more parking capacity outside the historic center to reduce vehicle idling, enhance pedestrian safety and protect historic buildings from additional wear and tear linked to traffic.

There is also a shortage of parking spaces downtown, with some reports stating there are only about 5,000 for the more than 100,000 visitors coming to San Miguel during holidays and popular events.

Downtown parking fees have also been increasing lately, with public lots and garages near the city center charging anywhere from 50 to 80 pesos per hour.

Construction materials company commits 5 billion pesos to SMA

Soprema Mexico, a global manufacturer and supplier of construction materials, recently began construction of a manufacturing facility within the Polígono Empresarial San Miguel industrial park east of the city. Its products include waterproofing, insulation and energy efficiency materials.

The company said it is making a long-term capital investment of up to 5 billion pesos (US $300 million). The project will initially create 250 direct jobs while offering opportunities to local suppliers and engineers. Subsequent expansion plans for a larger industrial campus in San Miguel are also being considered.

Soprema’s parent company was founded in France in 1908 and is still headquartered there. The Canadian arm is based in Quebec, with offices in Mexico City and Monterrey.

This local development dovetails with ongoing economic development projects and additional plans for the state of Guanajuato. There are currently 79 investment projects occurring within the state worth more than US $6.5 billion, boosting Guanajuato’s profile as an increasingly important industrial destination in Mexico.

Cathy Siegner is an independent journalist based in San Miguel and Montana. She has journalism degrees from the University of Oregon and Northwestern University.

World.title: Mexico’s military kills avocado-extortion ringleader ‘R5,’ one other in surprise shootout
World.content:
Mexican security forces on Monday shot dead an alleged cartel leader and one other person after they came under fire in the state of Michoacán, authorities said.

The alleged cartel leader who was killed was Luis Enrique Barragán Chávez, known as “El Güicho” (Wicho) and “R5.”

En Tocumbo, Michoacán, elementos de @Defensamx1 y una aeronave de @SEMAR_MX fueron agredidos con disparos de arma de fuego por integrantes de una célula delictiva. Durante el operativo, 2 agresores perdieron la vida, entre ellos Luis Enrique “N”, alias “El Güicho” y/o “R5”,… pic.twitter.com/BDaCAlsmFR — Gabinete de Seguridad de México (@GabSeguridadMX) September 1, 2026

Federal Security Minister Omar García Harfuch said in an X post on Tuesday morning that Barragán had been identified as the leader of the Cártel de Los Reyes (Kings Cartel) and the “main coordinator of extortion against avocado producers” in Michoacán.

According to Mexican authorities and the U.S. Department of State, which was offering a reward of up to US $3 million for information leading to the arrest of Barragán, the Cártel de Los Reyes is a faction of Cárteles Unidos, one of eight Mexican criminal groups designated as foreign terrorist organizations by the U.S. government.

Clash in Tocumbo

The federal Security Cabinet said on X on Tuesday morning that Mexican Army troops and a Navy plane came under fire on Monday in Tocumbo, a municipality in Michoacán on that state’s border with Jalisco.

According to García Harfuch, the attack occurred as Mexican Army and National Guard troops were carrying out an operation in Tocumbo in coordination with the Michoacán Attorney General’s Office and state police.

The security minister said that the security forces returned fire and “two attackers lost their lives,” including Barragán, who died around two months before his 40th birthday. The other victim wasn’t identified.

García Harfuch and the Security Cabinet noted that Barragán was subject to an arrest warrant for the purpose of extradition to the United States. The Security Cabinet said that authorities seized firearms, magazines and a quad bike during the operation in Tocumbo.

The death of Barragán came a month after another alleged leader of the Cártel de Los Reyes, Alfonso Fernández Magallón, was detained in the Michoacán municipality of Los Reyes. Barragán allegedly succeeded Fernández as the leader of the criminal group.

Barragán, a ‘well-known sicario,’ was wanted in the US on drug and firearms charges

In a statement published in August 2025, the U.S. State Department noted that an investigation in the United States carried out by Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) “led to an indictment charging Barragán in the District of Columbia with drug conspiracy offenses and firearms offenses in July 2023.”

“The indictment was unsealed in July 2025 in conjunction with the announcement of Treasury sanctions against Cárteles Unidos leaders as well as a Narcotics Reward Program (NRP) reward offer for Barragán,” the State Department said.

At the start of its statement, the State Department noted that HSI had identified Barragán as the “chief sicario,” or hitman, of the Cártel de Los Reyes.

It said that HSI had determined that Barragán used the proceeds from the sales of illegal narcotics in the United States to fund the Cárteles Unidos’ “combat operations” against the Jalisco New Generation Cartel, “and the projection of power in their area of control in Michoacán.”

“Drug proceeds were used to acquire small arms from the United States, hire local fighters and Colombian mercenaries, and the acquisition of heavy weaponry such as landmines, .50 caliber rifles, up-armored vehicles and the use of bomb-dropping drones,” the State Department said.

“Barragán was at the forefront of those combat efforts, becoming a well-known sicario and combat leader, working closely with other elements of Cárteles Unidos.”

‘A decisive blow to organized crime’

Michoacán Governor Alfredo Ramírez Bedolla acknowledged the death of Barragán in an X post on Tuesday morning.

“In Michoacán, there is no room for impunity or for those who threaten the peace of our families and the economy of our producers,” he wrote.

“My full recognition to the National Security Cabinet and our sincere gratitude to President Claudia Sheinbaum for her constant support to our state. Thanks to coordinated intelligence work and operations in Tocumbo between the Ministry of National Defense and the Michoacán Security Ministry we dealt a decisive blow to organized crime by neutralizing Luis Enrique ‘N’, alias ‘El Güicho’ or ‘R5’, the main extortionist of avocado growers in the region and a priority target with an extradition order,” Ramírez wrote.

Combating extortion — a widespread problem in Mexico — is a top priority for the federal government, which launched a national strategy against the crime in July 2025. Criminal groups have long targeted avocado and lime producers in Michoacán, a leading producer of those fruits.

In terms of total homicides, Michoacán ranked as Mexico’s 12th most violent state in the first seven months of 2026. The state recorded 477 murders between January and July, a 41.8% reduction compared to the same period of last year, according to the federal government.

Last November, the federal government began the implementation of “Plan Michoacán for Peace and Justice,” a 57-billion-peso (US $3.35 billion) initiative devised in response to the murder of the mayor of Uruapan on Nov. 1 and general insecurity in the state.

On Tuesday morning, the Security Cabinet said that “within the framework” of that plan, its coordination with state authorities allows criminal structures to be weakened, extortion to be combated and “those who generate violence” to be detained.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: CFE restores power in Yucatán Peninsula after 7-hour blackout reportedly caused by vandalism
World.content:
The Federal Electricity Commission (CFE) reported that service was restored in four southeastern states that were without electricity for approximately seven hours beginning Monday evening, blaming the lengthy blackout on vandalism.

As the 34-degree (93 F) day came to an end, cities across the Yucatán Peninsula were darkened after two high-voltage power lines were “damaged.” The power outage crippled commercial activities in Mérida, a city of nearly 1 million people, and left hundreds of businesses unable to process electronic payments, operate refrigeration systems or run air conditioning. Cancún, Playa del Carmen, Chetumal and parts of Chiapas and Campeche were also impacted.

#CFEInforma La Comisión Federal de Electricidad (CFE) informa que, tras las afectaciones en dos líneas de alta tensión por actos de vandalismo, se ha restablecido al 100% el suministro de energía a usuarios afectados en los estados de Yucatán, Quintana Roo, Campeche y Chiapas.… pic.twitter.com/OQoXlt3rB1 — CFEmx (@CFEmx) September 1, 2026

In a statement on social media issued at 3:08 a.m. Tuesday, the CFE reported that “following damage to two high-voltage lines due to acts of vandalism, the energy supply has been 100% restored to affected users in the states of Yucatán, Quintana Roo, Campeche and Chiapas.”

The state-owned electric utility said that once its “specialized personnel were deployed to the site,” they were able to quickly identify the problem as “damaged insulation strings” on one of the transmission structures. After several hours of “uninterrupted repair and restoration work,” power was restored to the region.

The explanation that the blackout was caused by vandalism targeting the insulators on two 400 kV high-voltage lines was met with skepticism by members of the public, dozens of whom responded to the CFE statement on X with critical comments.

The respondents recalled that former CFE director Manuel Bartlett (2018-2024) frequently blamed vandalism, illegal connections and sabotage to explain away widespread electrical grid failures and instability.

The lack of accountability fueling public skepticism is highlighted by a scandal in late 2020 where the CFE forged official documents to blame a Tamaulipas brushfire for a blackout affecting 10 million people.

Monday’s blackout affected more than 10 million people in southeastern Mexico while also partially impacting the neighboring country of Belize.

The region is no stranger to electricity insufficiencies due to the combination of extreme heat, low power generation and the lack of infrastructure to distribute natural gas. One year ago, a blackout left more than 2.2 million residents in the region without power for six hours, and rolling blackouts affected the area in May 2025.

With reports from The Yucatán Times, El País, Diario de Yucatán and LopezDoriga.com

World.title: Algeria Moves to Restore the Death Penalty for Setting Forests Alight
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

ALGERIA · SOCIETY

Key Facts —The order: President Abdelmadjid Tebboune has instructed the justice minister to submit an amendment to the penal code by 15 September introducing capital punishment for anyone convicted of deliberately setting fire to forested areas. He issued the directive on Sunday at a meeting with senior civilian and military officials. —The toll: Twelve people died and 54 were injured in the wave of wildfires across several eastern provinces. Five deaths were recorded in Jijel, four in Bejaia and three in Tizi Ouzou. —The scale of the burn: Algeria’s civil protection service counted 154 fires across the country in a single day, 36 of them in Bejaia province alone. Three days of national mourning were declared. —A moratorium since 1993: The death penalty already exists in Algerian law for several offences, but the country has observed a de facto moratorium on executions since 1993. Reinstating it in practice would be a first-order change. —What the law says now: Intentionally setting a forest fire currently carries up to 30 years in prison, and life imprisonment in certain circumstances. The proposed amendment would add the ultimate sentence. —The president’s suspicion: Tebboune said videos showing several fires starting at around one in the morning had raised questions about whether some were deliberate. He asked provincial governors to hand security services all available information. —The relief package: Tebboune ordered immediate compensation for affected families, with committees to assess damage. He also instructed authorities to restore electricity, gas, water and telecommunications, and told the housing minister to arrange repairs on fixed deadlines.

The Algeria death penalty is to be extended to arson, after President Abdelmadjid Tebboune ordered his justice minister to amend the penal code by 15 September. The directive follows wildfires in the country’s north-east that killed 12 people and injured 54.

What Tebboune actually ordered

The instruction was issued on Sunday during a high-level meeting on the response to the fires, attended by senior civilian and military officials and reported by state television. The justice minister has until 15 September to submit the amendment.

It would introduce capital punishment for anyone convicted of intentionally setting fire to forested areas. State television said any sentence would only be carried out once all avenues of appeal had been exhausted.

That last clause matters more than it looks. It is the sentence that makes the reform legally survivable and, in practice, slow.

The fires that prompted it

Algeria’s Interior Ministry said 12 people had died in the latest wave of wildfires across several eastern provinces. Fifty-four were injured, several of them critically.

The deaths were concentrated in the mountainous north-east: five in Jijel, four in Bejaia and three in Tizi Ouzou. The government declared three days of national mourning.

The intensity was unusual. Civil protection recorded 154 separate fires nationwide in one day, with 36 in Bejaia province alone, during an exceptional heatwave across North Africa.

Why the government suspects arson

Tebboune said videos showing several fires starting at around one in the morning had raised questions about their origin. He asked provincial governors to give security authorities everything they had.

Officials have pointed to arson as a contributing factor alongside drought and heat. No arrests or charges connected to the current fires had been announced when the directive was issued.

That gap is worth holding onto. The policy is moving faster than the investigation that would justify it.

What the Algeria death penalty change would mean in law

Capital punishment is already available in Algerian law for a range of offences. What has been absent since 1993 is execution: the country has observed a de facto moratorium for more than three decades.

Deliberate fire-raising currently attracts up to 30 years in prison, and life imprisonment in some circumstances. Adding the death penalty would place forest arson among the country’s gravest crimes.

The practical question is whether the moratorium holds. A statute that authorises execution is not the same as a state that carries one out, and Algeria has kept that distinction for a generation.

The recovery orders that came with it

Alongside the penal reform, Tebboune ordered immediate compensation for affected families, with committees to assess destroyed or damaged property. He set a deadline for restoring electricity, gas, water and telecommunications in the affected areas.

The housing minister was told to coordinate with construction companies on repairing damaged homes within fixed deadlines. The president said normal life in the burnt areas should resume within a week.

Those timelines are ambitious for terrain of that kind. They are also, politically, the part of the package residents will measure first.

The wider picture

North Africa is in the middle of a run of hotter, drier summers, and the Algerian fire season has repeatedly turned lethal. The policy instinct in such moments is to find intent behind catastrophe.

For readers outside the country, the significance is less about arson than about precedent. A state that has not executed anyone since 1993 is being asked to legislate as though it might.

Nothing here is legal advice, and the amendment has not yet been drafted, tabled or passed. The date to watch is 15 September, when the justice ministry is due to produce the text.

Frequently Asked Questions

What has Algeria ordered on the death penalty? President Tebboune instructed the justice minister to submit a penal code amendment by 15 September introducing capital punishment for deliberately setting forest fires. State television said sentences would only be carried out after all appeals were exhausted. How many people died in the Algerian wildfires? Twelve people died and 54 were injured across several eastern provinces. Five deaths were in Jijel, four in Bejaia and three in Tizi Ouzou. Does Algeria currently carry out executions? No. The death penalty exists in Algerian law for several offences, but the country has observed a de facto moratorium on executions since 1993. What is the penalty for forest arson in Algeria today? Intentionally setting a forest fire currently carries up to 30 years in prison, and life imprisonment in certain circumstances. The proposed amendment would add capital punishment. What relief did the government announce? Tebboune ordered immediate compensation for affected families, damage assessment committees, and the restoration of electricity, gas, water and telecommunications. The housing minister was told to arrange home repairs on fixed deadlines.

World.title: Hichilema Is Sworn In With the Election Petition Still Unresolved
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

ZAMBIA · POLITICS

Key Facts —A public holiday for the ceremony: The government declared Tuesday 1 September a public holiday for the swearing-in of President Hakainde Hichilema and Vice-President Mutale Nalumango. The ceremony was held at the National Heroes Stadium in Lusaka. —The margin: The Electoral Commission of Zambia declared Hichilema re-elected on 18 August with 60.49% of the vote. Brian Mundubile, who stood for the NRPUP as the Tonse Pamodzi alliance candidate took 37.87%. —Petition unresolved: The Secretary to the Cabinet said the seven-day window for filing an election petition had expired, clearing the way for the inauguration. The Constitutional Court confirmed it had received no challenge. —Why that is contested: The opposition has said it was unable to lodge a challenge after authorities sealed off the courts on the final filing day, citing security. No petition was therefore ever heard. —The economic record he is running on: The government points to inflation falling from about 24% at his 2021 inauguration to 6.5% in June 2026. It also cites roughly US$12bn of fresh mining investment. —Debt was the first-term project: Hichilema’s first term was dominated by restructuring Zambia’s defaulted external debt, alongside energy shortages and weak investor confidence. That work framed the country’s return to market access. —The unresolved case: Mundubile was charged with treason in late August, after surrendering to police following two weeks in hiding. Eleven opposition officials were detained in a raid on election night.

A Hichilema second term formally began on 1 September, when Zambia swore in the president and Vice-President Mutale Nalumango at Lusaka’s National Heroes Stadium. He returns with 60.49% of the vote and, unusually, with an emailed election petition still sitting before the Constitutional Court.

What happened on the day

The government declared 1 September a public holiday so Zambians could watch the ceremony, which was held at the National Heroes Stadium in Lusaka. It marks the start of a second five-year term.

Preparations were confirmed in the days before by the Zambian press, which reported the venue ready and the schedule fixed. Hichilema was declared re-elected by the Electoral Commission of Zambia on 18 August.

The margin was wide. He took 60.49% against 37.87% for Brian Mundubile of the Tonse Pamodzi alliance.

The petition nobody could file

Zambian law gives seven days for an election petition. The Secretary to the Cabinet confirmed that the window had expired and that the swearing-in would go ahead.

The Constitutional Court said it had received no challenge to the result. On the face of it, that is a clean legal path to inauguration.

The opposition’s account is different. It has said it could not lodge a petition because authorities sealed off the courts on the final filing day, citing security concerns, so no challenge was ever heard on its merits.

Both statements can be true at once, and that is the difficulty. The absence of a petition is not by itself evidence that the result was uncontested.

The economy behind the Hichilema second term

The government’s own account of the first term rests on stabilisation. It points to inflation falling from about 24% at the 2021 inauguration to 6.5% in June 2026, and to roughly US$12bn of fresh mining investment.

Debt was the defining work. Zambia defaulted in 2020 and spent most of the first term negotiating a restructuring with official and private creditors, a process that shaped everything from the exchange rate to the budget.

Energy shortages and weak investor confidence ran alongside it. Both are the kind of problem that eases slowly and returns quickly.

Copper is the whole argument

Zambia is Africa’s second-largest copper producer, and the metal is the country’s principal source of foreign exchange. The investment figure the government cites is essentially a copper figure.

That gives the second term a clear commercial test. Whether the announced capital converts into produced tonnes, and on what terms for the treasury, is the question investors will judge.

It also ties Zambia directly into the wider contest over the minerals needed for the energy transition. The Copperbelt is one of the places where that competition is most visible.

The politics that did not go away

Mundubile was charged with treason in late August, after two weeks in hiding and a surrender to police. Eleven opposition officials were detained in a raid on election night.

Those cases will run into the new term. They are the reason the inauguration reads differently at home than it does in a press release.

For a government that has built its external credibility on predictability, the handling of the opposition is now part of the risk picture. Creditors and miners tend to price political stability alongside geology.

What to watch in the new term

The first marker is the treason case and how it is conducted. The second is whether the mining investment pipeline produces commissioned capacity rather than announcements.

The third is fiscal. Restructuring bought Zambia room, and the question is whether the second term uses it for capital spending or for consumption.

None of this is a prediction. It is simply the short list of things that will tell readers, over the next year, which version of the first term the second one intends to continue.

Frequently Asked Questions

When did Hichilema’s second term begin? He was sworn in on 1 September 2026 at the National Heroes Stadium in Lusaka, alongside Vice-President Mutale Nalumango. The government declared the day a public holiday. What was the election result? The Electoral Commission of Zambia declared Hichilema re-elected on 18 August with 60.49% of the vote. Brian Mundubile of the Tonse Pamodzi alliance took 37.87%. Was the result challenged in court? None was filed by the deadline, and the opposition says it could not lodge one because the courts were sealed off on the final filing day. The Chief Justice then received a petition by email on 25 August and referred it to the Constitutional Court, which has not ruled. What does the government claim for the first term? It points to inflation falling from about 24% in 2021 to 6.5% in June 2026, and to roughly US$12bn of fresh mining investment. Debt restructuring was the defining task. What happened to the main opposition candidate? Mundubile was charged with treason in late August after surrendering to police following two weeks in hiding. Eleven opposition officials were detained on election night.

World.title: Ghana’s Gold Board Promises US$1.4 Billion of Dollars in September
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

GHANA · MINERALS

Key Facts —The September target: GoldBod says it will generate US$1.4bn of foreign exchange during September 2026. US$700m is earmarked for commercial banks and up to US$700m for the Bank of Ghana. —What August delivered: The board reported total earnings of US$1.315bn in August, the first month under the updated financing model. Of that, US$668.21m went to commercial banks and US$646.59m to the central bank. —The policy behind it: The Ghana Accelerated National Reserve Accumulation Policy, known as GANRAP, was formally implemented on 3 August 2026 after Cabinet and parliamentary approval. It sets a collaborative financing model for artisanal and small-scale mining. —How the money reaches the market: Bank allocations were made through spot sales and funded forward arrangements intended to ease exchange-rate pressure. The rest was transferred to build state reserves. —A refining rule starts the same week: From 1 September, artisanal and small-scale gold must be refined in Ghana before it can be exported. GoldBod has said non-compliance could bring suspension or revocation of licences. —The refining capacity question: Ghana has four licensed gold refineries, and GoldBod has announced supply contracts with only two of them. No Ghanaian refinery sits on the London Bullion Market Association’s Good Delivery List. —A projection, not an outturn: The September number is a target published by GoldBod itself, and the August figure is the board’s own reported performance. No independent audit of either was cited in the statement.

Ghana gold foreign exchange earnings are targeted at US$1.4bn for September 2026, with US$700m destined for commercial banks and up to US$700m for the Bank of Ghana. The Ghana Gold Board published the figure on 31 August, alongside a reported US$1.315bn for August.

What the Ghana gold foreign exchange plan says

The statement came from GoldBod’s Finance and Trading Directorate and was carried by Ghanaian outlets including Rainbow Radio and The Herald on 31 August. It sets out a split between market liquidity and reserve accumulation.

Half the projected September flow is intended to reach commercial banks to support stability in the foreign-exchange market. The remainder is to go to the central bank to build reserves.

The board framed the arrangement as a statutory mandate to generate foreign exchange for the country. It said it would continue to work transparently with stakeholders.

Where GANRAP came from

The Ghana Accelerated National Reserve Accumulation Policy took formal effect on 3 August 2026, after approval by Cabinet and Parliament. It is the framework under which the August and September numbers are being reported.

GoldBod says it ran structured consultations with the Ministry of Finance, the Bank of Ghana, commercial banks and primary market participants before implementation. The stated purpose is a collaborative financing model for artisanal and small-scale mining.

That focus matters because Ghana’s small-scale sector supplies a large share of the gold the state buys. Financing it directly is how the board intends to keep volumes coming.

The August numbers, read carefully

GoldBod reported US$1.315bn of foreign exchange earnings for August, its first full month under the updated model. US$668.21m was injected into the banking sector through spot sales and funded forward arrangements.

A further US$646.59m was transferred to the central bank for reserve accumulation. The September target would represent a modest increase on that base.

These are the board’s own figures, published in its own statement. No external verification was cited, and the release did not give a cedi equivalent for the dollar amounts.

The refining rule that starts alongside it

From 1 September, GoldBod requires gold from artisanal and small-scale mining to be refined inside Ghana before export. The board has said non-compliance could lead to the suspension or revocation of licences.

The policy intent is to keep more of the margin at home, which is the same logic driving resource-nationalist moves elsewhere on the continent. The obstacle is capacity.

Ghana has four licensed refineries and GoldBod has announced supply contracts with two. No Ghanaian refinery is currently on the London Bullion Market Association’s Good Delivery List, which is the benchmark most international buyers rely on.

Why this matters beyond Accra

Gold has become the central pillar of Ghana’s external accounts, and the reserve strategy built on it has been credited with much of the cedi’s recent strength. State gold buying has also been expensive: the International Monetary Fund put losses on the earlier purchase programme at more than US$1.7bn.

That history is the reason to read a projection as a projection. The August figure is the first data point under the new framework, and one month is not a trend.

For investors, the number to watch is not the target but the realised split between banks and reserves over the coming quarter. If the bank allocation slips while the reserve share holds, the pressure will show up in the street rate before it shows up in the statement.

What to watch next

The first test is whether the September outturn lands near US$1.4bn, and whether GoldBod publishes it with the same granularity. The second is whether refinery supply contracts widen beyond two of the four licensed plants.

Accreditation is the third. Without a Good Delivery listing, Ghanaian refined output faces a narrower set of buyers than the policy assumes.

None of this is investment advice, and official figures on programmes of this kind are frequently revised. Readers should treat the published targets as statements of intent from the issuing body.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much foreign exchange does GoldBod expect in September 2026? GoldBod says it will generate US$1.4bn during September. US$700m is earmarked for commercial banks and up to US$700m for the Bank of Ghana. What did GoldBod report for August 2026? Total earnings of US$1.315bn. Of that, US$668.21m went to commercial banks through spot sales and funded forwards, and US$646.59m to the central bank. What is GANRAP? The Ghana Accelerated National Reserve Accumulation Policy, formally implemented on 3 August 2026 after Cabinet and parliamentary approval. It sets the financing model behind these flows. What changed for gold exporters on 1 September? Gold from artisanal and small-scale mining must now be refined inside Ghana before export. GoldBod has said non-compliance could bring suspension or revocation of licences. Can Ghana’s refineries handle the volume? Ghana has four licensed refineries and GoldBod has announced supply contracts with only two. No Ghanaian refinery is on the London Bullion Market Association’s Good Delivery List.

World.title: Brazil and South Africa Talk Trade as US Tariffs Push Them Together
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

SOUTH AFRICA · GEOPOLITICS

Key Facts —A US$2bn relationship: Bilateral trade between the two countries reached about US$2bn in 2025. Brazil is now South Africa’s largest trading partner in Latin America and its second-largest in the Americas, according to Business Day. —Tariffs did the pushing: South Africa faced a 30% United States tariff on many exports from August 2025, the highest rate on the continent, before a partial reversal this year. Brazil was hit with 25% on most imports from July 2026. —What they agreed to work on: The eighth South Africa-Brazil Joint Commission named trade, critical minerals, manufacturing and technology as the ground for deeper co-operation. It met in Pretoria, co-chaired by ministers Ronald Lamola and Mauro Vieira. —The quarrels stayed outside: South Africa accuses Brazil of dumping frozen poultry, and its cane growers list Brazil among the subsidised-sugar exporters undercutting them. Officials told Business Day those disputes were not on the table. —The deficit is wide: South Africa exported R5.2bn to Brazil in 2025 and imported R27.3bn, on figures published by Business Leadership South Africa. Trade currently runs under the SACU-Mercosur preferential agreement. —A missing piece of homework: No serious modelling of the bilateral supply response has been published, BLSA chief executive Busi Mavuso wrote on 31 August. She also noted the talks were led by the foreign ministry rather than the trade department. —Minerals are the prize: Lamola said demand for the minerals needed for the energy transition was likely to increase fourfold by 2040. Both governments say they want more processing done at home.

A closer Brazil South Africa trade relationship is being negotiated around a shared problem: American tariffs on both economies. Meeting in Pretoria, the two governments named trade, critical minerals, manufacturing and technology as the ground for deeper work, and quietly left their poultry and sugar disputes for another day.
