World.title: Burnham promised hope. Reality is already getting in the way
World.content:
He pledged to shake up England’s privatized water sector as part of a “10-year plan” this fall. He promised to impose his predecessor Keir Starmer’s social media ban on under-16s “at pace.” He repeated his long-held vows to radically reform the social care system, move powers and officials out of Whitehall, release public land for a wave of house-building and “end” rough sleeping — while still bringing down the welfare bill. “Working together to build a new sense of optimism around the country, we can make this next decade better than the last,” he said.

The parliamentary chamber began to empty, MPs turning to other duties and their bladders, as the hardiest stayed behind in the hope they would extract yet another commitment from the prime minister.

As the session wore on, Burnham hinted he could one day scrap England’s system of local taxation, which is based on property valuations from 1991. In the third hour he even promised to save Jodrell Bank, a locally-beloved cluster of deep space radio telescopes near Manchester that has had its funding cut.

The new prime minister was not offering a free-for-all and, like any minister, swerved more invitations to commit policy than he accepted. He insisted he will make tough choices.

Yet he is also enjoying a practical by-effect of being a new leader: He hasn’t yet had to disappoint all the people he will eventually disappoint.

Rhetoric vs. reality

The 125 questions he took showed that the difficulties and trade-offs that come with power are already coming into view.

World.title: Pressure mounts on Europe as Trump deals push pharma to the US
World.content:
Industry leaders in Europe warn that if the U.S. continues to sign more deals with companies — designed to drive down prices for American citizens while boosting U.S. investments — European patients will feel the effects.

Since the most-favored nation policy will see Washington copy some EU countries’ prices, companies are opting not to launch new drugs in Europe to maintain higher prices in the U.S. where they can make bigger profits. In addition, companies are increasingly choosing America for research and manufacturing.

“Companies may hesitate to launch in Europe or in Japan or Canada if they think that the price in Europe or Japan or Canada will be lower than the price they could obtain in the U.S.,” Adrian van den Hoven, director general of Medicines for Europe, told POLITICO. “That's the risk for Europe going forward.” Medicines for Europe represents the generics industry, which largely makes cheaper off-patent medicines. Two large generics firms that also make branded drugs were included in the nine new deals.

Meanwhile, Europe’s current biggest offering to entice industry to stay local — a proposed patent extension for certain biotech drugs — is too little too late, some argue. Industry says the patent extension comes with too many conditions and it won’t come into effect in time to stop the sector from pivoting more to America where market conditions are more favorable.

The patent extension and other industry perks in the proposed Biotech Act are a step in the right direction, said Alexander Natz, secretary general of the European Confederation of Pharmaceutical Entrepreneurs. But “it’s probably too late if we wait for the Biotech Act” to take effect, likely in a couple of years, he said.

Capturing more companies

The latest deals mark a shift away from the previous 17 deals with multi-billion dollar big pharmaceutical companies and include a mix from small specialist firms with only a handful of licensed drugs to vast generic drugmakers.

World.title: Germany blames Russia for drone incursion, announces retaliatory measures
World.content:
The attempted attack in August involved three drones carrying explosive material spotted at or near the Leipzig-Halle Airport in eastern Germany, including one drone that was found near a Ukrainian Antonov plane used to transport munitions.

Standing alongside Wadephul, German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said the German government determined Russia is responsible even as investigations remain ongoing.

“The attack involved tools such as the drone configuration, various components, explosives and cyber technology that we recognize from other Russian hybrid operations and its war against Ukraine,” Dobrindt said.

Wadephul announced a series of domestic countermeasures, including the closure of Russia’s Bonn consulate on September 18, stricter entry controls for Russian nationals and the termination of the agreement governing the Russian House in central Berlin — a cultural institution suspected of serving as a hub for espionage operations and whose Russian operator is under EU sanctions.

Germany will also propose new EU sanctions targeting Russian individuals connected to hybrid attacks, while pushing to increase measures targeting Russia’s shadow fleet, Wadephul said. A senior German government official also said Berlin would advocate that the EU reduce the number of 90-day tourist visas issued to Russian citizens and restrict the freedom of movement of Russian diplomats.

The announcement comes as EU foreign ministers are set to meet in Ireland on Tuesday night and Wednesday. “The matter, including additional sanctions, will be prepared by Foreign Ministers at their upcoming meeting,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen wrote on social media after the German announcement.

World.title: Leuven mayor bans Europa League match against Israeli team
World.content:
Violence and hooliganism are not uncommon at European-level football matches, nor are occasional orders that games should take place in neutral venues, behind closed doors or with certain fans banned from attending for safety reasons.

The war in Gaza, though, has politicized such decisions as they relate to Israeli clubs, at the same time as exacerbating tensions around the visits of Israeli fans to some parts of Europe.

In Amsterdam in November 2024, supporters of Israeli club Maccabi Tel Aviv were involved in violence across the city before and after a match with Ajax, with dozens of arrests and several people hospitalized.

Keeping boisterous groups of opposing teams’ football fans away from each other and under control is already a challenge for police, and adding the potential for political, antisemitic and racist provocation into the mix stretches their ability to keep the peace.

“We have full confidence in the Belgian security authorities and their ability to ensure that a football match can take place safely and securely,” said the Israeli embassy in Brussels. “Should assistance be required, Israel would be happy to provide it.”

This is not the first time Belgian authorities have blocked a match involving an Israeli team on security grounds. In 2024, Brussels refused to host Belgium’s Nations League game against Israel, citing the risk of major demonstrations and counter-demonstrations. The game was eventually moved to Debrecen, Hungary, and played behind closed doors. Ridouani had also previously refused to allow both the Belgian women’s and men’s national teams to play Israel at Leuven’s Den Dreef stadium.

World.title: Les datacenters énergivores se développent en Europe, la résistance aussi
World.content:
Une résistance croissante pourrait toutefois venir contrecarrer les ambitions de l’entreprise. Un groupe d’opposants locaux — inquiets de la consommation énergétique vorace du centre de données et méfiants face à la mainmise d’un mastodonte américain de la tech — se bat pour empêcher son extension.

“Nous voulons vraiment leur donner du fil à retordre”, assume Harald Müllner, un expert en informatique originaire de Linz, une ville voisine, et qui a cofondé un collectif local regroupant des scientifiques, des artistes et des militants opposés au centre de données. “Ils doivent comprendre que ça ne convient pas à la population.”

Leurs manifestations et leurs pétitions contre les projets de Google reflètent une tendance observée de l’autre côté de l’Atlantique, où les démocrates surfent sur une vague croissante de rejet à l’égard des centres de données à l’approche des élections de mi-mandat américaines de cette année. Le président Donald Trump, quant à lui, a pris le parti des Big Tech, affirmant lundi dans un post sur son réseau social que les communautés s’opposant aux datacenters “finiront par être arriérées et pauvres”.

En Europe, des militants s’attaquent à des projets en France, tandis qu’en Italie, les habitants manifestent contre certains projets. En Irlande, où les centres de données consomment déjà un cinquième de l’électricité totale, les opposants ont tenté — sans succès — d’en faire bloquer la construction devant les tribunaux.

Mais jusqu’à présent, les inquiétudes suscitées par les centres de données en Europe se sont heurtées à la crainte des gouvernements de voir le continent prendre du retard par rapport aux Etats-Unis et à la Chine dans la course à l’intelligence artificielle.

“Nous ne pouvons pas réclamer une plus grande souveraineté européenne en matière d’IA, tout en dressant sans cesse de nouveaux obstacles qui entravent l’infrastructure même sur laquelle elle repose”, a déclaré Elisabeth Zehetner, secrétaire d’Etat autrichienne à l’Energie, à propos des demandes visant à renforcer la réglementation des centres de données de grande envergure, comme celui de Kronstorf.

World.title: What's behind France's plan to survey school children on sexual violence?
World.content:
Ringing school bells marked the start of the new year academic year in France on Tuesday. This year, the government has introduced a string of unprecedented measures, including a ban on mobile phones in primary and secondary schools, as well as new steps to tackle sexual violence.

 

For the first time, France's annual school questionnaire on bullying — which has been handed out to pupils since 2023 — will include questions on sexual violence. Pupils will be able to choose whether or not to they wish to remain anonymous in this questionnaire, which will be distributed in November.

Speaking to French broadcaster BFMTV on 25 August, France's education minister Édouard Geffray, said that around 10 million pupils, ranging from primary to secondary school, would complete the form, designed "with school staff, parents' associations and a committee of experts, including child psychiatrists". According to the minister, the results could be "seismic".

Teachers will collect the forms first. If any responses raise concerns, school leaders are then expected to step in, either by reporting the case to the relevant regional education authority or, in more serious situations, referring it to the justice system.

Reaction to alarming figures

This initiative comes in the wake of numerous child sexual violence scandals in France, particularly in supervised childcare services. In Paris alone, there are 203 criminal investigations underway into alleged acts of violence, including sexual violence, in schools and in after-school settings, according to the latest official figures dated 26 August.

Despite these alarming figures, schools are still the main place where child sexual abuse reports are filed, with on average 80,000 reports a year, according to France's education minister.

Estimates made in 2023 by the CIIVISE (the Independent Commission on Incest and Sexual Violence against Children) assessed that around 160,000 children are victims of sexual violence every year in France, with 77% of this abuse occurring in a family environment. That amounts to one child being raped or sexually assaulted every three minutes.

Parents' doubts and fears about initiative

According to France's education minister, questions about sexual violence will be tailored to pupils' ages. Despite this, parents have mixed feelings.

For Samuel Bougnat, a father of a three-year-old, the measure is a step in the right direction, "I think school has a role to play in providing support and in reporting possible violence, because school should be a sanctuary, a place where children can feel confident enough to talk about things that may be happening at home"."

Another father of two young children who preferred to remain anonymous also backed the measure, "personally, I think it is pragmatic given that all children are supposed to go through school at some point; so if there is one place where we can spot things that are problematic and dangerous for children, it is there."

"As a parent, I will be paying close attention to how these forms are rolled out through, especially to ensure that they are appropriate for younger children", he added.

Others, like Caroline Varas, who has a four-and-a-half-year-old son, are less convinced. "I am not entirely sure that school should be responsible for this. I think it should be collaborative work: with independent parents' associations, the local council and the school."

"If it is only the school dealing with it, they will cover themselves, protect themselves. I found out afterwards that there had been violence – not sexual violence, but violence – in my child's school. There is a missing intermediary between the school and parents", she added.

Child protection organisations react with caution

Laura Morin-Baudet, who heads L'Enfant Bleu, a Paris-based non-profit that fights child abuse, says she "welcomes" the fact that the education ministry is taking up the issue of child sexual violence, but also voiced doubts about the practical side of things.

"It all depends on the conditions children answer these questions in. If the child feels comfortable, has the feeling that their friend sitting next to them cannot necessarily see their answers, then perhaps, indeed, they will end up saying something. But on the other hand, if they have the slightest doubt, if they are afraid, if they are unsure where these documents will go, we unfortunately know that they will not necessarily confide."

For Laura Morin-Baudet, alongside any such questionnaires, it is still key to carry out prevention and raise awareness in schools.

"We know just how poorly trained teachers and childcare professionals are in this area. Our organisation regularly receives calls from professionals who tell us: 'I have observed this and that, what can I do, how should I act?' So we know there is that need."

"Sometimes signs can manifest themselves through words, but it can also be through behaviour. It may be a child who suddenly becomes very agitated when they were not before, or conversely a child who withdraws completely. And that is where an adult's gaze can interpret things and build up relationship of trust."

Teachers' unions welcome initiative but question format

According to Jean-Rémi Girard, president of the National Union of Lycées and Collèges, schools and higher education (SNALC), "the vast majority" of teachers support the initiative.

"For us, the most important thing is that school should be a safe place for our pupils and, in fact, for everyone. That does not mean we are the ones who will do the work of the justice system, quite clearly. But we are nonetheless able to talk to pupils, to go and see a little what is happening, to take an interest in children's living conditions and to gather information so that we can then pass the baton to the police and the justice system."

"Sometimes very young children are not aware of how serious what has happened to them is. With the form, very simple questions will allow us not to make a diagnosis, but at least to identify a first point that needs attention."

For her part, Béatrice Laurent, secretary of the education union UNSA Éducation, speaks of a "dilemma".

"We cannot be against a programme that allows children to report violence they may have suffered. But the immediate question is whether a written questionnaire is the right format."

"Our concern also relates to how these questionnaires will be processed. Is there enough staff in the education system to deal with the reports that children are going to make? It would be truly tragic for children to disclose what has happened to them and for nothing to happen afterwards."

France's education ministry did not respond to Euronews' questions about the specific details of the questionnaire, or about how the justice system would intervene if the results turned out to be "seismic", as the country's minister has suggested.

The ministry said that work to prepare the questionnaire is underway and that it was therefore premature to provide more precise answers.

World.title: Zelenskyy warns ‘Russian airspace will effectively be closing’
World.content:
Following almost a week of relentless Russian attacks on Kyiv and non-stop air raid alerts, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy issued a stark warning to international airlines and insurers: "Russian airspace will effectively be closing."

 

In his evening address on 1 September, Zelenskyy said the consequences of the war Moscow launched more than four years ago could no longer be confined to Ukrainian territory and that Kyiv's ever-growing drone operations would soon render Russian airspace unsafe.

“It was from Russia that the first missiles and the first drones came, and they crossed our country’s border from Russian airspace,” Zelenskyy said. “This escalation cannot and will not remain confined to Ukrainian territory.”

His warning was directed not only at Moscow but at airlines, insurers and foreign governments whose carriers continue to fly through Russian airspace and serve airports in Moscow, St Petersburg and other major cities.

“Today, we want to warn every airline that uses Russian airspace, every insurer, and everyone who still uses Russia’s key airports: Russian airspace is becoming completely unsafe,” he said.

Zelenskyy stressed that Ukraine would not threaten civilian aircraft, but the sheer scale of Ukrainian UAV activity would have to be taken into account.

“Ukraine does not threaten civilian aviation as such - not a single civilian aircraft,” he said. “There will simply be drones in Russia’s skies on a scale that has to be taken into account.”

“Russian airspace will effectively be closing — the war started by Russia is closing its skies," he added.

Ukraine’s airspace has been closed to civilian aviation since 24 February 2022, when Russia launched its full-scale invasion.

Russian civilian aviation, by contrast, has continued operating throughout the war, despite increasingly frequent disruptions and temporary airport closures during Ukrainian drone attacks.

Kyiv’s long-range operations have targeted military facilities and infrastructure supporting Moscow’s war effort, including airfields, missile units, oil refineries and other energy facilities.

Zelenskyy stressed that that would not change, saying Ukraine did not want innocent lives to be lost.

“We are warning our partners: the safe days in Russia’s skies are over,” he said, while calling on foreign ambassadors in both Kyiv and Moscow to relay the message to their governments.

Ukraine’s foreign ministry and other government agencies would provide international organisations with full information about the dangers in Russian airspace, he added.

Almost a week of attacks on Kyiv

Zelenskyy’s warning comes after almost a week of sustained Russian attacks on Ukrainian cities, with Moscow increasingly relying on jet-powered drones launched in repeated waves both day and night.

Kyiv and its surrounding region have been among the main targets, with repeated air-raid alerts disrupting transport, businesses and daily life across the capital.

The attacks point to a shift in Russian tactics. Rather than concentrating its largest attacks in massive overnight barrages of drones and missiles, Moscow has increasingly sent smaller waves of drones at intervals throughout the day, prolonging air-raid alerts and placing sustained pressure on Ukrainian air defences.

Officials in Kyiv said Russia was increasingly deploying jet-powered drones alongside ballistic missiles, presenting Ukrainian defences with a particularly difficult challenge.

Zelenskyy’s message is now that Russia can no longer expect the air war it has waged over Ukraine to stop at its own border.

“Drone-infested skies are no place for civilian aviation," he said.

World.title: Spanish government approves €309 million aid package for Ceuta amid migrant crisis
World.content:
The migrant crisis in Ceuta continues to dominate Spain's political agenda.

 

The Council of Ministers on Tuesday approved an extraordinary funding package worth €309 million for the autonomous city, aimed at safeguarding jobs, supporting businesses, strengthening security and ensuring public services.

Government spokesperson Elma Saiz presented the measures alongside First Vice-President Carlos Cuerpo and Territorial Policy Minister Ángel Víctor Torres. The announcement came on the eve of a demonstration in the city that has exposed divisions in the PSOE and prompted Podemos to call a separate anti-racism rally.

The package, Cuerpo explained, amounts to around 16% of the city's GDP over the four remaining months of 2026.

The money is divided into four areas: €21 million for healthcare, education, justice and water treatment; more than €90 million for defence and the national security forces; €118 million for humanitarian care of unaccompanied migrant minors; and €80 million in direct support for businesses, incentives for trade and tax cuts.

Cuerpo, who also serves as Economy Minister, said the aid package represents a "shock response" designed to meet the demands of social organisations and the city government.

He said that the main aim of the decree was "to give confidence" to both companies and workers.

Cuerpo also stressed that, before the migration crisis, Ceuta was going through a "period of economic dynamism" that had helped to correct some of the "structural deficits" the city had struggled with for decades.

Direct aid for businesses and the self-employed

Of the €80 million allocated for businesses, €36.6 million is earmarked for direct support: €5,000 per self-employed worker and between €10,000 and €150,000 per company, depending on turnover.

Applications can be submitted from Monday 14 via the Tax Agency website, with the first payments aiming to arrive in early October.

The government has estimated that the measure will benefit 2,600 self-employed workers and 1,400 companies. This is supplemented by €14 million in consumer and tourism vouchers, €1 million for the Plan Ceuta Exporta, and another €1 million to promote the city as an international tourist destination.

The package also includes permanent measures: Corporation Tax relief rises from 50% to 60% for companies in Ceuta and Melilla that maintain their activity and jobs, alongside improvements to personal income tax (IRPF) for the self-employed, totalling €12 million.

Employers' Social Security contributions are to be subsidised from 50% to 75% for permanent contracts linked to training, at a cost of €12.2 million over four months.

The government will also set up an ICO-backed loan guarantee scheme worth up to €50 million, introduce exemptions for companies that make use of the job retention scheme (ERTE) and provide an extraordinary benefit for self-employed workers who are forced to stop working.

The president of the Ceuta, Juan Jesús Vivas, warned of the seriousness of the situation a month ago, when the Government approved a first package of €168 million euros for the territory.

Vivas reiterated this in a new text, published by PP leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo, in which he denounced an "attack on its territorial integrity" and described a city "overwhelmed and on the brink of collapse."

Vivas calls for Spanish unity on Ceuta Day

Vivas has also addressed Spaniards across the country in a message marking Ceuta Day, which is celebrated on 2 September, amid the fallout from the migrant crisis.

In his letter, Vivas called for national unity and solidarity and thanked people for the support shown to Ceuta in recent weeks.

"Ceuta has lived through its toughest month this August," he added in the text, in which he described recent events as "an unprecedented outrage" against the territory.

But whatever happens, he insisted that the city would "never" be abandoned.

A Ceuta Day overshadowed by crisis

Vivas also acknowledged that this year's 2 September celebrations would be different from those of previous years.

However, in his view, the situation the city is facing has made this day "particularly significant" and has presented an opportunity to strengthen ties and unity among Spaniards.

The president also referred to the rallies scheduled for 8 pm in municipalities across Spain following a call by the Spanish Federation of Municipalities and Provinces (FEMP).

He stressed that these demonstrations were not intended to serve partisan interests and are "not marked by political colours or ideologies."

Their purpose, he said, was to send a message of unity and support to Ceuta.

Migrants who crossed from Morocco into Spain return to a beach after being expelled from the area the previous day, as Spanish police escort them in the Spanish exclave. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved.

Another of the key messages in the letter is that the defence of Ceuta goes far beyond the territory itself.

"The cause is not exclusively Ceuta's; it is the cause of all Spain," he said, linking the defence of the city to protecting territorial integrity and democratic values.

"We have never stopped feeling you at our side," Vivas continued, while also expressing gratitude for the support shown towards the city during "its most difficult moment."

He added that such displays had been "a source of encouragement and hope" and had helped send Ceutans a clear message: "We are not alone".

World.title: US launches new strikes in southern Iran, Tehran responds with attacks across region
World.content:
The US military said it launched waves of sustained attacks on Iranian Revolutionary Guards (IRGC) targets along the southern Iranian coast on Tuesday, leading to Tehran launching missile and drone strikes on "military installations" in Jordan, Bahrain and Kuwait, while threatening a wider response.

 

Tehran's semi-official media said its troops fired missiles and drones in response to US strikes, and explosions were reported over the southern Jordanian city of Aqaba while sirens sounded in Mafraq.

Jordan's Armed Forces said in a statement that they intercepted 13 ballistic missiles that entered the kingdom's airspace, while Kuwait's army issued emergency alerts that it is intercepting an "Iranian aggression".

The IRGC has issued a statement via Iranian media saying that the strikes had "tightened the grip on the Strait of Hormuz" and that the US would "regret" its actions.

Iranian state media claimed that the US first bombed civilian sites along Iran’s southern coast and hit a civilian airport, with explosions heard in the areas of Bandar Abbas, Sirik, Qeshm island, Asaluyeh, Lavan, Jask, Jiroft and other locations.

Tehran claimed that at least four people, including a child, were killed and several wounded when a US strike hit a home where a wedding ceremony was being held in Kuhestak in southern Iran.

Iran’s Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei threatened with "unforgettable lessons for the American enemy” in a post on X.

US Central Command (CENTCOM) said the strikes followed "recent attempted attacks by the IRGC against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and against American service members deployed to the region."

In a post on his Truth Social platform, US President Donald Trump warned Tehran that if it retaliates for what he called "this very justified attack," Iran will "be hit again at a much harder and higher level."

Trump told Fox News on Tuesday that it notified its Gulf allies before the strikes and that they focused heavily on efforts to undermine radar installations undergoing repairs that had been decimated by earlier US-Israel strikes in the six-month war.

Trump, in a phone call with the network, said the US military had been monitoring Iran’s efforts to rebuild radar systems and waited until the work was almost completed before carrying out the strikes.

Earlier Tuesday, Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian said his country was ready to return to a ceasefire agreement brokered with the US in June if Washington was willing to abide by the terms.

World.title: Ryanair's Boeing 737 stairs tied to hundreds of passenger falls, study says
World.content:
Ryanair's Boeing 737 hides a hazard just outside the cabin door: its retractable onboard stairs.

 

Passengers who have used them have faced a significantly higher risk of falling than those using stairs provided by airports. That is the conclusion of a study by Italy's National Agency for Flight Safety (ANSV), published in August 2026.

The study analysed falls reported in Italy during boarding and disembarkation between 2023 and 2025. Of 104 incidents, 85 involved passengers who used the forward integrated stairs of Boeing 737 aircraft, accounting for 82% of cases, according to Corriere della Sera.

The scale of the figures is even clearer when set against total passenger numbers. Over the same period the Irish airline carried around 27% of all passengers in Italy. The other carriers, which make up the remaining 73%, recorded 19 falls between them.

The trend is not confined to Italy. Since 2021 Ryanair has registered 489 falls on stairs, 360 of them, or 73%, on the Boeing 737's integrated stairway. According to ANSV, that is three times as many falls as those recorded on airport stairways.

To track and analyse the incidents, ANSV used the ECCAIRS system, the digital platform run by the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA). The system collects and analyses aviation safety data from EU countries.

Why the stairs are riskier

For disembarkation, airlines often hire mobile stairs from airports. Ryanair's Boeing 737 instead has the option of an integrated system that can be deployed while parked, allowing passengers to disembark without airport handlers. This cuts disembarkation times and ground-service costs.

The integrated stairway has 12 steps, about 61 centimetres wide and 20 centimetres high, with a tread depth of 25 centimetres and an inclination of 35 degrees.

ANSV's investigation found the dimensions "are at the limits for step height and steepness" compared with those used by airport operators, "who have lower steps and, usually, a less pronounced inclination, and platforms and treads that are considerably larger."

FILE - In this Sept. 12, 2018 file photo, a Ryanair plane parks at the airport in Weeze, Germany. FILE - In this Sept. 12, 2018 file photo, a Ryanair plane parks at the airport in Weeze, Germany.

It also notes that the first step of the stairway is asymmetrical for passengers on the way down because of the shape of the fuselage in relation to the step.

According to Ireland's air accident investigation unit (AAIU), EU regulations do not impose requirements on the size of integrated stairs because they are not deemed critical to flight operations.

ANSV's study began with three incidents in Genoa, Venice and Bologna, in which three people suffered "serious injuries".

In Genoa on 22 March 2025, one person was taken by ambulance to hospital after a fall that occurred "most likely due to the inattention of the passenger," according to ANSV's reports.

Two days later in Venice, another passenger suffered serious injuries after falling from the integrated stairs. According to staff, the passenger was carrying two suitcases and was not holding the handrail. In the Bologna incident, the passenger also fell while carrying two bags.

After these incidents, Ryanair updated its disembarkation protocol, and since 23 July cabin crew have been repeating the warning to use the handrail also in the language of the country of origin and destination.

The problem with the integrated stairs on the Boeing 737 had already been examined by the aviation safety agencies of Ireland and Spain (CIAIAC) after falls in 2021 in Dublin and in 2024 in Alicante.

Following those incidents, the Spanish agency urged Boeing to redesign the stairway, reducing its steepness and increasing the surface area of the steps. CIAIAC also called on Ryanair to abandon use of the integrated system and rely solely on stairs provided by airport operators.

No investigation carried out so far has concluded that the system is defective. ANSV has endorsed the Spanish recommendations to Boeing and Ryanair, while attributing the falls to human factors such as inattention and failure to use the handrail.

World.title: SCO challenges West as diverse group of nations pursues multipolar future
World.content:
The Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO), a diverse group aiming to balance the West’s global influence, has called for a more representative and fairer multipolar world order as its summit in Kyrgyzstan ended on Tuesday with a run of headlines.

 

The 25th gathering of the 10 members — China, India, Iran, Pakistan, Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan — brought together regional leaders as “dialogue partners” from Central Asia, the Caspian region, the Middle East and wider Asia in a broad forum of meetings to address a rapidly changing multipolar world, even amid significant disagreements and often diverging interests.

The Iran war and Russia’s all-out invasion of Ukraine defined the summit’s focus, with disruptions in global supply lines and emerging alternatives through Central Asia and the Caspian, as well as the rapid geopolitical shockwaves and realignments they have generated.

In a surprise moment with global impact, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi told Russian President Vladimir Putin directly, on live television, to end his war against Ukraine.

"Every single day spent in war pushes humanity backwards, ” Modi said unexpectedly to a visibly tense Putin. “We need to move from endless war to the end of war, to the end of hostilities.”

“This is very important for all of humanity," Modi added.

"We have to move in that direction, which is also essential for the welfare of humanity. It is humanity’s call to resolve all issues peacefully as soon as possible," the Indian premier told the Russian president.

"This is India’s message — the message from the land of Gandhi, the land of Buddha: a message of peace, a message of humanity."

Putin did not reply to Modi, but in a speech later at the summit said that "today, 1 September, is the day World War II began."

"We must do everything to exclude from world practice any provocation of armed conflicts," Putin added. Russia’s war in Ukraine is now longer than World War II in duration.

Members of the SCO Plus meeting. Press service of Kyrgyzstan President

In another snub for the Kremlin, a bilateral meeting between Putin and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping produced no progress on a Siberian natural gas pipeline that Moscow urgently needs as the country’s infrastructure and economy reel from continuous Ukrainian strikes on key energy targets across Russia.

The Russian president however received the public gratitude of his Iranian counterpart Masoud Pezeshkian, who thanked Putin "for your positions at every stage.”

Putin said that Russia is providing Iran with assistance and “supplying the needed goods,” and that “Russia stands in solidarity with the people of Iran, who are defending their interests. He further said he "admires their courage and steadfastness” in their fight against the US and Israel.

"Today we are experiencing an erosion of the foundations upon which international order is built," Pezeshkian said.

"If such actions are met with no effective response from the international community, what state can be certain that its sovereignty and security will be protected in the future against the use of force?"

The Iranian delegation pushed for maximum results at the SCO summit, with Pezeshkian also meeting his Azerbaijani, Indian and Pakistani counterparts, while Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi met his counterparts from China, Pakistan, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan and Russia.

China and Turkey laud multilateralism

China, which sees the SCO as an alternative to Western-aligned organisations like the G7, has recently shown it wants to expand the organisation's scope and influence, while Russia and Iran joined the summit to build relations with non-Western partners and seek support and recognition.

In his speech at the summit, China’s Xi said the SCO should “foster an environment of universal security,” while criticising “hegemony, unilateralism, and protectionism” which run “counter to the tide of history.”

Xi further urged the SCO leaders and partners to “shoulder the responsibility of the times,” as multipolarity is an “irreversible trend” and that “dominance by just one or several countries, or bloc politics are not true multilateralism.”

Turkey, which holds partner status within the SCO, also seeks to use the platform to strengthen its position in the region, viewing its partnership in the organisation as part of a balanced foreign policy that maintains its traditional ties with the West through NATO while strengthening its influence in Eurasia.

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan told the summit that the SCO is “a rising star in every field” and that with its “3.5 billion people and $35 trillion in gross domestic product (it) is an indispensable element of a multipolar order."

Calling the SCO a “complement to the UN,” Erdoğan said the organisation “has a structure that aligns with our multidimensional foreign policy centred on regional ownership,” adding that “as Türkiye, we are taking responsibility for resolving conflicts around us through dialogue and diplomacy.”

Erdoğan highlighted one of the new thrusts of the SCO summit participants: alternative transport and energy corridors, as the war with Iran disrupted traditional avenues.

"We believe that the organisation can play a role not only in ensuring peace and stability, but also in establishing uninterrupted and secure transportation corridors, which are vital for the prosperity of our peoples, and in areas such as energy supply security," the Turkish president said.

Billions in Central Asia and Caucasus projects

The leaders of Central Asia and the South Caucasus pushed relentlessly during the summit to maximise the economic opportunities for their regions as the Iran war and wider Middle East disruptions place them at the forefront of new global trade and connectivity solutions.

Azerbaijan’s President Ilham Aliyev and Armenian Premier Nikol Pashinyan held a new round of their peace talks in Bishkek, with Aliyev saying “the South Caucasus is becoming a zone of peace.”

Pashinyan said transport corridors and regional connectivity are now developing toward the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP).

Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev told the summit that trade among SCO countries has reached $1 trillion and that much more remains to unlock the full potential of cooperation and resource use.

Uzbekistan's President Shavkat Mirziyoyev proposed establishing a bank for inter-regional projects, natural resource management, digital services and healthcare.

Mirziyoyev agreed with his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping to raise bilateral trade from $18 billion in 2025 to $30 billion in the coming years through a portfolio of joint investment projects and industrial cooperation.

"The existence of multiple centres of political influence is an important condition for advancing a political pluralism on the international stage," Tajikistan's President Emomali Rahmon said.

New security centre approved

Away from the diplomacy, the summit closed Kyrgyzstan's year as chair with a package of institutional decisions. Leaders signed the Bishkek Declaration and a protocol amending the SCO's Founding Charter, which Kyrgyz Foreign Minister Jeenbek Kulubaev said would create the basis for a more flexible bloc.

On security, members approved the rules for a Universal Centre for Countering Security Challenges based in Tashkent and an anti-drug centre in Dushanbe.

A unit to fight transnational organised crime will open in Bishkek under that centre, the first permanent SCO body on Kyrgyz soil.

Members also agreed to complete consultations "in the shortest possible time" on a long-discussed SCO development bank, with a view to signing its founding document, although they concluded no deal in Bishkek.

Leaders adopted further documents on artificial intelligence, climate, energy and information security, a declaration on nuclear safety, and a decision to develop cooperation with the African Union.

Kyrgyzstan said it held around 200 events during its chairmanship, more than 50 of them in the country itself, and marked the anniversary by naming a 4,050-metre peak in the Ala-Archa range "SCO Peak".

Pakistan now takes the chairmanship and will host the next summit in Islamabad.

World.title: Von der Leyen pledges response to Russian hybrid attacks ahead of Rutte meeting
World.content:
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she stands in "full solidarity" with Germany after officials in Berlin formally attributed a high-profile drone incident to Russia at a press conference on Monday.

 

Von der Leyen said she would use a meeting with NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte on Wednesday to discuss the matter, with additional sanctions to be prepared by foreign ministers at an upcoming meeting.

"We will keep the EU united despite these escalating and serious acts," she said in a statement posted on social media platform X on Monday.

"The German government has taken strong measures. And the message is clear: hybrid attacks will not go without a clear response."

The “short notice” bilateral was confirmed by European Commission Chief Spokesperson Paula Pinho on Tuesday, who said the meeting would also occur in the context of Europe and NATO strengthening defence cooperation.

A NATO official told Euronews the meeting would centre mostly on how to deepen coordination against hybrid threats.

In the wake of the news from Germany, Rutte posted a similar statement on X, stating that NATO stands in full solidarity with Berlin and "the evidence is clear" that Russia was to blame.

"NATO will continue to strengthen our ability to deter and defend all Allies against any threat—including malign actions like those seen in Leipzig and elsewhere across the Alliance," he said.

Von der Leyen's comments came after Germany's Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt announced on Monday that the "means to carry out the act" of a drone sabotage incident occurring in August is "known to use from other hybrid operations conducted by Russia and its war against Ukraine."

"The German government therefore concludes that Russia is responsible for the hybrid attack in Leipzig on 4 August," he said.

Germany has ordered the closure of the Russian consulate in Bonn, while the Russian House in Berlin will also be shut down. Foreign Affairs Minister Johann Wadephul said Russia’s actions form part of a “long series of attempts at destabilisation, disinformation, threats, sabotage and aggression directed at Europe."

The Russian embassy in Germany has issued a statement denying Berlin's claims and threatening "consequences" for the new sanctions.

On 4 August, a drone was found in the security zone of the Leipzig/Halle Airport near a Ukrainian cargo aircraft used to transport military supplies. Later, a second unmanned aerial vehicle also collided with an aircraft, with the plane unable to land.

Merz has previously vowed a response to the incidents, with action coordinated between EU and NATO allies.

The Russian Foreign Ministry also released a statement in late August condemning Europe for putting the blame on Moscow, noting that the accusations came before an investigation had been completed.

Kallas: Russia wants to scare us away from supporting Ukraine

Meanwhile, the EU’s foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said Russia was hitting Europe with increasing kinetic hybrid incidents aiming to “scare us away” from supporting Ukraine.

“They will not succeed,” she said, following a defence ministerial meeting in Wicklow, Ireland. Kallas said it was obvious the risks from these incidents were rising, and “clearly we are not doing enough to stop this.”

Irish Foreign Minister Helen McEntee, delivering the press conference alongside Kallas, said “support for Ukraine and pressure on Russia” remains central to Ireland’s six-month EU council presidency.

“We are now starting to see threats materialise as recently as the last 24 hours, where our colleagues in Romania and Latvia and Estonia, and of course Germany, have spoken of incursions into their own airspace, but also into their own land domain,” she said.

Romania and Estonia both reported drone incursions occurring on Tuesday. Several improvised explosive devices were found near coal-fired power plant in Germany also on Tuesday.

On his way into the talks, Estonian Defence Minister Hanno Pevkur said Europe must prepare itself for more Russian hybrid warfare incidents.

"They are testing always this threshold — where is this red line," he said, adding that Europe must keep a “very clear” head.

Elsewhere, French President Emmanuel Macron and Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni expressed their solidarity with Germany following the Leipzig incident.

"France stands in full solidarity with Germany and supports the adoption of new European sanctions against Russia," Macron wrote in a post on X on Tuesday.

Meloni added: "Attempts to intimidate us or to drive a wedge between Allies will not succeed: hybrid actions against any one of us are a matter of concern for all of us, and will be met with a united response."

World.title: Russia's Starlink copycat has failed so far but still threatens Ukraine
World.content:
None of the 16 satellites Russia launched on 19 July as part of its Rassvet programme, Moscow's attempt to build its own version of Starlink to guide the drones and missiles it has used against Ukraine for more than four years, have reached their planned orbit, according to the Institute for the Study of War (ISW), citing data from live satellite tracker N2YO.

 

Most of the satellites are sitting at altitudes of 300 to 400 kilometres, "well short of the intended 870-kilometer operational altitude for the Rassvet satellites," the report said.

At least two satellites appear to be heading for reentry into Earth's atmosphere.

Those flying at lower altitudes face greater atmospheric drag, burn through fuel faster and have shorter operational lifespans than those flying higher, meaning the affected satellites are unlikely to last as long as Russia had planned, even if they stabilise.

Satellite internet has become central to how both sides fight this war.

Ukraine's access to Starlink has let its forces fly reconnaissance and strike drones, coordinate artillery and stay connected in areas where Russian strikes have destroyed ground infrastructure.

The stakes involved are not abstract. Since Russia's full-scale invasion began in February 2022, the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine (HRMMU) has verified at least 16,874 civilians killed and 51,173 injured, as of the end of July.

HRMMU said in a report published on 13 August that July 2026 was the deadliest month for Ukrainian civilians since March 2022, with at least 437 killed and 2,610 injured, driven by a sharp rise in aerial bombardment and glide bomb attacks alongside continued long-range missile and drone strikes on cities far from the front line.

The mission's monthly reports also recorded successive records for short-range drone casualties near the front in April and May.

A functioning Rassvet constellation would extend Russia's ability to direct strikes over greater distances and with greater precision, which is why the programme's repeated failures matter well beyond the technical details.

A troubled launch record

Of the 16 Rassvet satellites launched on 24 March, 12 reached their intended altitude of 550 kilometres and remain there, according to the report.

Those satellites already give Russian forces two daily windows of connectivity with ground terminals, lasting up to 90 minutes in total over Ukraine.

Moscow appears to be rushing the programme to compensate for the loss of Starlink access. Ukraine's defence ministry said in early February that Starlink terminals being used illicitly by Russian forces had been deactivated after Kyiv and SpaceX moved to a "whitelist" system restricting the network to verified terminals.

"Russia may have been unprepared to accelerate constellation deployment at this pace and will likely face additional delays," the ISW report said.

But the threat has not gone away. ISW warned that the existing satellites "may allow Russian forces to conduct more precise strikes against Ukraine using remotely controlled unmanned systems" during the windows when connectivity does work — a reminder that Russia does not need a fully functioning constellation to keep inflicting harm, only a partially working one.

Falling short of scale

Bureau 1440, the Russian aerospace firm developing the satellites, has said it plans "dozens" more launches to deploy hundreds more satellites.

Serhii Beskrestnov, then an adviser to Ukraine's defence minister, said on 31 May that Russia would need at least 200 to 250 satellites in orbit to achieve continuous, stable connectivity, and that Moscow was unlikely to hit that target in the near term.

The report attributed Russia's bottleneck to its reliance on the Soyuz-2.1b, "a costly and scarce asset."

The country has carried out only six to eight Soyuz-2.1b launches across all space and commercial missions since 2022, a tempo that ISW said would allow for "a maximum of 128 Rassvet satellites per four years," and only if every launch succeeded and none were diverted elsewhere.

So far, only 37.5% of launched Rassvet satellites have reached a sustainable operational altitude.

Ukraine targets the supply chain

Ukrainian forces have also gone after the infrastructure behind the programme, in an apparent effort to slow a system that would extend Russia's ability to deliver deadly strikes in Ukraine.

Ukrainian forces struck the Progress Space Rocket Center, which produces Soyuz-type launch vehicles, overnight between 14 and 15 August.

A further strike was attempted against the Plesetsk Cosmodrome on 23 August, two days before Russia launched a Soyuz-2.1b vehicle reportedly carrying a GLONASS-K1 satellite, part of Russia's GPS alternative.

Both Rassvet batches were launched from Plesetsk, and the report concluded that Ukrainian strikes "threaten not only Russia's limited supply and production of launch vehicles but also the scarce launch infrastructure to place satellites into orbit" — infrastructure that, if it succeeds, will make Russia's war on Ukraine much more lethal.

World.title: What the SDF’s dissolution means for Syria’s Kurds and neighbouring Turkey
World.content:
Nearly a week after the Syrian Democratic Forces agreed to dissolve, the consequences are beginning to take shape for Syria's Kurds and neighbouring Turkey. As the former US-backed force is absorbed into the Syrian state, questions remain over what the country's Kurds have secured in return – from language and political rights to protections for women – and what the end of more than a decade of Kurdish-led autonomy means for Turkey's own conflict with Kurdish militants.

Advertising

SDF leader Mazloum Abdi announced the force's dissolution last Tuesday, saying its fighters would be integrated into the Syrian army.

At its height, the predominantly Kurdish force numbered around 100,000 fighters and controlled nearly a fifth of Syrian territory in the northeast, including major oil fields and fertile land. Under SDF rule, Kurds gained cultural and political rights denied to them under previous governments in Damascus.

“It means the end of Kurdish autonomy. After more than one decade of freedom, now they are under the control of Damascus,” said Syria expert Fabrice Balanche of Lyon University, who frequently visited the region.

Kurdish rights

“There are no guarantees for the Kurdish language because it's just a presidential decree: ‘let the Kurds use their language and teach Kurdish in schools,’ but there is nothing in the constitution,” Balanche said.

The decree, issued by President Ahmed al-Sharaa in January, recognised Kurdish as a national language and allowed it to be taught in schools in areas with significant Kurdish populations.

It also restored citizenship to Kurds who had been left stateless under measures stemming from a controversial 1962 census and made Nowruz, the Kurdish New Year festival, an official national holiday.

The Education Ministry followed up on 27 August with rules providing for three Kurdish-language classes a week in public and private schools in areas with significant Kurdish populations, with marks counting towards pupils' final grades.

‘Words and promises not enough’ as Syria’s Kurds face uncertain future

Abdi was also appointed as an adviser to al-Sharaa on Friday, days after announcing the SDF's dissolution. It remains unclear whether the role will be more than ceremonial.

But questions remain over what the end of the Kurdish-led administration will mean for women. The SDF and affiliated institutions used a system in which governing bodies were jointly headed by a man and a woman.

“During these 10 years of autonomy, men and women were equal,” Balanche said. “In the region’s administration. It was always a co-presidency. In Raqqah, for example, the mayor was Leyla Mustafa, a woman, and the co-president was a man. Now that is no longer the case.”

Balanche also said the change could threaten restrictions on polygamy introduced under the Kurdish-led administration. Another unresolved question is what will happen to female SDF fighters as the force is absorbed into Syria's armed forces, which currently have no female troops.

Shifting alliances

For years, the SDF was Washington's main partner on the ground in Syria in the fight against the Islamic State group. But its position weakened as the United States built closer relations with Syria's new rulers.

A Syrian government offensive in January seized large areas held by the SDF and pushed the Kurdish-led force back into negotiations over integration with Damascus.

Washington, meanwhile, has increasingly embraced al-Sharaa's government, dismantling broad sanctions against Syria in 2025 and last week removing the country from its list of state sponsors of terrorism.

Turkey has emerged as one of al-Sharaa's main foreign allies and has long pressed for the SDF to disarm and integrate into the Syrian state.

Ankara considers the SDF a terrorist organisation linked to the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK), which launched an insurgency against the Turkish state in 1984. The SDF has rejected Turkey's claim that it is an extension of the PKK.

A year after Assad's fall, Syrian hopes for transitional justice are fading

The United States and European Union designate the PKK as a terrorist organisation, but not the SDF.

Turkey has carried out several cross-border military operations against the SDF in northern Syria since 2016 and still has thousands of troops stationed in the country. Ankara says those forces will remain until the security threats it faces have been eliminated.

The SDF's dissolution therefore achieves a longstanding Turkish objective in Syria. Turkey's ruling AK Party welcomed the move last week as an important step towards strengthening Syria's unity.

“Stability in Syria means Turkey perhaps being able to divert some of the resources it's been spending on counterterrorism into other areas of its defense that are absolutely necessary at a time like this, a time of regional turmoil,” said Turkey expert Asli Aydintasbas of the Washington-based Brookings Institution.

Turkey's Kurdish conflict

The SDF's dissolution could also remove an obstacle to the fragile peace process between Ankara and the PKK.

The process is intended to end the PKK's decades-long armed campaign against the Turkish state through the group's disarmament and dissolution.

Jailed PKK leader Abdullah Ocalan called on the group to disarm and disband in February 2025, and the PKK announced three months later that it would do so. A group of militants symbolically burned their weapons at a ceremony in northern Iraq in July 2025.

Turkey's parliament passed a law in August establishing a legal framework for the PKK's disbandment. Kurdish politicians have said broader democratic and legal reforms will also be needed for lasting peace.

Macron to become first Western European leader to visit post-Assad Syria

For Ankara, however, the process does not stop at Turkey's borders. It has repeatedly insisted that the SDF must also dissolve, because it regards the Syrian force as part of the same militant movement as the PKK.

The SDF has disputed that characterisation, with Abdi saying in 2025 that the PKK's decision to disarm did not apply to his forces in Syria.

The dismantling of groups Ankara regards as PKK affiliates across the region is essential to the process, said Middle East expert Serhan Afacan of Istanbul's Marmara University.

“The PKK should not exist anywhere in the region. This is what Ankara has been saying for more than a year,” Afacan said.

“If there is going to be any kind of peace process or reconciliation, the PKK is not supposed to exist anywhere in this region, in Turkey, in Iran, in Iraq, Syria.”

World.title: Ukraine: Russia threatens 'devastating' Baltic response
World.content:
Skip next section 'Russian airspace is becoming completely unsafe,' Zelenskyy warns

09/02/2026 September 2, 2026 'Russian airspace is becoming completely unsafe,' Zelenskyy warns

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned airlines flying across Russia, saying that Ukraine's drone operations would make the airspace unsafe.

"Russian airspace is becoming completely unsafe," Zelenskyy said in a statement on Tuesday evening. He said that Ukraine was not threatening civilian aviation or individual aircraft.

"There will simply be drones in Russia's skies on a scale that has to be taken into account," he said.

Just last week, Zelenskyy threatened the deployment of up to 1,000 long-range drones per day.

Russian President Vladimir Putin branded Zelenskyy's comments "a declaration of state terrorism."

"They are asking us to resume negotiations... but you don't negotiate with terrorists," Putin said in a televised news conference.

Ukraine has been defending itself against a full-scale Russian invasion since February 2022 and has repeatedly managed to strike targets deep inside Russia with drones as part of its defense efforts.

World.title: Germany says Russia behind attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport
World.content:
Investigators believe an explosives-laden drone was deliberately targeting a Ukrainian cargo aircraft at Leipzig/Halle airport in early August. The German government said on Tuesday that it held Russia "responsible."

The German government said on Tuesday that it held Russia "responsible" for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport on August 4.

"The federal government concludes that Russia is responsible for the hybrid attack in Leipzig," said Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt at a press conference in Berlin .

Leipzig airport attack: What has Germany said?

"The means used — such as the drone configuration, components, explosives and detonation systems — are known to us from other hybrid operations by Russia and its war against Ukraine," added Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul.

He said the attack fit the pattern of a "long series of destabilization operations" against Europe.

Authorities discovered a drone fitted with explosives and a detonation mechanism on the evening of August 4 in the security area of Leipzig/Halle Airport between Ukrainian cargo aircraft and believe a second drone may have collided with a DHL aircraft nearby.

Last week, German media reported a third drone, also loaded with explosives, had also been discovered at the airport.

German federal prosecutors described the incident as a "serious attack on Germany's transport and logistics infrastructure."

"Taken together, police investigations, patterns of the crime and intelligence findings substantiate Russian responsibility for the attempted attack at Leipzig Airport," said Interior Minister Dobrindt on Tuesday.

"We do not view Leipzig as an isolated incident, but rather see it in the context of other hybrid actions," he continued. "We assume that Germany will be the target of further hybrid attacks by Russia."

The airport is ​a cargo and military logistics hub used by NATO and Ukraine's Antonov Airlines for military supplies Image: Hendrik Schmidt/dpa/picture alliance

How will Germany respond?

Dobrindt insisted that Germany is "not at war" but that it is "a daily target of hybrid warfare."

Therefore, he said, Germany would respond to the hybrid attack in Leipzig in a "proportionate and measured, yet resolute manner."

Foreign Minister Wadephul said Germany's response would be coordinated closely with European Union and NATO partners.

"We are tightening entry controls for Russian nationals" and Berlin would propose the listing of more Russian individuals for European Union sanctions, Wadephul said, as the Russian ambassador to Berlin was summoned.

In addition to a strengthening of internal security, he also announced additional measures including the closure of the Russian consulate in the western city of Bonn from September 18 and the rescinding of a contract enabling the operation of the "Russian House," a Russian cultural center in Berlin.

"Our message to the Russian leadership is clear," Germany's top diplomat said. "We are sticking to our security course. The attack on Leipzig shows that this is necessary. We will not allow our social cohesion to be divided by Russian attacks. We remain ready to react along with our partners when the protection of our population demands it."

Finally, he said that Germany would continue to support Ukraine in its "defensive battle against Russian aggression."

Germany blames Russia for attempted terror attack in Leipzig To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

How have NATO and the EU responded?

"NATO stands ​in full solidarity with Germany after the Russian hybrid ​attack in Leipzig on 14 August," ⁠said NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, adding that the alliance would continue strengthening its ability to deter and defend ‌its ⁠allies ⁠against threats.

"Russia's attempts to intimidate us, to undermine our unity and our willingness to support Ukraine are futile and will fail," he added.

"The German government has taken strong measures and the message is clear: hybrid attacks will not go without a clear response," said European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.

"We are united in our resolve to stand against Russian aggression," she continued. "We will deter anyone who seeks to undermine our freedom and security. Russia is seeking to sow distrust and fear among our societies. But it will fail. And we will stand by Ukraine for as long as it takes."

The European Union's foreign affairs chief Kaja Kallas said earlier on Tuesday that it was "clear" that Russia was involved in the drone incident, but declined to comment further until Germany had identified those it believes were responsible,

Kallas said Russia was becoming increasingly provocative, raising the question of what could be done to deter Moscow from escalating tensions any further.

Third drone found in suspected Leipzig hybrid attack To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

How have Russia and Ukraine responded?

Russia's President Vladimir Putin rejected Berlin’s allegations, claiming Germany's leadership was attempting use the incident to deflect from their own failings and dissatisfaction among voters with "the need to counter an aggressive Russia."

Putin also claimed Russia was being set up.

"But where is the proof? Well, the proof has been planted," Putin told reporters in the early hours of Wednesday in Kyrgyzstan.

Ukraine meanwhile, welcomed Berlin's measures against Russia following the failed drone attack at Leipzig airport.

Ukrainian Ambassador to Germany Oleksii Makeiev praised Berlin's response late on Tuesday.

"I welcome Germany's resolute response to the Russian attack in Leipzig," Makeiev wrote on social media platform X.

Kyiv has been in close contact with Berlin to secure critical infrastructure against drones, a coordinated approach against Russia's "shadow fleet" and further sanctions against Moscow, he said.

Edited by: Elizabeth Schumacher and Wesley Dockery

World.title: Iran war: US, Tehran trade fire in new flare-up
World.content:
09/02/2026 September 2, 2026 Air alert sirens sound in Bahrain, Kuwait intercepts Iranian drones

Sirens warning of potential aerial threats sounded in Bahrain early on Wednesday amid the latest escalation between the US and Iran.

Bahrain's Ministry of Interior said in a post on X: "A danger is present. The Ministry of Interior calls upon citizens and residents to adhere to calm, head to the nearest safe place, and follow the news through official channels, to safeguard public safety.

Bahrain is home to a major US naval base where the 5th Fleet is headquartered and has previously been targeted by Tehran.

Kuwait, another US ally in the Mideast region, also said it repelled attacks by "hostile" Iranian drones.

World.title: Iran: US launches fresh strikes as hostilities flare again
World.content:
Explosions were reported in and around the Strait of Hormuz, as well as at an airport in southern Iran. US President Trump described the strikes as "large and powerful." Iran said the US will "regret" its latest attacks.

Hostilities in the Strait of Hormuz flared up again on Tuesday evening as the United States launched fresh strikes on Iranian targets in and around the strategic waterway.

"Explosions were heard again in Bandar Abbas city and Qeshm island," Iranian state television reported, adding that blasts were also heard on Lavan island, home to one of Iran's Gulf oil export terminals.

Oil prices rose in the wake of the latest attacks with US crude up by as much as 5%.

The US military's Central Command (CENTCOM) confirmed the strikes, saying they were in response to "recent attempted attacks by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and against American service members deployed to the region."

US President Donald Trump said the strikes, which he described as "large and powerful," were retaliation for "failed" Iranian attempts to lay mines in the Strait of Hormuz and the firing of "eight missiles" towards a US military base in Jordan, all of which he claimed were shot down.

"If the failed Nation of Iran retaliates for this very justified attack, they will be hit again at a much harder and higher level," Trump wrote in his latest social media threat. "But it will not be the biggest attack of them all. That is waiting in the wings."

Iran: IRGC vows to respond to US strikes

An IRGC spokesman, quoted by the Fars state news agency, said the US would "regret" its latest attacks, which state television said included a strike on Jiroft airport in southeastern Iran, about 300 kilometers (186 miles) inland from the Strait of Hormuz.

Iran's joint military command said its armed forces would deliver what they described as "crushing and devastating blows" against the US, while state media said the army had launched operations against unspecified US targets in the region.

The Tasnim news agency said a "decisive operation by Iran's armed forces in response to the US enemy has begun. The US bases and interests in the region are being targeted by Iranian missiles and drones."

G20: US threatens further sanctions on Iran

Meanwhile, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Tuesday that his department was planning to impose fresh sanctions on Iran.

"We are probably going to announce a bank sanction this week, and we will announce one the week after," Bessent said on the sidelines of the G20 meeting of finance ministers in North Carolina.

"We are speaking to our allies here, who have all come forward, and we have had a great show of support."

He also said the US was considering airplane leasing companies and other companies which continue to do business with the IRGC.

"We have zero tolerance," he said. "We are going to economically asphyxiate this regime."

Iran's Pezeshkian meets Putin

The latest flare-up comes just hours after Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said earlier on Tuesday that Tehran would reciprocate any US move that signals a return to the collapsed interim ceasefire deal.

Pezeshkian, speaking after the US and Iran had already resumed exchanges of fire for the first time in over a month, accused Washington of "reneging on its commitments" under the agreement, which fell apart in June, with both sides accusing the other of violating the agreement's terms.

Pezeshkian was speaking on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, where he also met Russian President Vladimir Putin on Tuesday.

Putin reportedly told Pezeshkian that Russia stood in solidarity with Iran, and that the two countries would maintain their economic relationships despite the current turbulence.

Pezeshkian thanked Putin and criticized the US for having "no right" to impose sanctions on other countries.

World.title: Congo's Ebola caseload tops 6,000 as concerns grow
World.content:
The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo has surpassed 6,000 confirmed cases, with nearly 3,000 deaths. As the virus spreads, authorities are racing to contain one of the deadliest outbreaks in history.

The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) continues to escalate, with confirmed infections now topping 6,000 and the death toll reaching 2,911, according to government figures.

The outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo strain of the Ebola virus, has spread to around 60 zones in six provinces, raising fears that the virus is outpacing efforts to contain it.

"Around 60 health zones are now affected, every week more are added to the list. And the same pattern is repeated everywhere: initially, there is resistance and denial, followed by gradual acceptance," DW correspondent Jonas Gerding reported from Bunia, the capital of the Ituri province, the epicenter of the latest Ebola outbreak in Congo.

"Unfortunately, a lot more people will die until this Ebola outbreak gets under control," he added.

Health experts have said the situation is particularly worrying in eastern Congo, where conflict and insecurity are making it harder for response teams to reach affected communities.

Ebola outbreak in DR Congo outpaces efforts to contain it To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"This outbreak is the fastest-growing Ebola epidemic on record. It is growing faster and wider than the response to contain it, but it can be stopped," UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres told journalists last week.

The United Nations has appealed for more funding as humanitarian agencies struggle to keep pace with the increasing number of cases.

"International attention, political focus and resources are still lagging behind the reality unfolding on the ground," Guterres said, warning that the world "must also overcome another virus — the virus of indifference."

Vaccination campaign gathers momentum

As researchers continue trials aimed at developing a licensed vaccine for the Bundibugyo strain, Congolese authorities have rolled out a vaccination campaign focused on front-line health workers.

The vaccine was originally developed for a different Ebola variant, but officials hope it will provide some protection against the current outbreak.

Health Minister Samuel Roger Kamba said more than 50,000 doses had already arrived in the country.

"We will cover all the provinces that are around Ituri, moving in a ring towards the center of the outbreak, that is to say towards Ituri. But we have enough doses for all healthcare providers," he said on August 28.

Some health workers remain confident despite uncertainty over how effective the vaccine will be against the Bundibugyo strain.

"It is a vaccine that has already proven itself. We are talking about Ebola Bundibugyo, of Ugandan origin. But the vaccine that they want to administer to us was the vaccine that had succeeded for the Zaire type," said health worker Arnaud Batumbu.

"Since both cases involve a viral disease, I hope the vaccine will work for us now as well," he added.

Communities seek protection

Residents in hard-hit areas say they are ready to take the vaccine if it is properly explained to them.

"I will be ready to get vaccinated if only someone explains to me the importance of this vaccination," Clemency, a student in Tshopo province, told DW.

Health workers are worried about the spread of the virus Image: Xinhua/dpa/picture alliance

Others are calling for wider access. "Children need to be vaccinated too. They go back to school; there are many of them in class," said local resident Carine Lobwadji

Some community members also fear vaccine supplies may not be enough.

"I have learned that this is an insufficient quantity. I ask the authorities to add other doses for Tshopo and that we vaccinate everyone, especially those who will voluntarily agree, since some are afraid," said Onyeka Treasure, a photographer.

Violence hampers response

The latest outbreak is unfolding against a backdrop of violence and mass displacement in eastern DRC, complicating efforts to stop transmission.

Ebola response teams have reported attacks while carrying out their work, including during operations to safely handle Ebola-related deaths.

"We demand greater security so we can operate in the field and do our work without endangering our lives," Floribert Magene, a member of an Ebola response team, told The Associated Press on Monday after an attack in Ituri province.

Magene said his team was assaulted near Mambasa while responding to a call to secure a body.

Economic toll grows

Beyond the health emergency, the outbreak is worsening economic hardship for many families.

Schools have reopened in towns such as Bukavu and Bunia, but many parents are struggling to afford basic school supplies.

DR Congo launches Ebola trial for high-risk contacts To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Stationery shop owner Furaha Mpangu Esperance told DW that demand has collapsed as families prioritize food and other essentials.

"In any case, it doesn't work. The situation is serious because there are no customers. We have even lowered the prices but there is no one to buy. Before, we even sold 10 boxes, 20 boxes a day. Today not even three boxes, not even two! The situation is critical," he said.

To reduce disruption to education, the government has proposed radio-based learning for children unable to attend school.

"For us, it's a double objective: to ensure that children continue to go to school, despite the epidemic, and to ensure that distance learning is the device that will help them," Education Minister Raissa Malu told DW.

Schools have enforced protective measures, like hand-washing Image: DW

Teachers, however, say many areas lack the infrastructure needed for effective distance learning.

"We, the teachers, are ready, but we don't have the tools. In sensitive areas, even picking up frequencies is quite a problem," said Patrick Girinegi, president of the Ituri teachers' inter-union alliance. "The first-grade children can't read, nor do the parents. Several schools don't have printers or computers. How will it go?"

Many students and parents would rather see classrooms remain open with stronger health measures in place.

"It's easy for me to understand when it's my teacher himself who explains it to me. Saying that the child stays at home to listen to the radio, I don't think it's going to work. We [must] find ways to go to school without contaminating ourselves," said Viviane Tshipamba, vice-president of the Ituri children's committee.

Despite the challenges, health authorities point to a positive sign: more than 1,360 people have recovered from Ebola so far. For many Congolese, those recoveries offer hope that with stronger support, increased vaccination rates and improved security, the outbreak can still be brought under control.

Marcus Loika, Gaston Mukendi and Mitima Delachance contributed to this article.

World.title: Germany terminates lease for Berlin's Russian House
World.content:
Germany has announced the termination of the lease for the Russian House in the heart of Berlin. Critics have long said it is a hub for propaganda and espionage.

Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has announced that the contract under which the Russian House is operated will be rescinded. This is one of several measures in retaliation for Russian involvement in the attempted airport drone attack at the Leipzig/Halle Airport on August 4.

The Russian House is centrally located on Friedrichstrasse in the heart of the German capital. As a throwback to a bygone era of friendly German-Russian relations, it has long been the subject of fierce disagreements and a bone of contention in Berlin.

The massive seven-story building covering an area of almost 30,000 square meters opened in 1984. At that time, back in the days of the East German state, its role was to celebrate friendship with the Soviet Union through concerts, film screenings and book readings. It even had its own small bookstore.

French authorities have previously linked the building to possible activities by Russian intelligence services.

"In light of the measures taken against German cultural institutions and organizations, the federal government is comprehensively and continuously reviewing the legal basis of the Russian House under international treaty law,” said German Foreign Ministry spokesperson Martin Giese at a press conference in Berlin at the beginning of August.

Back then, in response to a question from DW about the organization's future activities, Giese emphasized that the fate of the Russian House is linked to that of the Goethe Institut in Moscow, and that any action taken against one would also have direct consequences for the other.

German tax money for Russian propaganda?

The property on Friedrichstrasse belongs to Germany, yet the building is run by the Russian agency Rossotrudnichestvo, the Federal Agency for the Commonwealth of Independent States, Compatriots Living Abroad and International Humanitarian Cooperation.

Rossotrudnichestvo, whose primary purpose is to promote the Russian language abroad, currently has dozens of similar institutions worldwide. The German Foreign Office has repeatedly stated that the employees of the institute have diplomatic status in Germany.
