World.title: The Tisza’s message reaches Tiszalök: What the PET Cup found beneath the trees – PHOTOS
World.content:
When the PET Cup fleet reached Tiszalök on 22 August, the boats had already spent eight days travelling along the Bodrog and Tisza. The finish line marked the end of a demanding competition, but the final stretch revealed a more troubling reality: tonnes of waste remain hidden in floodplains even when no recent flood has carried it there. The expedition therefore raised a question that reaches beyond the event itself. How much of the pollution comes from upstream, and how much is created or abandoned locally? I spoke with Viktória Doró from the PET Kupa press office for this article.

Author: Zoltán Rokonál

A record with an uncomfortable meaning

The VII Bodrog–XIV Tisza PET Cup took participants from Olaszliszka to Tiszalök between 15 and 23 August. Twelve teams worked along the riverbanks and floodplains, collecting and sorting 18.9 tonnes of waste. That result exceeded the previous record of 17.5 tonnes, set on the same route in 2024 with 15 teams. Eleven of the participating teams had already taken part in earlier editions, giving them valuable experience in locating waste deposits that are difficult to see from the water.

Such a result is not easy to interpret. A larger amount of collected rubbish does not automatically prove that the river has become more polluted. It may also indicate that volunteers have become more efficient at finding material that has accumulated over a long period.

This distinction was especially relevant in 2026. Neither the Bodrog nor the Tisza experienced a major flood wave capable of transporting large quantities of new waste into the area. Much of what the teams discovered was already lying in the floodplain. Organisers said some deposits may have remained there for years or even decades.

The finding adds another layer to the familiar story of Tisza pollution. Waste arriving from the upper reaches of the river, including from the direction of Ukraine, remains a serious regional issue. Earlier clean-up campaigns have also shown the scale of the challenge. In a previous Daily News Hungary report, volunteers removed more than six tonnes of waste from the River Tisza.

At the same time, the latest route showed that not every discarded object can be blamed on the current. Some rubbish had never needed the river to carry it.

What was found near Tiszalök

The final section between Tiszaladány and Tiszalök covered approximately nine river kilometres. During that part of the journey, the teams collected 2,120 kilograms of waste, including 522 bags, eight tyres and numerous larger objects.

Behind those figures lies a considerable amount of manual labour. Volunteers had to enter dense vegetation, search difficult sections of the floodplain, remove objects from bushes and transport everything back to collection points. A bag of plastic bottles may appear insignificant on its own, but hundreds of such bags represent many hours of work.

Compared with other parts of the route, the Tiszalök section was not the most heavily polluted. Nearly seven tonnes were collected between Tokaj and Tiszaladány in just two days. The Bodrog section between Olaszliszka, Szegi, Bodrogkeresztúr and Tokaj produced almost 9.9 tonnes, while the Tisza section accounted for a further nine tonnes overall.

The uneven distribution illustrates why a single total cannot fully describe the condition of a river. Waste gathers in particular locations where vegetation, currents, earlier floods and human activity create natural traps.

If you missed it: Tiszalök’s hydropower plant stops operating as drought pushes River Tisza to a critical point

When the river is not responsible

One of the most troubling discoveries was an illegal waste deposit along the Bodrog. According to the organisers, the arrangement of the rubbish made it clear that people had taken it to the riverbank rather than the water carrying it there. The same area had been visited during the 2024 expedition, yet some sections appeared to contain even more waste this time.

The list of objects found elsewhere was equally revealing: tyres, parts of car bodies, refrigerators and other bulky items. These discoveries challenge the idea that the Tisza is merely a conveyor belt transporting waste from distant places into Hungary.

The reality is more complicated. Pollution can cross national borders, but it can also originate beside a local road, fishing spot or riverside shelter. Abandoned rubbish may remain hidden for years until a clean-up team exposes it.

That difference has practical consequences. International cooperation is necessary to address pollution entering Hungary from upstream countries. Local enforcement and waste-management systems are just as important when the source is illegal dumping within the country.

A competition built around environmental work

The PET Cup differs from a conventional clean-up campaign because its participants do not simply walk along the bank with bags. They build boats from recovered waste and use them to travel the river. Navigation, team challenges, quizzes and other activities form part of the programme, creating a structure that combines physical work with education and community-building.

The 2026 competition was won by Siemens Energy, followed by TOMRA and PETardáltak. A separate “Hero” award recognises the team collecting the largest amount of waste per participant.

Competition may seem unusual in an environmental programme, yet it helps maintain motivation during long and exhausting days. Teams return to the river year after year, become familiar with the terrain and develop practical knowledge about where waste tends to accumulate.

Young volunteers and participants involved in community-service programmes also encounter the problem directly. Seeing plastic trapped beneath vegetation can leave a stronger impression than learning about river pollution only through statistics or classroom discussions.

Stay up-to-date with our Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

Collection cannot replace prevention

The event’s success also exposes its central contradiction. The more effectively the PET Cup finds and removes waste, the more clearly it demonstrates how much rubbish has entered the natural environment.

That cannot be the final measure of progress. A future in which larger teams collect larger quantities every year would not represent a solution.

Prevention must therefore accompany clean-up work. Better waste management, stronger action against illegal dumping, cooperation among countries in the Tisza basin and systems that intercept waste before it reaches the floodplain are all necessary.

Recovery and recycling can extend the value of the work. At the Kisköre River Rescue Centre, collected material is sorted and prepared for further use. Earlier PET Cup projects also transformed recovered plastic into prototypes such as kayaks.

Still, recycling has limits. A bottle that is eventually processed after spending years in a floodplain has already caused unnecessary environmental damage. The most effective waste is the waste that never reaches the river.

What the arrival means for Tiszalök

Tiszalök was more than the endpoint of a sporting event. The town’s position along the route makes it a place where the consequences of upstream pollution, local dumping and floodplain accumulation become visible at the same time.

Repeated PET Cup arrivals can also influence how nearby communities relate to the river. A bottle floating past a bridge may be easy to overlook. Hundreds of bottles pulled from bushes create a different impression. So do abandoned tyres, refrigerators and illegal dumps.

Physical contact with the problem can change behaviour. Someone who has spent hours removing plastic from a floodplain may think differently the next time they hold a disposable bottle. That personal experience is one of the event’s most lasting effects.

Daily News Hungary has also previously reported on PET Cup clean-up expeditions, including an earlier campaign in which the Plastic Cup removed 8.2 tonnes of waste from the Tisza. Together, these reports show that the issue is not limited to dramatic waves of floating rubbish. It also involves hidden floodplain deposits, local responsibility and the long-term challenge of preventing waste from entering the river system.

The finish line is not the end

At Tiszalök, the boats arrived, the waste was weighed and sorted, and the results were announced. The competition had its winners, and the eight-day journey was complete. The environmental problem, however, remained.

The 18.9 tonnes collected during the expedition represent a significant achievement. So do the 2.12 tonnes removed from the final nine-kilometre section. Yet the most important figure may be the amount that volunteers did not reach.

The latest PET Cup showed that two explanations can exist at once. Some waste travels from far away, carried by the river across borders. Other rubbish is left much closer to home by people who treat the floodplain as a place where unwanted objects can disappear.

Volunteers can continue to remove what they find. Lasting progress will depend on reducing what reaches the river in the first place.

World.title: Police: Five men beaten and kept as modern-day slaves in Hungary for years
World.content:
They were promised work and accommodation, but allegedly ended up working 10–12 hours a day without pay, rest days or regular financial support, and were reportedly beaten and threatened if their performance was deemed inadequate, according to the police.

Men allegedly forced to work without pay

Hungarian police have arrested a 55-year-old man suspected of human trafficking and forced labour after five men were allegedly exploited at a property in Vecsés, near Budapest, for around two years.

According to the Pest County Police Headquarters, the victims were initially promised employment and accommodation. Instead, investigators say they were forced to work long hours under threats and physical abuse.

The men were reportedly accommodated at a property in Vecsés. On weekdays, they were taken to Budapest to carry out construction and electrical work, while in Vecsés they were made to perform tasks related to animal husbandry.

They allegedly worked 10 to 12 hours a day without proper rest periods or days off. Despite carrying out the work for around two years, they reportedly received no wages or regular financial support.

If you missed it: Hungarian man beats and tortures partner, forcing her to dig her own grave

Victims allegedly lived in fear

Police say the investigation revealed increasingly serious details after one of the alleged victims filed a report at the Budapest Police Headquarters’ 18th District Police Station late on 26 August.

Officers from Monor arrived at the Vecsés property shortly after midnight and began gathering information. The subsequent questioning of the alleged victims reportedly shed further light on the conditions in which they had been living and working.

According to investigators, the men were kept in a state of fear and were allegedly assaulted when their performance did not meet expectations.

One man was reportedly forced to continue working despite a musculoskeletal injury. Another was allegedly punched several times and was so frightened that he did not dare seek medical attention for his injuries.

Suspect denies the allegations

Police arrested the 55-year-old Lajos T. shortly after the report was made. He was taken into custody and prosecutors sought his pre-trial detention, which was subsequently ordered by the court. The suspect denies committing the offences and has lodged a complaint against the allegations.

Police are still searching for his alleged accomplice. The Pest County Police Headquarters is investigating the case on suspicion of human trafficking and forced labour committed against multiple victims. The investigation is ongoing.

World.title: Hungary’s new 2026 budget reveals a massive multi-billion-euro hole
World.content:
The Tisza government has submitted a revised 2026 budget that dramatically increases both state revenues and expenditure, while the projected deficit rises to HUF 7,110 billion (approx. EUR 19 billion), which is far above the figure originally approved under the previous government.

New government unveils dramatically revised budget

Hungary’s Ministry of Finance submitted the revised 2026 budget to Parliament on 31 August, just before the deadline. The overhaul was deemed necessary after the new government reviewed the country’s finances following the April change of government, 444.hu writes.

The previous administration had approved the 2026 budget last summer, based on assumptions that have since proved unrealistic, including economic growth of more than 4% and a significantly lower deficit.

According to the revised figures, the state is now expected to collect HUF 41,915 billion in revenue this year, compared with HUF 39,562 billion in the original budget.

At the same time, expenditure is projected to reach HUF 49,025 billion, up from HUF 43,781 billion. This leaves a projected deficit of HUF 7,110 billion, compared with the HUF 4,218 billion originally budgeted.

The government plans to reduce the deficit-to-GDP ratio to around 7.5% by the end of the year, compared with the 8.3% figure identified during its review of the inherited budget.

EU funds expected to boost revenue

One of the biggest changes on the revenue side is the amount expected to come from EU programmes. The revised budget forecasts HUF 3,708 billion in revenue from EU programmes, more than double the HUF 1,800 billion originally planned.

However, several other revenue streams are now expected to perform worse than initially forecast. Corporate tax revenue is projected to be almost HUF 250 billion lower than originally planned, while excise duty revenue is expected to fall by around HUF 220 billion. VAT revenue is forecast to come in nearly HUF 400 billion below the original estimate.

If you missed it: PM Magyar: Hungary has met all conditions to access frozen EU funds

State assets and other spending drive expenditure higher

Expenditure has increased much more sharply than revenue. The largest increase concerns spending related to state assets, which is now expected to exceed HUF 1,770 billion, more than HUF 1,400 billion above the original allocation.

This is particularly notable because only around HUF 120 billion had actually been spent from this budget line during the first half of the year, suggesting significantly higher spending could take place during the second half.

Other expenditure is also expected to rise by almost HUF 1,000 billion to around HUF 1,540 billion, while interest payments are also projected to be somewhat higher. Spending connected to EU programmes is expected to reach HUF 3,467 billion, also above the amount originally budgeted.

Government increases emergency reserves

The revised budget also strengthens the state’s reserves by a total of HUF 756 billion. Around HUF 500 billion will go towards a newly established Havaria Fund, designed to help deal with challenges including drought and the energy crisis.

A further roughly HUF 250 billion will increase contingency reserves, which had previously stood at less than HUF 750 billion. At the same time, the government plans to save around HUF 120 billion on spending by central budgetary institutions and centrally managed appropriations, reducing the planned amount from HUF 13,550 billion to HUF 13,427 billion.

Stay up-to-date with our Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

What about the promised extra money for healthcare?

The revised budget also provides a clearer picture of one of the Tisza government’s major election promises: increasing state healthcare funding by HUF 500 billion a year. The answer is more complicated than the headline figure might suggest.

According to Portfolio, the revised budget increases the Health Insurance Fund’s expenditure allocation from around HUF 4,945 billion to more than HUF 5,112 billion, representing an increase of approximately HUF 167 billion. Compared with the actual HUF 4,902 billion spent by the fund in 2025, the new allocation represents an increase of around HUF 210 billion.

The healthcare treatment and prevention budget rises from HUF 2,886 billion in the original 2026 budget to HUF 3,004 billion in the revised version — an increase of only around HUF 50 billion compared with the previous government’s original plan. The figures therefore depend heavily on what is being compared.

For example, spending on combined specialist healthcare services is projected at HUF 1,409 billion in the revised 2026 budget. Compared with the HUF 909 billion originally allocated for 2025, this represents an increase of exactly HUF 500 billion.

However, the previous government had already increased this spending allocation significantly for 2026, meaning the entire HUF 500 billion increase cannot be attributed to the new government.

The revised budget therefore does not provide a straightforward HUF 500 billion increase in healthcare spending attributable to the Tisza government. The promised 20–25% pay rise for healthcare professionals also cannot yet be clearly identified in the revised 2026 budget.

World.title: Industrial climber dies after falling from Hungarian government office roof
World.content:
A worker died after falling from the roof of a government office in Szeged on Tuesday. Police have launched an investigation into the fatal workplace accident.

Worker fell from Szeged government office

A fatal workplace accident occurred in Szeged on Tuesday around midday, when an industrial climber fell from the roof of the Csongrád-Csanád County Government Office, Szegeder reported.

The worker fell onto the roof of the Vármegye Restaurant next to the government office and died at the scene, according to local reports.

The man is believed to have fallen from a height of at least 15 metres. Local reports said he suffered a serious head injury, which may have contributed to his death, although the exact cause of death has not yet been officially established.

Photographs from the scene show ropes hanging from the government office building, apparently used by the worker during his work. Workers were also seen setting up a protective covering at the site following the accident.

Police investigate circumstances of fatal fall

The circumstances that led to the industrial climber falling from the roof remain unclear. Police told local media that the worker fell for reasons that are currently unknown.

The Csongrád-Csanád County Police Headquarters has launched an investigation into endangering safety in connection with employment. Experts have been involved in the investigation to establish what happened and whether any safety rules may have been breached. The investigation is ongoing.

World.title: Hungarian police seize thousands of documents in investigation into state Eximbank deals
World.content:
Police have seized thousands of pages of documents from Hungary’s Ministry of Economy and Energy as part of a criminal investigation launched following an audit of the state-owned Eximbank. The probe concerns suspected abuse of office and mismanagement of funds.

Thousands of pages seized from ministry

Hungarian police have seized thousands of pages of documents from the Ministry of Economy and Energy as part of an investigation into alleged irregularities at the Hungarian Export-Import Bank (Eximbank).

The National Bureau of Investigation (NNI) of the Rapid Response Police launched criminal proceedings after the ministry filed complaints based on information uncovered during an examination of Eximbank’s operations.

Police said on Tuesday that investigators seized the documents from the ministry on 31 August. The material had been collected during the ministry’s internal review and could provide further evidence concerning the alleged offences under investigation.

The case involves suspected abuse of office and mismanagement of funds.

If you missed it: Hungarian government seeks Eximbank investigations over EUR 2.74 billion in deals

Four controversial deals under investigation

Prime Minister Péter Magyar announced in July that the Ministry of Economy and Energy had filed criminal complaints concerning four deals dating from the previous government.

One concerns a HUF 59 billion (approximately EUR 161 million) financing deal connected to the Sofitel hotel and a company close to the business interests of István Tiborcz, the son-in-law of former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán.

According to Magyar, Eximbank made the relevant decision within just two days, allegedly failing to comply even with its own internal rules. The ministry filed a complaint over suspected mismanagement and other potential criminal offences.

A second case involves HUF 126 billion (around EUR 344 million) and an African project linked to Hungarian construction company Duna Aszfalt. The project involved plans to build an expressway between Zambia and the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Magyar also said the company had obtained financing from the state-owned Hungarian Development Bank in connection with the project.

The third case concerns the Dunakeszi Vehicle Repair Company’s Egyptian project, for which the Egyptian state railway was reportedly granted a HUF 176 billion (approximately EUR 480 million) loan from the Hungarian state.

The fourth investigation centres on a EUR 1 billion general-purpose loan granted to North Macedonia.

Stay up-to-date with our Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

Investigation launched after Eximbank review

The complaints were filed in July after the ministry reviewed the activities of Eximbank and identified information it considered potentially relevant to criminal proceedings. Police investigators are now examining the evidence gathered in the case, including the thousands of pages seized from the ministry.

The investigation is ongoing, and the seizure of the documents does not in itself establish that any criminal offence was committed. Further decisions will depend on the findings of the investigation.

World.title: Extraditing Hungarian MOL’s head to Croatia? Péter Magyar gives cryptic answer at Bled forum
World.content:
Hungary and Croatia could be preparing for a new round of high-level talks over the long-running dispute surrounding Croatian oil company INA and Hungary’s MOL Group.

Péter Magyar was asked about oil giant MOL’s chief

Speaking at the Bled Strategic Forum in Slovenia, Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar said Hungary was ready to negotiate with Croatia and that a “new chapter” could begin in relations between the two countries.

Magyar said he had held a brief meeting with Croatian Prime Minister Andrej Plenković in Bled. The two leaders agreed that their foreign and economic ministers should begin talks on the relationship between INA and MOL. Magyar also suggested that a meeting between the two prime ministers could take place in the foreseeable future.

“We are ready to negotiate. Naturally, everyone will defend their own national interests, but that is normal. At the same time, we all see that there is an opportunity to open a new chapter in relations between the two countries,” Magyar said, according to Croatian outlet Jutarni List.

What about Zsolt Hernádi ?

The issue of MOL chairman and chief executive Zsolt Hernádi remains one of the most sensitive aspects of the dispute. Magyar was asked directly whether Hungary would be prepared to extradite Hernádi to Croatia, where a European arrest warrant has been issued against him. However, the Hungarian prime minister did not give a straightforward yes or no answer.

Instead, he referred back to his comments about opening a “new chapter” in Hungarian-Croatian relations. “I have already answered the question by saying that there is an opportunity to open a new chapter between Croatia and Hungary. Both countries have their own obligations that need to be settled. That is my answer,” Magyar said. His response leaves unclear whether Budapest’s position on Hernádi could change. For now, there is no explicit confirmation that Hungary intends to extradite the MOL chief.

Stay up-to-date with our Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

INA dispute has strained relations for years

The relationship between MOL and INA has been a major source of tension between Hungary and Croatia for more than a decade. MOL acquired 25 per cent plus one share of INA in 2003 and subsequently increased its stake. It now holds 49.08 per cent of the Croatian oil company, while the Croatian state owns 44.84 per cent.

The dispute has centred on control of INA, corporate governance and the possibility of Croatia buying back MOL’s stake. The two sides have also been involved in arbitration proceedings. Plenković said the unresolved INA-MOL issues had held back wider Hungarian-Croatian relations, despite strong economic, tourism and energy links between the two countries. “I think we are now in a position where we can try to resolve this issue, and afterwards move on,” the Croatian prime minister said.

Stay up-to-date: Péter Magyar in Bled about crisis management, budget deficit, EU affairs, illegal migration, regional cooperation

Hernádi case remains unresolved

Croatian authorities have accused Hernádi of bribery in connection with MOL’s acquisition of management rights at INA. He has rejected the allegations. His legal case has become closely linked to the wider political and corporate dispute between Budapest and Zagreb.

The latest statements from both prime ministers could signal a renewed attempt to resolve the INA conflict. Whether the proposed talks can deliver a lasting settlement — and whether Hernádi’s case will form part of any broader agreement — remains uncertain.

World.title: Bucharest association launches app for people caring for stray cats
World.content:
Last week, the Părinți de Cireșari Association announced the launch of CatChat, an app dedicated to stray cats in Bucharest. Through the app, people can find out whether a cat on the street is already being cared for by someone.

The idea came about when an abandoned cat from a Bucharest neighborhood was treated with antibiotics by members of the association, who later found out that the feline was already being treated for the same condition. After the cat was treated by members of the association, it returned to the yard some time later, wearing a collar around its neck. They put a note on the collar to find out whether the feline had an owner or was being cared for by someone, and the answer came from a neighbor.

“That was when we realized we had a problem: cats roam around the neighborhood, but we, the people, don't really know who takes care of them, or whether anyone takes care of them. That's how CatChat came about,” representatives of the Părinți de Cireșari Association said, cited by Buletin de București.

The app has two functions. The basic one is the PisID function, through which users can register cats in the community and see whether they are already being cared for by someone. Users can also see how many unsterilized cats there are in the community.

The app includes an “identity card” for each cat, containing its identifying features (fur, eyes, age, sterilization status, etc.), while the map shows the cats nearby, with their photos. A missing cat appears with a red alert on the map, and those who see it can report its appearance so that the people searching for it can be contacted. According to association representatives, the project's purpose is to encourage communities to pay more attention to the animals around them and, at the same time, to facilitate communication between the people who care for them.

According to the Părinți de Cireșari Association, the app also has a “less serious” function. More specifically, based on the descriptions entered in PisID, cats have their own “chat,” which operates at night, when people are sleeping. The cats' conversations are fictional, written with AI only from the cats' public profiles, without using users' personal data.

For now, CatChat is available on the App Store for iPhone users. The app is free, without ads and without subscriptions. Moreover, it can be used across the country.

World.title: Italian branch of Bucharest Exchange-listed tech group Simtel announces first projects
World.content:
Romanian engineering and technology group Simtel (BVB: SMTL), one of the leading players in Romania’s renewable energy sector, announced the signing of the first two projects by Simtel Italia, the subsidiary opened by the Group in Milan in June 2026.

The two projects have a cumulative value of approximately RON 15 million and a total installed capacity of over 15 MWp, according to a company press release sent on Tuesday, September 1.

The projects are located in the Abruzzo and Emilia-Romagna regions and involve the provision of light EPC services for an independent renewable energy producer (Independent Power Producer – IPP) controlled by a US infrastructure investment fund. Works commenced in August 2026 and are expected to be completed by the end of the year.

In addition to the projects already secured, Simtel Italia is participating in tender procedures for photovoltaic projects with a cumulative capacity of approximately 300 MWp and battery energy storage systems (BESS) totaling approximately 90 MWh.

The current pipeline supports the company’s objective of securing projects with a total capacity of more than 200 MWp by the end of 2026, to be implemented in stages over the following period, according to the same source.

“Italy provides us with access to a sizeable market, with a significant need for new generation and storage capacities and an investment framework conducive to long-term development. The pipeline built within a short period of time, the profile of our first client and the scale of the projects currently under tender reinforce our confidence in the subsidiary’s potential to make a meaningful contribution to the Group’s revenues and profitability,” stated Mihai Tudor, CEO of Simtel Group.

Based on the projects secured and the commercial opportunities currently at various stages of the tendering process, Simtel Italia’s management estimated revenues of approximately RON 40 million for 2026. For 2027, the company aims to significantly accelerate its activity and achieve revenues of up to approximately RON 250 million.

The Simtel Italia team currently consists primarily of project managers responsible for coordinating and monitoring construction sites, while tendering, engineering and procurement activities are supported by Simtel’s specialists in Romania. Over the next 12 months, the company plans to expand its local team by recruiting professionals with experience in the energy sector and to make the Milan office fully operational.

“Our experience during the first few months confirms that Italy represents one of Europe’s most significant opportunities for renewable energy investment. The plan of national transmission system operator Terna envisages investments of approximately EUR 23 billion by 2030 for the development and modernization of the electricity grid, while the definitive FER-X mechanism aims to support up to 37.15 GW of new renewable energy generation capacity,” stated Guglielmo Martino, CEO of Simtel Italia.

(Photo source: press release)

World.title: Romania's first digital identity wallet to launch in January 2027
World.content:
ROWallet, Romania's first digital identity wallet, was officially announced by the Ministry of Internal Affairs on Tuesday, September 1. The app will be available starting next year on iPhone and Android and will allow users to store official documents on their phones.

ROWallet promises to become an essential tool for citizens and residents, according to the ministry. “The idea is simple: ROWallet will function as a digital wallet in which the user can add documents originating from official sources, following an initial identity verification with the electronic identity card,” the institution said, cited by Libertatea.

Romania’s digital wallet was adapted after RoEUDIW, the open-source solution developed by Germany, the government announced this June. However, all personal data will be stored exclusively on the national infrastructure.

The installation process is straightforward. First, the user downloads the official ROWallet application once it becomes available. Then they confirm their identity “through a secure enrollment process, using the electronic identity card.” After enrollment, the user can add their digital documents, which are issued directly by the institutions that issue them. Finally, when a service requests certain information, the user decides what exactly to transmit.

When a public or private institution requests certain information, the user will be free to choose what data they want to share, without having to disclose the entire document. For example, to prove that they are over 18, the user can transmit only this information, without providing their full date of birth.

ROWallet also promises reduced bureaucracy, removing the need to present physical copies of documents. Moreover, access to the application is protected through authentication methods such as PIN, fingerprint, or facial recognition, increasing security. If the phone is lost or stolen, the digital wallet can be deactivated, and the data can be recovered on another device through a secure authentication process.

The application also uses advanced certification mechanisms to verify the validity of documents and the identity of entities requesting information.

According to the authorities, ROWallet has the potential to transform the way Romanians interact with institutions and companies. For example, the process of signing documents, accessing banking services, or interacting with public authorities will become much simpler and faster, directly from the phone. Moreover, documents and digital identity in ROWallet will be recognized in all European Union member states.

“It is important that the data will be stored locally on the phone, and the application provider will not have access to it. In addition, users will be able to access a history of the data shared to know exactly what information was transmitted and to whom,” the MAI's official statement said.

Although the project has been officially launched, the application is not yet available for download. The first test version is scheduled to be available on October 31, 2026, followed by a restricted beta stage on December 22, 2026. The official launch of the final version, ROWallet v1, is scheduled for January 14, 2027.

At this time, interested users can visit the project's official website, where more information and documentation are available. According to the MAI, the success of ROWallet will depend on cooperation with public and private institutions, which could adopt the system to reduce bureaucracy and improve access to services.

The ministry underlined that ROWallet is an optional solution, allowing users to choose between traditional and digital methods for managing documents.

radu@romania-insider.com

(Photo source: MAI on Facebook)

World.title: Damaged drone reportedly found in field in eastern Romania
World.content:
A damaged drone was found on Tuesday, September 1, in a field near Viișoara, Vaslui county, around 30 kilometers from Romania’s border with Moldova, according to News.ro. Authorities have isolated the area and launched an investigation into the aircraft’s origin and how it reached the site.

A local resident reportedly discovered the drone outside the village and notified police. Preliminary information indicated that the aircraft might be carrying explosives, although this had not yet been confirmed.

A Romanian Intelligence Service (SRI) bomb disposal team was sent to inspect and secure the drone. Police and gendarmerie personnel were also present at the site, according to media reports.

“We are waiting for the results of the inspections,” Vaslui prefect Andrei Șerban told Agerpres.

Police were notified about the discovery at 10:15 a.m. The Prosecutor’s Office attached to the Iași Court of Appeal was informed and will investigate the circumstances surrounding the incident.

Authorities had not yet determined when the drone came down or where it originated.

Romania has been facing a sharp escalation in unauthorized drone incursions linked to the war in neighbouring Ukraine this year. According to the latest Ministry of Defense data, the country registered 25 separate incidents in 2026 alone.

Last week, for example, residents within a radius of approximately 300 meters were temporarily evacuated after a drone was found crashed into a walnut tree near a house in Ciușlea, Vrancea County.

irina.marica@romania-insider.com

World.title: President says Romania seeks stronger US economic ties, backs EU integration of Moldova and Ukraine
World.content:
Romanian president Nicușor Dan presented the country's main foreign and security policy lines on Tuesday, September 1, during a meeting with the heads of Romanian diplomatic missions from across the world.

In a subsequent message on Facebook, the head of state outlined three major points of focus for Romania’s foreign policy: development of economic relations with the United States of America, strengthening of bilateral defense partnerships and firm support for the European path of the Republic of Moldova and Ukraine.

The head of state stressed that the strategic relationship with the US must go beyond the sphere of military cooperation and attract significant economic capital to Romania. “The partnership with the US is very important for Romania. We have made progress and, beyond the security partnership, we want a more significant economic presence of American companies in Romania,” Nicușor Dan said.

On the second point, Dan said that Romania is focusing on bilateral partnerships with a defense component that would strengthen the guarantees provided by multilateral alliances. “Regarding hybrid threats, both the kinetic side and the disinformation side, these issues must continue to be part of our concerns,” the head of state added.

Regarding the European agenda, the current year is marked by essential negotiations on the future financial framework of the bloc. The president expressed his hope that the Multiannual Financial Framework will be finalized as soon as possible, ideally by the end of this year.

Moreover, Romania will remain an active promoter of the European Union's enlargement and of strengthening the EU's internal security architecture, according to the president.

“We are interested in the enlargement process, especially for the Republic of Moldova, as well as for Ukraine and the Western Balkans. At the same time, we are interested in the security architecture within the EU,” Nicușor Dan explained.

Dan also reiterated Romania's commitment to supporting Ukraine and international measures aimed at ending hostilities. He further noted that Ukraine celebrated Romanian Language Day for the first time this year.

“We want the war in Ukraine to end as soon as possible and a solid peace in the region. For this, we support Ukraine and support forms of special economic pressure on Russia. We support the European integration process for Ukraine, Moldova and the Western Balkans,” the president concluded.

radu@romania-insider.com

(Photo source: presidency.ro)

World.title: VGP acquires 294,000 sqm plot for new industrial park in Oradea
World.content:
Pan-European real estate developer VGP announced that it acquired a 294,000 sqm land plot near Oradea in western Romania for a new logistics and industrial park. VGP Park Oradea is planned to offer an initial lettable area of 133,000 sqm for logistics, light industrial, and commercial activities.

The site is located close to the DEx16 expressway and the Borș border crossing with Hungary. It also offers access to Oradea International Airport and the city’s railway station.

VGP said the location would provide connections to major European transport routes for companies involved in cross-border distribution, manufacturing, and regional supply chains.

The planned park will be designed to accommodate different technical requirements from prospective tenants. It is targeting BREEAM Excellent certification and compliance with the EU Taxonomy. Sustainability features are expected to include photovoltaic panels, electric vehicle charging stations, smart metering systems, and measures to improve biodiversity at the site.

The acquisition expands VGP’s Romanian portfolio, which also includes industrial and logistics parks in Arad, Brașov, Bucharest, Timișoara, and Sibiu. The company said demand in Romania was being supported by manufacturing growth, e-commerce expansion, and the diversification of regional supply chains.

VGP entered the Romanian market in 2007. Since then, it has acquired more than 1.7 million sqm of industrial space, representing nearly 900,000 sqm of potential lettable area.

irina.marica@romania-insider.com

(Photo source: press release)

World.title: Romanian-made watch enters major watchmaking competition Grand Prix d’Horlogerie de Genève
World.content:
A watch created in Târgu Mureș, central Romania, is set to take part in Grand Prix d’Horlogerie de Genève 2026, one of the most important watchmaking competitions in the world.

Grand Prix d’Horlogerie de Genève is considered one of the major benchmarks of contemporary watchmaking and is frequently dubbed the “Oscar of watchmaking.” Every year, the competition brings together creations by renowned manufacturers and independent watchmakers from around the world.

The 2026 edition marks the first year with Romanian participation in the competition. Genesis, the watch created by Romanian watchmaker Alin Constantin Mureșan and entered in the competition, is inspired by the vaults of Transylvanian fortifications and local craftsmanship.

The Genesis dial is inspired by the vaults and arches of Transylvanian fortifications. The brass piece was processed, engraved, finished, and colored in the workshop in Târgu Mureș. The hands of the watch were also made in the same place. Their shape refers to the weapons that defended the fortresses and fortifications of Transylvania, while the finish was designed to reproduce the shine of the metal. The strap is made by a Transylvanian artisan. The watch uses a Swiss movement, according to the same source.

The model is entered in the Challenge category and brings international attention to Romanian independent watchmaking. For Alin Constantin Mureșan, founder of Constantime Watches, participation in Geneva is also a way of making elements related to Romania's history and identity known around the world.

“We have many things in Romania, and especially in Transylvania, that deserve to be shown to the world: architecture, symbols, crafts and stories. I don't just want to make watches in Romania. I want them to speak about Romania,” he said.

radu@romania-insider.com

(Photo source: press release)

World.title: Romania among top beer producers in EU in 2025
World.content:
Romania was the ninth largest beer producer in the European Union in 2025, according to data published on Monday, August 31, by Eurostat.

Germany was the main beer producer in the EU the same year, with 7.4 billion liters of beer (21.6% of the EU's total production). Spain ranked second (5.3 billion liters; 15.5%), followed by Poland (3.5 billion liters; 10.2%). The list of the top five producers was completed by the Netherlands (2.4 billion liters; 6.9%) and France (2.1 billion liters; 6.0%).

The next places were occupied by Belgium (1.992 billion liters of beer), Czechia (1.922 billion liters), Italy (1.725 billion liters) and Romania (1.594 billion liters of beer).

Most of the beer produced last year in the EU, 32.3 billion liters, contained more than 0.5% alcohol, while low-alcohol beer (below 0.5%) and alcohol-free beer accounted for 2.1 billion liters.

In Romania's case, most of the beer produced in 2025 (1.491 billion liters) contained more than 0.5% alcohol, while low-alcohol beer (below 0.5%) and alcohol-free beer accounted for 103.954 million liters.

Aside from producing, Romanians also enjoy drinking beer. According to Visual Capitalist, Romanians drank 87.4 liters of beer per capita in 2024, ranking ninth in the world. The Czech Republic (148.8 liters per capita), Lithuania (110.6), and Austria (104.6) took the first three spots in the ranking. European countries dominated the list, accounting for 25 of the 35 highest beer-consuming nations.

Earlier this summer, Romania’s Chamber of Deputies approved a bill allowing for the sale of beer and even wine in stadiums during competitions and public gatherings. The project was mainly initiated by deputies from the Social Democratic Party (PSD) and far-right representatives from the Alliance for the Union of Romanians (AUR) and United for Romania parliamentary groups.

World.title: ‘Polish Annexation’ Hoax Campaign Spotlights Czech Disinformation Vulnerability
World.content:
A podcast interview with investigative journalist Lukas Valasek for Seznam Zpravy on Monday laid out a well-organised, large-scale disinformation campaign that pushed the notion Poland was preparing to invade and annex a small border area with its southern neighbour around the twin towns of Ciezyn/Tesin.

“It is the first ever operation of this scale,” assessed Valasek. “If we understand this whole thing as a test from a potential Russian actor on how the Czech Republic will respond to a wave of disinformation, then I think that the Czech political scene, and especially the government, did not quite pass.”

The campaign relied on paid Facebook ads, AI-generated images, a fake website mimicking Czech Radio’s iRozhlas.cz, as well as fake social media accounts of both ordinary citizens and top officials – including Czechia’s ambassador to Poland.

The apparent goal, most have deduced, was to spark fears of a land grab and property seizures while stirring up historical grievances between the two EU and NATO countries linked to a controversial 1958 border treaty between Poland and then-Czechoslovakia.

According to Czech security expert Bohumil Kartous, the campaign bears all the hallmarks of a Russian-backed hybrid operation, exploiting “a fragment of truth” – the lingering, albeit relatively minor Czech-Polish border dispute – to place it “in a completely different context of fear over losing property”.

“The goal is precisely to trigger a dispute within this pro-Ukrainian coalition,” according to Kartous.

It appears to have mostly missed the mark. Poland was fastest to respond, with both Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk and his Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski quickly dismissing the claims of imminent annexation as absurd and orchestrated.

As a symbol of Czech-Polish unity, Prime Minister Tusk posted an image of friendship between the countries’ most famous cartoon characters, the Polish dog Reksio and the Czech mole Krtek, captioning: “Reksio and Krtek have known this for a long time, Poland and Czechia are true friends.”

But over the border the response took longer and was more muddled, with finger-pointing now underway to determine who was to blame for these failings. It took several days for the Czech Foreign Ministry to unequivocally reject “the spread of false information about alleged Polish territorial claims to the Czech Republic”.

Czech President Petr Pavel also weighed in: “This is a targeted provocation. And I’m very glad that people are not listening to this provocation on either side of the border,” going on to assure that “Poland is one of the Czech Republic’s closest and most important partners.”

Czech hesitancy

Yet late last week, Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis lashed out against his intelligence services, saying he had only heard about the ongoing hoax campaign through the media.

On Monday, he again pointed the finger at the Office for Foreign Relations and Information (UZSI) and blamed Czechia’s envoy in Poland, Bretislav Dancak, for the failed response.

Although evidently failing to drive a wedge between Prague and Warsaw, security experts said such a campaign could be used to test both Polish and Czech responses to hybrid threats and influence ops.

Highlighting the decision to entirely scrap the Strategic Communications Department (Stratkom) shortly after taking office, on top of reducing the number of ministerial experts focused on disinformation, many argue the Czech government only has itself to blame.

“If, by chance, there had still been any strategic communication of the state, analysts would have caught [the disinformation campaign] long before and the top representatives of the state could have communicated it,” argued former Stratkom chief Oldrich Bruza. “At least we have our Polish brothers.”

Opposition politicians, too, have accused the government of bringing this upon itself. “We have repeatedly warned about this,” said former foreign minister Jan Lipavsky. “For ideological reasons, the government is liquidating the state’s capacities for combating disinformation and influence operations at the very time when someone is using them against the Czech Republic.”

Hints of Russian involvement abound, but officials have so far refrained from unequivocally accusing Moscow of being behind the operation. Intelligence services in both Poland and Czechia are still investigating the matter.

But in Prague the finger-pointing continues. “We don’t need a Strategic Communications Department,” argued Prime Minister Babis. “We have [intelligence] services here that are supposed to work for the state, for the people and for the interests of the state.”

While failings at the top were evident, the response from the local population did not disappoint, with social media quickly flooded with montages of Reksio and Krtek as long-time chums, nipping in the bud any fears of cross-border animosity.

World.title: Postponement of Serbian Activists’ Subversion Trial ‘Absurd’, Lawyer Says
World.content:
The Higher Court in Serbia’s second city Novi Sad has again postponed the trial of the “Novi Sad 12” – 12 activists who are accused of plotting subversion ahead of a anti-government rally in the capital Belgrade last March amid an ongoing student-led mass protest campaign.

The accused – five former activists of the opposition Movement of Free Citizens, PSG, and seven members of the activist group Students Against Authoritarian Rule, STAV – are charged with “preparing an attack on Serbia’s constitutional order” and calling for the violent overthrow of the authorities.

The charges arise from discussions between the indictees that were recorded at a meeting ahead of the March 2025 rally, which became the largest in Serbian history.

The hearing has been postponed from September 4 to October 30 because an assessment of defendant Lazar Dinic’s fitness to stand trial has not been completed, after Dinic failed to attend a hearing in May, which caused the first postponement.

But Mihailo Pavlovic, the lawyer for one of the defendants, Mila Pajic, told BIRN that there were not sufficient grounds to postpone the hearing, and that the court decision was “completely nonsensical and irrelevant” and represented “the unnecessary prolonging of the proceedings”.

Six of the defendants who are members of STAV have been in exile since March 2025, are will be tried in absentia. Serbia sought international arrest warrants for them, but Interpol declined to issue them in July, concluding that the case was political in nature.

In the meantime, proceedings to confiscate their travel documents were also initiated but were later discontinued after the prosecutor withdrew the request, Pavlovic told BIRN.

“We are now in an absurd situation: these people are outside the country and detention orders against them remain in force, while at the same time the prosecutor himself has withdrawn the request to have their passports confiscated,” he said.

World.title: A Question of Justice: What I Learned from Watching Ratko Mladic’s Trial
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp

When news broke that Ratko Mladic had died in UN detention in The Hague, the headlines brought back the familiar images of the 1990s: the “Butcher of Bosnia”, the war criminal, the commander who became synonymous with the Srebrenica genocide.

For me, however, his death brought back a different image: an older man sitting a few metres away from me in a courtroom, stripped of his uniform and subjected to the quiet and slow rhythm of international criminal procedure.

My encounter with Mladic began not behind the bench but behind the glass of the public gallery in 2015. I was studying for a master’s degree in public international law and went to the International Criminal Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia, ICTY, excited to see a trial that until then I had known mostly through lectures, books and documentaries.

World.title: Bulgaria’s Former Interim PM Andrey Gyurov Confirms Presidential Bid
World.content:
After months of speculation, Bulgaria’s former interim Prime Minister Andrey Gyurov announced on Tuesday that he will run in the presidential elections on October 25. He will likely be the main rival to acting President Iliana Iotova who will be seeking a full mandate.

“The answer is yes, I will run, but the more important question is ‘why’… I don’t dream of a career, I dream of us leaving our children a united, honourable and modern Bulgaria, which is centred around the economy of knowledge and its biggest asset – the people,” said Gyurov.

“We can’t let our differences turn us into mutual enemies. Bulgaria can do so much better,” he added.

His two-month stint as caretaker prime minister in early 2026 was marked by a crackdown on fraudulent voting ahead of the general elections in April and the signing of a cooperation agreement with Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky in March.

Gyurov will run with the former chief secretary general to the Interior Ministry, Georgi Kandev, as his designated vice-president.

The duo – expected to lead a pro-EU and reformist campaign in opposition to the government of current Prime Minister Rumen Radev – announced their campaign in their common home town of Gotse Delchev in south-west Bulgaria, named after a revolutionary Ottoman-era hero celebrated in both Bulgaria and North Macedonia.

The announcement ended months of speculation over their political futures. Rumours started as early as April, while Gyurov was still interim prime minister, with his name widely mentioned as a potential presidential candidate by analysts and fellow politicians.

Since his caretaker term, Gyurov has been noticeable for his carefully curated social media and public presence: from visiting festivals and endorsing cultural events to running in marathons and reuniting with his baseball youth team – moves seen as aimed at engaging pro-EU, liberal, urban voters.

Born in 1975, he built a career spanning banking and financial academia, moving from work as an analyst and credit-risk expert in Vienna to lecturing and directing financial programmes in Bulgaria.

He entered parliamentary politics in November 2021 as a member of the reformist and then newly-founded We Continue the Change party, which the won the general elections. He left the party in 2023 and was then appointed deputy governor of the Bulgarian National Bank.

In 2026, he left that position to become interim prime minister, chosen by President Iliana Iotova – herself in a new role after Rumen Radev left the president’s office to successfully run in the general elections with his Progressive Bulgaria party.

Now, Gyurov and Iotova, supported by Progressive Bulgaria and the Bulgarian Socialist Party, will be the main opponents in the 2026 presidential elections.

Gyurov’s designated vice-president, Kandev – also born in 1975 – has held various positions in the Interior Ministry since 1999. He left his last position as chief secretary in June, claiming he had been subjected to political pressure by Radev’s office, but the issue was ultimately left unexplained.

A month and a half before the elections, it’s unclear whether the two men will be supported by the otherwise fragmented centre-right. The Democratic Bulgaria party and Gyurov’s former partners from We Continue the Change have previously stated that they will support their bid.

The lack of a candidate from the longstanding dominant party GERB might also be to their benefit, but Boyko Borissov’s party has yet to make its opinion public.

World.title: Russian Suspected of Triple Homicide in Montenegro Dies by Suicide
World.content:
Montenegro police officer. Photo illustration: EPA/Boris Pejovic.

A Russian citizen suspected of killing three people at a shooting range in Danilovgrad, central Montenegro shot himself dead on Tuesday after opening fire on police when he was found near the coastal town of Herceg Novi, authorities said.

The victims, killed by the Russian national on Monday, have been identified as Podgorica residents Nemanja Kapor, 20, and Petar Globarevic, 24, and Danilovgrad resident Momir Radonjic, 67.

Police identified the suspect as 30-year-old Russian citizen Mikhail Nikolaevich Shabunin.

Police Director Lazar Scepanovic said on Tuesday that officers had located Shabunin in a wooded area above the Topla neighborhood of the coastal town of Herceg Novi.

“After the suspect was surrounded and found himself in a hopeless situation, he opened fire in the direction of police officers and then committed suicide using a firearm,” Scepanovic said.

Police said Shabunin had visited the Ceska Zbrojevka shooting range in Danilovgrad in the days before the killings.

“He carried out a test shooting at the range, entered the building and committed the killings,” Scepanovic said. “After that, he drove away in one of the victims’ vehicles.”

Police later found the vehicle that Shabunin allegedly used to leave the crime scene in Rogami, near Podgorica. They believed Shabunin later travelled by taxi from Podgorica toward Herceg Novi.

Scepanovic had described the suspect as dangerous and said he had taken a firearm and ammunition with him after the killings.

The Ceska Zbrojevka shooting club told state broadcaster RTCG that the three victims were its employees and had been at work without weapons and without the possibility of defending themselves.

Police initially urged residents to remain indoors while the suspect was at large and warned people to avoid contact with unknown persons and report any suspicious behaviour.

Authorities have not disclosed a possible motive or provided further details about the circumstances leading up to the killings.

“Police officers are continuing their activities in cooperation with the Higher State Prosecutor’s Office in Podgorica to establish all the circumstances of the incident, including its cause and motive, and to fully clarify the entire situation,” the statement said.

Prime Minister Milojko Spajic expressed condolences to the victims’ families. He said September 1 and 2 would be declared days of mourning in Montenegro.

World.title: Animals in Tirana Zoo Struggle in Sweltering Summer Heat
World.content:
In Britain, the BBC reported that some zoos were using paddling pools, iced water and iced fruits to keep animals cool.

Iced fruits have also been deployed at Tirana Zoo, said zoo director Evis Rrahmani.

Rrahmani said the zoo has plans to enhance its enclosures, “to make them more diverse to provide mental stimulation for the animals”.

“We intend to improve it, but it takes time,” she acknowledged.

Research-based news website The Conversation recently raised the issue with an article under the headline ‘Are Zoos Ready for the Changing Climate’. It argued that extreme heat should be treated as a “foreseeable animal welfare risk”.

“This might involve expanding shaded areas, creating climate-controlled refuges, improving ventilation, installing misting systems and water features, and monitoring temperature and humidity in real time,” it suggested.

“But infrastructure alone will not be enough. Zoos may also need to adapt their daily management practices, adjusting feeding and enrichment schedules and modifying routines to minimise heat exposure during the hottest parts of the day,” it cautioned.

“To be honest, we don’t have [enough] water in Tirana; everyone struggles to get it, not just us. But since our water consumption is higher, it stands out more in our case,” wildlife veterinarian Vasili said.

Indrit Osmani from Animal Rescue Albania, ARSA, said securing enough water and shade was only the bare minimum.

“If an animal is kept in captivity, the responsibility extends far beyond merely providing the minimum conditions for survival,” said Osmani, who stressed that ARSA opposes keeping animals in captivity.

“A modern zoo should not be judged solely by the quality of its infrastructure or the fact that the animals have access to water, food, and shade,” he said. “It must be evaluated based on whether the entire living environment is adapted to the biological, social, and behavioral needs of each species and the individual animals housed there.”

“Extreme temperatures can cause heat stress, dehydration, fatigue, and behavioural changes. Naturally, the impact varies depending on the species, age, and condition of each individual.”

“Modern animal welfare standards require that animals have the ability to make choices and exercise some control over their environment, including access to varied microclimates, shaded areas, and indoor spaces, as well as the opportunity to escape continuous exposure to heat.”

World.title: Montenegro Greenlighting Solar Plants Despite Warnings of Biodiversity Damage
World.content:
In ratifying the Paris Agreement in 2017, Montenegro committed to cutting greenhouse gas emissions by 55 per cent by 2030 and raising the share of renewables to 50 per cent of gross final energy consumption.

Renewables accounted for 41 per cent in 2024, while solar plants generated 4.51 per cent of Montenegro’s electricity in 2025.

Documents analysed by BIRN show that since March 2023 the Montenegrin government has issued private investors with more than 40 sets of urban and technical requirements for solar power plants.

The Ministry of Spatial Planning, Urbanism and State Property has meanwhile issued construction permits for six projects.

The government issues the urban and technical requirements after consulting relevant institutions. Investors may then be required to prepare an EIA assessing the project’s potential environmental impact and setting out measures to prevent or reduce damage.

For projects under state jurisdiction, the Environmental Protection Agency approves the EIA, while local authorities decide on municipal projects, based on the findings of an assessment commission.

Once the final design has been prepared and reviewed, the investor can apply for a construction permit.

BIRN found that the company Obnovljivi Izvori Energije received a construction permit for the Predis solar power plant in Cevo, near Cetinje, even though its EIA warned that the project could permanently destroy black hornbeam and manna ash scrub, as well as two proposed Natura 2000 habitats.

The assessment argued that the habitats were widespread and that their eradication at the project site “would not have significant negative consequences for their distribution or survival”.

Likewise, MEnergy received a construction permit for a 385-megawatt solar plant on the border between Cetinje and Niksic, even though four prospective Natura 2000 habitats and 70 species on the IUCN Red List were recorded at the site.

The EIA says the project will have a major negative impact on habitats and plant and animal species, while noting that the biodiversity is not unique to the area. “Some habitats will be destroyed, others degraded,” the assessment reads.

“The composition of existing plant and animal communities will change.” Avramoski said areas containing proposed Natura 2000 habitats, endemic species and IUCN Red List species require particular caution.

“The fact that an area is not yet formally protected does not mean that it is ecologically low- value or automatically suitable for development,” he said. “At the same time, the presence of important biodiversity values does not automatically mean that every project is impossible.”

But, he added, such projects must undergo “rigorous, transparent and science-based assessment”.

“Where significant impacts cannot be avoided or adequately mitigated, the project should be redesigned, relocated, or not proceed in its proposed form.”

Government speeds up permitting

World.title: Women Survivors of Bosnia’s War Watch Tributes to Mladic with Despair
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp

"I do not hate them," 82-year-old Kada Hotic tells BIRN over the phone. "I am just wondering what kind of person you have to be to celebrate a war criminal."

Hotic was answering the call from hospital, where she was undergoing medical checkups while trying to follow the reactions to the death last week of Ratko Mladic, the convicted war criminal who was serving a life sentence for the Srebrenica genocide.

Hotic lost her husband, a son and two brothers in the genocide in July 1995. More than 50 other members of her extended family were killed in a series of systematic killings executed after Mladic’s forces overrun the UN-declared “safe zone” of Srebrenica, committing crimes which were classified as genocide by international and domestic courts.

World.title: Has the Much Anticipated Croatian Robotaxi Failed?
World.content:
September the 2nd, 2026 – Has the Croatian robotaxi story ended? It has been revealed that Mate Rimac’s Verne may need to return 89.7 million euros if it is determined that the project has indeed failed.

The company Verne, which has been engaged in developing the much anticipated robotaxi project, is prepared to return 89.7 million euros in advance payments drawn from the National Recovery and Resilience Plan if the evaluation of what has been achieved so far in the project shows that the contracted obligations have not been fully met. “The company is prepared to return all funds,” Verne said in its announcement.

an ongoing procedure

The Verne project, partially financed from the National Recovery and Resilience Plan (NPOO), officially ended on the 31st of August, but the key part of the procedure is still to come, the final evaluation that will show whether all contracted obligations have been fulfilled. Sinisa Malus reports for Poslovni that the company has stated, as touched on above, that it is prepared to return all funds if the competent authorities determine that the objectives have not been fully achieved, according to the announcement. The company has so far drawn 89.7 million euros in advance payments from the NPOO project, while it has raised more than 140 million euros from various private investors.

The Verne robotaxi project has therefore formally ended, but the procedure is not finished. Within one month, Verne must submit a report on all activities carried out, costs incurred and final results achieved. On the basis of that documentation, the competent authorities will carry out the final evaluation and determine what of the contracted obligations has actually been fulfilled.

what we know so far

The delivery of all prototypes of fully autonomous electric vehicles envisaged by the project has been verified, testing has been carried out, and regulations have been adopted. “The project ended on the 31st of August. The company is now submitting, within one month, a report on all activities carried out, costs incurred and final results achieved. On the basis of that report, the competent authorities will make the final evaluation of the project, i.e. an assessment of what has been successfully fulfilled in the project,” Verne stated.

According to the company’s claims, some of the objectives have already passed the verification of the competent institutions. The delivery of all prototypes of fully autonomous electric vehicles envisaged by the project has been verified, appropriate testing has been carried out, and regulations governing autonomous driving have been adopted. However, three remaining objectives still need to receive a final assessment, and the outcome of the project will largely depend on them. These are: the issuance of 50,000 free vouchers for rides in fully autonomous vehicles to persons with disabilities, the production of fully autonomous electric vehicles adapted to the needs of passengers with disabilities, and the establishment and operational readiness of specialised infrastructure.

multiple amendments have already been made

“In the implementation of the project so far, the competent institutions have verified that all verification prototypes of fully autonomous and electric vehicles have been successfully delivered, that appropriate testing has been carried out, and that regulations on autonomous driving have been adopted,” the company stated. They add that the public will be informed after the competent authorities complete the procedure of assessing the success of the project.

The main result of the project, for which Project 3 Mobility was approved 179.5 million euros from the National Recovery and Resilience Plan, was supposed to be a fully autonomous electric vehicle of the fifth level of autonomy. That objective did not change even after multiple amendments to the contract and extensions of deadlines. The Ministry of Maritime Affairs, Transport and Infrastructure particularly emphasised this back in April, when the last annex to the contract was signed.

The fifth level represents the highest level of autonomy. Such a vehicle does not need a driver and is not limited to predefined areas or driving conditions. Neither Verne nor any other company in the world has a vehicle of that level of autonomy today.

there are still many unknowns in the story

As Mate Rimac revealed recently, the fact is that Verne has, in addition to EU funds, also attracted more than 140 million euros in private funds. The robotaxi is already driving the streets of Zagreb. Uber is a strategic partner, and Pony.ai is the technology partner. Verne will be the owner of the fleet and the operator of the service, Pony.ai will provide the autonomous driving solution, while Uber will integrate the service into its global ride-hailing network, which will be an additional option alongside the Verne application. Together, the companies are building a commercial robotaxi service in Zagreb, and over time also in additional European and international markets, with plans to expand to a fleet of thousands of autonomous vehicles in the coming years.

“It’s difficult even to determine precise deadlines for when this will become a profitable business. It’s a kind of adventure, but all partners see potential in it. It will be a great story, but realistically it will take quite a lot of time. It wouldn’t be particularly serious to forecast now when this will be a sustainable business model,” was Rimac’s answer to the question about the profitability of the robotaxi business itself.

World.title: Petition Launched After Removal of Lokrum Nudist Beach
World.content:
September the 2nd, 2026 – A petition has been launched by dissatisfied local people following the removal of a favourite Lokrum nudist beach.

The decision to remove the signs marking out the way to a favourite Lokrum nudist beach has sparked a wave of reactions among residents of Dubrovnik. Morski reports that after the signs were taken down, a group of people decided to take concrete steps and launched a petition calling for a solution that would allow the long-standing practice to continue.

“With this petition, we wish to encourage those responsible to find a legal framework for the lawful continuation of the tradition of naturism on the island of Lokrum. Back during the mid-1960s, with the establishment of the Lokrum Reserve, signs designating a swimming area for nudists were put up by the institution above the cliffs on the eastern side of the island of Lokrum.”

As a reminder, the public first learned about the removal of the signs from a reaction by Professor Igor Legaz, who confirmed on the 26th of August that the signs pointing to the Lokrum nudist beach had been removed, noting that the nudist beach in that area had operated contrary to the applicable regulations.

“This concerns a stretch of coastline about 300 metres long, characterised by a series of large natural stone slabs, which has been under general use since yesterday. For that reason, I thank the Management of the Lokrum Reserve and the director for the step they have taken, because that ‘special-purpose beach’ on the island of Lokrum had in any case been established contrary to the provision of Article 80, paragraph 2, point 2 of the Maritime Domain and Seaports Act,” Legaz said.

While part of the public welcomes the alignment of the situation on the ground with the Maritime Domain Act, the initiators of the petition emphasise the historical and cultural significance of that section of the coast and appeal to the competent institutions to find an appropriate model that would allow the lawful retention of the naturist tradition on the beautiful island of Lokrum.

World.title: September Sea Temperature Records Broken in Split and Komiža
World.content:
September the 2nd, 2026 – The September sea temperature records have been broken in both Split and Komiža, with strong warmth still beating down on the Croatian coast.

The sea was unusually warm along a large part of the Croatian coast on the first day of September. According to DHMZ data, at 14:00 yesterday, the temperature measured in Split was 28.0 degrees, in Komiža 28.2 degrees, and near Dubrovnik it also stood at 28.2 degrees. Index reports that the sea is even warmer on Mljet. In Malo jezero at 2 p.m. as much as 30.2 degrees was measured, in Veliko jezero 29.9 degrees, while on the open sea near Mljet the temperature was 28.8 degrees.

september records have been broken in split and Komiža

Data from both Split and Komiža is particularly interesting. According to the DHMZ bulletin for September 2025, the previous absolute September maximum in Split was measured at 27.3 degrees, measured on the 2nd of September 2015. In Komiža, the record was also 27.3 degrees, set on the 2nd of September 2024. Yesterday afternoon’s 28.0 degrees in Split is therefore 0.7 degrees higher than the previous September record, while Komiža with 28.2 degrees exceeded the old record by as much as 0.9 degrees. These are operational DHMZ data, so the final values will be confirmed after data processing. For comparison, during the whole of September last year the highest measured value in Split was 25.0 degrees, and in Komiža 24.6 degrees. Even in the very warm September of 2024, the maximum recorded in Split was 27.0 degrees. The average sea temperature in Split that September was 24.0 degrees, a full 1.7 degrees above the climatic average for the period 1991–2020.

a mere 1.4 degrees lower than the absolute record for that particular station

Yesterday afternoon’s 28 degrees in Split is only 1.4 degrees lower than the absolute record for that specific station. In Split back on the 15th of July 2024 a temperature of 29.4 degrees was measured. Values from Mljet should not be directly compared with the long-term series from Split and Komiža. Malo and Veliko jezero are measured by automatic sensors and aren’t part of the same long-term series of the four stations – Rab, Split, Hvar and Komiža – that DHMZ uses in monthly analyses of September sea temperatures. Surface sea temperature at the classic stations is measured approximately 30 centimetres below the surface.

World.title: Croatia Records Modest Tourism Growth in First Half of 2026 as EU Nights Rise 1.7%
World.content:
September the 2nd, 2026 – Eurostat reports that Croatia has recorded modest tourism growth throughout the entire first half of 2026, as EU overnight stays rise.

Over the first six months of 2026, tourist accommodation establishments across the European Union recorded 1,321 million overnight stays, a 1.7% increase compared with the same period in 2025 (1,299 million nights), according to official data released by Eurostat on 1 September 2026. Eurostat reports that while the EU as a whole continued its recovery and expansion, growth was highly uneven across member states. The strongest increases were recorded in Ireland (+14.6%), Malta (+9.9%) and Slovakia (+5.9%). Nine countries registered declines, with the sharpest falls in Cyprus (–7.7%) and Romania (–6.7%).

Croatia, long one of Europe’s leading tourism destinations, registered only a mild increase of approximately 0.5% in overnight stays during the same period. This placed the country near the bottom of the group of member states that still achieved positive growth, just ahead of Finland and the nine countries that recorded outright declines.

international visitors drive the numbers up

Foreign (non-resident) tourists accounted for 48.9% of all overnight stays in the EU in the first half of 2026. Nights spent by international visitors grew by 2.5%, nearly three times the increase recorded by domestic guests (+0.9%). Dependence on foreign visitors varies dramatically across the bloc. Malta (95.2%), Cyprus (92.6%) and Luxembourg (87.7%) recorded the highest shares of foreign overnight stays, while Germany (18.5%), Poland (19.8%) and Romania (23.0%) remained heavily reliant on domestic tourism.

Croatia’s modest 0.5% growth comes against a backdrop of strong overall EU performance and particularly rapid expansion in several smaller markets. The figures cover the traditionally quieter first half of the year, before the peak summer season. Full-year results will depend heavily on performance in July, August and the shoulder months of September and October. Eurostat’s data underlines that while tourism demand in Europe remains resilient, competition for visitors is intensifying and growth is no longer automatic even for established destinations.
