World.title: Salaries rise 7% while house prices climb 12.4%: Is it worth buying home in Azerbaijan?
World.content:
Buying a home in Azerbaijan

The average price of a 65-square-metre flat in Baku is now around 178,000 manats (about $105,000). Someone earning the country’s average monthly salary of 1,174 manats (about $690) would have to save their entire income for 12 and a half years to afford it. But once the cost of food, rent, transport and other everyday expenses is taken into account, this calculation is purely theoretical.

According to an August review by the Central Bank, house prices rose by 8.6% year-on-year in the second quarter of 2026. Prices for newly built homes increased by 12.4%, while those on the secondary market rose by 8.6%. Rents increased by 7.4%. Over the same period, average nominal wages rose by 7%.

Wage growth is failing to keep pace with house prices

In Azerbaijan, the average nominal wage rose by 7% over the year, or about 77 manats (around $45), reaching 1,174.4 manats. At the same time, prices for newly built homes increased by 12.4%. This means new homes became 5.4 percentage points more expensive than the rate at which average wages increased.

The gap shows that housing affordability for potential buyers has not improved. The rise in wages increased a worker’s annual pre-tax income by around 920 manats (about $541). Meanwhile, a 12.4% increase in house prices means that a flat costing 170,000–180,000 manats would have become roughly 19,000–20,000 manats (about $11,200–11,700) more expensive over the year.

It should also be noted that 1,174 manats is the average nominal wage across the economy as a whole. The figure is calculated before taxes and social contributions and does not reflect the actual income of most workers.

How many years would it take to buy a 65-square-metre flat?

The m2map platform, which analysed more than 82,000 active listings in August, estimated the median asking price in Baku at 2,735 manats (about $1,609) per square metre. At that price, a 65-square-metre flat would cost 177,775 manats.

According to July data from the Azerbaijan Chamber of Appraisers, the median price per square metre for newly built homes was 2,812.5 manats (about $1,655), compared with 2,616.7 manats (about $1,540) on the secondary market. This puts the price of a flat of this size at roughly 170,000 to 183,000 manats (about $100,000–108,000), depending on the segment.

At the national average monthly wage of 1,174.4 manats, 177,775 manats is slightly more than 12 and a half years of a worker’s total earnings. Using Baku’s average wage of 1,487 manats (about $875), the period falls to around 10 years. But this is only a theoretical calculation, assuming a person spends none of their salary on anything else. In reality, someone on an average income would need considerably longer to save the full price of a flat.

If a buyer can save 20% of their salary, it would take around 50 years to accumulate the full cost of the property. To save the down payment required under a standard mortgage, which in this case would be around 28,000 manats (about $16,500), would take almost eight years.

The average wage also does not reflect the incomes of all workers. According to data from the State Statistics Committee, during the first five months of the year, average monthly wages were 763 manats (about $449) in retail, 825 manats (about $485) in education, and 800 manats (about $470.50) in tourism and catering. For workers in these sectors, a mid-range flat in Baku is equivalent to around 18–19 years of their combined earnings.

Does a mortgage make housing more affordable – or more expensive?

The maximum amount available under a standard mortgage from the Mortgage and Credit Guarantee Fund is 150,000 manats (about $88,235), with a loan term of up to 25 years, an annual interest rate of 8% and a minimum down payment of 15%. However, 85% of the 177,775-manat price of the flat exceeds the loan limit, meaning the buyer would have to provide at least 27,775 manats from their own funds.

If the remaining 150,000 manats were borrowed for 25 years at 8% interest, the monthly payment would be around 1,158 manats (about $681.20). Over the full term, the borrower would repay more than 347,000 manats (about $204,000) to the bank. Including the down payment, the total cost would exceed 375,000 manats (about $220,600). Insurance, property valuation, notary fees and other associated costs are not included.

A monthly payment of 1,158 manats is almost equal to the average salary across the country and represents 78% of the average salary in Baku. Under the Fund’s rules, mortgage payments must not exceed 70% of borrowers’ combined income after tax. This means that a Baku resident earning a single average salary would find it practically impossible to service such a mortgage alone.

In a household where two people earn the average Baku salary, the monthly mortgage payment would account for 39% of their combined nominal income. After tax, the share would exceed 40%. According to OECD and Eurostat methodology, housing costs exceeding 40% of disposable income are considered an excessive housing burden.

Under the subsidised mortgage scheme, the annual interest rate is 4%, the loan term can be up to 30 years, and the maximum loan amount is 100,000 manats (about $58,820). Although the monthly payment would be around 477 manats (about $280.60), buying a 65-square-metre flat at Baku’s average price would require around 78,000 manats (about $45,882) in the buyer’s own funds. The lower interest rate therefore does not solve the main problem for families without substantial savings.

Is renting cheaper?

The median advertised rent in Baku is 11 manats (about $6.50) per square metre per month. Renting a 65-square-metre flat would therefore cost around 715 manats (about $420.60) a month – 443 manats (about $260.60) less than the monthly payment on a standard mortgage. However, this still amounts to around 48% of the average salary in Baku, excluding utility bills.

If an investor bought such a flat for 178,000 manats and rented it out for 715 manats a month, the gross annual rental yield would be around 4.8%. After accounting for maintenance, periods when the property is vacant and other associated costs, the actual return would be even lower. Buying a flat with a mortgage and then renting it out therefore generally does not allow the owner to cover the full cost through rental income alone. The model may make sense primarily for investors with substantial capital who are betting on further increases in property prices.

What is driving prices higher?

The Chamber of Appraisers attributes the rise in new-build prices to strong demand in the mid-to-upper and premium segments, the availability of mortgage financing and the perception of housing as an investment asset. The Chamber’s land price index also points to rising prices and limited supply in premium areas. This may put additional pressure on the cost of newly built homes.

At the same time, according to the State Statistics Committee, investment in residential construction fell by 2.7% in real terms in the first half of the year. These figures strengthen the suggestion that demand, growing faster than household incomes, is running up against limited supply.

State-backed mortgages make housing more affordable for some families: in the first half of the year, 2,242 families received mortgage loans worth a total of 226.3 million manats (about $133.1 million). Since 2019, just over 10,000 families have used the rent-to-own scheme. However, it remains unclear whether these programmes are large enough to curb the overall rise in property prices.

Buying a home in Baku today is therefore more affordable for a household with two stable official incomes, substantial savings for a down payment or another property that can be sold than for someone living on a single average salary. Those who qualify for subsidised mortgages and have tens of thousands of manats in savings are also in a stronger position.

For everyone else, the choice is essentially between increasingly expensive rent and taking on long-term, substantial debt.

Buying a home in Azerbaijan

World.title: ‘Occupation is off’: Russian state media RIA Novosti on Georgian PM Kobakhidze’s remarks
World.content:
RIA Novosti on Russia-Georgia relations

Russia’s state-run news agency RIA Novosti has responded to remarks by Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze, saying that Tbilisi had decided to reassess the history of its relations with Moscow.

The article, published on 24 August 2026 under the headline “Occupation is off”: Another country refuses to consider Russia an enemy, focused on Kobakhidze’s remarks about the Treaty of Georgievsk.

Background

On 18 August 2026, Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze said that Georgia’s decision to sign the Treaty of Georgievsk had been a “civilisational choice”.

His main argument was that King Erekle II’s decision ultimately ensured the physical and political survival of the Georgian nation. According to Kobakhidze, Christian Georgia, surrounded by Muslim states, chose to align itself with Orthodox Russia.

Kobakhidze argued that the decision was not only justified but also “the only correct and only possible” choice at the time. He said Russia honoured the terms of the treaty during Erekle II’s lifetime:

“While Erekle II was alive, he ensured that the agreement was upheld to the end, and almost 20 years passed between the signing of the Treaty of Georgievsk and the annexation of Georgia. For two decades, our country effectively survived.”

The Treaty of Georgievsk was an agreement between the Kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti and the Russian Empire, signed on 24 July 1783. Under the treaty, King Erekle II accepted the protection of Russian Empress Catherine II, while Russia pledged to defend the Kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti and preserve its territorial integrity. The treaty formally preserved the internal independence of the Kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti and did not declare it part of the Russian Empire. However, in 1801, the Russian Empire abolished the Kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti and incorporated it into its territory.

What RIA Novosti says in its article

The Russian state-run news agency says Kobakhidze presented Georgia’s decision to accept the Russian Empire’s protection as the only way for the Georgian people to survive Ottoman and Persian aggression.

The article quotes the views of several political experts, including Nino Skvortsova, whom the agency describes as a “Tbilisi-based political analyst”.

According to Skvortsova, Kobakhidze’s focus on the reign of Erekle II serves not only to reinterpret history but also to justify the government’s current policies.

“Kobakhidze is trying to place Erekle II back in his historical context. For him, the king is important as a ruler forced to choose between major powers while his country’s existence was under threat,” the expert says.

In her view, this approach allows parallels to be drawn with the current policies of the ruling Georgian Dream party:

“Modern Georgia is also caught in competition between major powers, while the authorities justify their actions by the need to preserve peace, sovereignty, traditional identity and freedom of foreign policy manoeuvre.”

RIA Novosti also quotes another expert, Artur Ataev, who says that Georgian Dream is trying to raise a new generation free from old stereotypes. Ataev argues that the opposition, in turn, wants Georgia to follow the example of Ukraine, the Baltic states and other former Soviet republics.

“Today, this is one of the main topics of debate in Georgian society. There are even calls to recognise the independence of Abkhazia and South Ossetia,” Ataev says.

He argues that Georgian society and the political elite are gradually changing, but that the restoration of diplomatic relations with Russia is unlikely in the near future.

“After all, most Georgians still see Russia as an occupier,” the expert concludes.

RIA Novosti on Russia-Georgia relations

World.title: More than 5,000 sheep worth $1.7m stolen from property in rural Qld
World.content:
Approximately 5,500 dorper sheep worth more than $1.7 million have been stolen from a property in rural Queensland.

Police are appealing for public assistance after the dorper ewes and rams were stolen between February and May this year from a property outside of Blackall on the Blackall-Isisford Road.

Detectives from the Rural and Stock Crime Squad are asking anyone who may have seen a flock of dorper sheep "matching the description" to come forward.

The sheep are fitted with white National Livestock Identification System (NLIS) tags, the police said in a statement.

The statement added police are particularly interested in speaking with anyone who observed "suspicious stock movements, livestock transport activity, or other unusual behaviour in the area".

Detective Senior Sergeant Paul Elliot from the Rural and Stock Crime said livestock theft remained a significant concern for police in rural Queensland.

"Livestock theft can result in substantial financial losses and place additional pressure on farming businesses already facing challenging conditions," Detective Senior Sergeant Elliot said.

"Livestock theft investigations can be complex, often spanning large geographical areas, which is why we work closely with producers, saleyards, transport operators and industry stakeholders to identify offenders and disrupt criminal activity."

World.title: Tourist left bruised after being charged twice by wild buffalo
World.content:
Two tourists from Victoria say they had the fright of their lives this week, when they were attacked by a buffalo at a gorge near the outback Northern Territory town of Katherine.

Hattie Frdelja and Emma Hipwell, both 21, were walking the 13-kilometre trail to Butterfly Gorge in Nitmuluk National Park, 300km south of Darwin, on Monday when they came face to face with a feral buffalo.

NT Parks and Wildlife says almost 350 buffalo were removed from the park in May. (ABC Rural: Daniel Fitzgerald)

"[It was] literally just right in front of us, maybe five or 10 metres away," Ms Frdejla said.

The couple said they froze after seeing the buffalo and then heard warning shouts from other hikers further down the track.

"I looked at him and could tell in his eyes that he was definitely happy to have a go," Ms Hipwell said.

Emma Hipwell and Hattie Frdelja say they were lucky not to come off any worse following an encounter with a wild buffalo. (ABC News: James Elton)

Ms Frdejla said the buffalo then "pushed her over" before running away.

"[He] did a U-ey and came back and picked her up … and tossed her onto the ground," she said.

"We just screamed and screamed and yelled 'Help! Help!'."

Ms Frdelja said the other nearby hikers, who had already managed to escape the buffalo, came to the couple's aid.

Emma Hipwell says the incident was a case of being in the wrong place at the wrong time. (ABC News: James Elton)

"The people down the track were so lovely and ran straight up, and they said the buffalo had actually charged at them as well but they ran down the gorge," she said.

Ms Hipwell described the encounter in an enclosed area leading into the gorge as a case of "just bad timing".

"If we were further up I reckon he would've just picked a side and we would've moved, or if we were further down we would've been able to outrun him," she said.

“He was already spooked and we were in his way – he had nowhere to go, we had nowhere to go, so he just went straight for Em,” Ms Frdelja added.

Ms Hipwell said she was left with bruising and scratches down both sides of her hips and legs.

Emma Hipwell and Hattie Frdelja were part-way through a three-month tour of Australia when they came face to face with the wild animal. (ABC News: James Elton)

"It didn't tickle," she said.

Ms Frdejla said the pair would now continue their three-month tour of Australia after taking a break to recover from the ordeal in Katherine.

The Northern Territory has hundreds of thousands of feral buffalo, which can weigh up to 1,200 kilograms, concentrated mostly in wetland areas of the Top End.

In 2023, a 73-year-old man was hospitalised after being gored by a buffalo near Borroloola on the Gulf of Carpentaria.

An NT Parks and Wildlife spokesperson said buffalo were managed through annual aerial removal programs, with almost 350 of the animals removed from Nitmiluk in May.

World.title: Breaking: Tasmania's Mount Lyell copper mine to reopen in boost for west coast
World.content:
A South African company plans to restart the historic Mt Lyell copper mine on Tasmania's west coast, creating more than 300 jobs.

The mine near Queenstown was a cornerstone of the region's economy for more than a century.

Coroner rules mine deaths 'avoidable' A coroner investigating three deaths within six weeks at the Copper Mines of Tasmania mine says two of them could have been avoided if basic safety principles had been observed.

But it entered care and maintenance in 2014, after three workers were killed within six weeks, and a rockfall damaged underground infrastructure.

The mine had been operated by Copper Mines of Tasmania before it was acquired by mining company Sibanye-Stillwater in 2023.

Today Sibanye-Stillwater has announced it has secured board approval to resume operations.

'Beating heart of Queenstown'

The West Coast Council Mayor Shane Pitt said it was "fantastic news" for the entire community.

"Before its closure in 2014, Mt Lyell was the beating heart of Queenstown, and its reopening will breathe new life into our region," he said.

"The west coast backs those who back us, and I look forward to a long and rewarding partnership with Sibanye Stillwater."

The mine has been described as the "beating heart" of Queenstown. (ABC: Selina Bryan)

Tasmanian Labor said along with the 300 jobs, it would create "flow-on benefits for local contractors, accommodation providers, hospitality businesses and retailers".

"Mt Lyell is part of the fabric of Queenstown, and its restart will provide a major boost for the broader west coast economy, with benefits felt across the state," a spokesperson said.

Production to restart in 2029

According to a company report published yesterday, work at the project is scheduled to begin early next year, before production commences in early 2029.

This will first require capital investment of around $490 million.

It plans to mine 26,000 metric tonnes of copper, 16,000 troy ounces of gold and 116,000 troy ounces of silver from the site each year.

It believes the mine can operate for another 23 years.

It is hoped reopening the mine will result in 300 new jobs. (ABC News: David Hudspeth)

Sibanye-Stillwater said the mine would be powered by hydropower, would cover the mine's "existing and previously disturbed footprint", would utilise "increased automation" and would have clearly defined future and environmental closure responsibilities.

The environmental impacts of the mine, under previous ownership, have been a long-standing issue.

According to the Federal Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water in 2021, the nearby lower King and Queen rivers remain heavily affected by historic mining practices.

It said they were now "essentially lifeless", due to acidity and high metal concentrations.

The surrounding hills have been stripped bare of vegetation, partly due to toxic fumes from smelting.

"Sibanye-Stillwater will be responsible for meeting environmental, rehabilitation, and closure obligations that arise from both the restart and future operations, in accordance with applicable regulations," the company states on it website.

"The group is currently evaluating opportunities such as mine-water treatment and reuse, progressive rehabilitation, and the engineered placement of potentially acid-forming material in suitable existing mining voids."

World.title: Prosecutors allowed to seek death penalty in Charlie Kirk murder case
World.content:
A judge has ruled that Tyler Robinson, the man accused of fatally shooting conservative activist Charlie Kirk last year, should face trial on murder charges in a case eligible for the death penalty.

Utah District Court Judge Tony Graf made the ruling at a hearing on Tuesday, local time, where prosecutors laid out what they called "overwhelming" evidence that a capital trial of Mr Robinson was warranted for the murder of one of the US political right's most prominent figures.

Mr Robinson has pleaded not guilty.

Utah County attorneys accused the former apprentice electrician of firing the single shot that killed Mr Kirk as he held one of his trademark campus debates that helped propel him to national prominence.

Mr Robinson faces seven charges, among them aggravated murder for endangering the lives of others at the event, which carries the death penalty in Utah.

Charlie Kirk was speaking at Utah Valley University when he was shot. (Reuters: Trent Nelson, The Salt Lake Tribune)

Utah County prosecutor Ryan McBride presented video of what he said was Mr Robinson taking up a sniper position at Utah Valley University in Orem on September 10, 2025, before he shot Mr Kirk.

He displayed pictures that he said showed Mr Robinson created a "great risk of death" to others, with Mr Kirk's security detail only feet away from Mr Kirk when he was shot.

Mr McBride said the four rounds in Mr Robinson's rifle demonstrated that the shooter was prepared to fire more rounds if the first missed, further endangering others.

"He lay down in a prone position, and he would have seen this mass of people of 3,000 plus people there for the event, took aim, put his crosshairs on Charlie Kirk, and fired," Mr McBride told the court.

DNA evidence disputed

Defence lawyer Staci Visser said the shooting endangered no-one but Mr Kirk, arguing the crime did not meet the standard of aggravated murder.

Ms Visser said the assailant did not engage with anyone else or reload the weapon, but simply fired the gun and ran away.

"There is one act. There is one shot. There is one bullet. There is one victim," Ms Visser told the court.

"There was no evidence that would suggest that anyone else was threatened."

During the hearing, the prosecutor cited test results that showed Mr Robinson's DNA was on the alleged murder weapon. Defence lawyer Michael Burt questioned the reliability of that testing.

Right-wing activist and Trump ally Charlie Kirk shot dead at Utah university Charlie Kirk, a friend and political ally of Donald Trump with millions of online followers, was shot while taking questions from a crowd of students in Orem, south of Salt Lake City.

Mr McBride alleged that Mr Robinson, who was in a relationship with his roommate, targeted Kirk for his political views against gay marriage and transgender rights.

He cited a text message from Mr Robinson in which he allegedly told his roommate he shot Mr Kirk because "some hate can't be negotiated out".

Among those in the packed courtroom were Mr Kirk's parents, Robert and Kathryn, and his wife, Erika, who has taken leadership of the late activist's conservative youth organisation.

A co-founder of conservative youth organisation Turning Point USA, Mr Kirk was credited with energising young voters behind President Donald Trump's 2024 re-election campaign.

His killing, captured in a video that spread widely on social media, is among a series of attacks on US political figures in recent years that have fuelled debate over political violence in a deeply polarised country.

At a memorial following Mr Kirk's shooting, Erika Kirk said she forgave the alleged shooter.

She has not commented on the death penalty charge.

Reuters

World.title: Live: Ray Hadley faces cross-examination in radio 'rival' Alan Jones's trial
World.content:
Retired 2GB radio host Ray Hadley has begin facing cross-examination at Alan Jones's indecent assault and sexual touching trial.

Veteran broadcaster Alan Jones has pleaded not guilty to 22 charges related to the alleged offending, with the trial in the NSW Local Court now in its fourth week.

Live Moment Live updates, reactions and contributions from ABC readers. Staff told to 'dig up dirt on Hadley', trial hears Mr Hadley said a 2GB colleague, who he described as a "double agent" told him Mr Jones requested that his staff "dig up dirt on Hadley". Defence barrister Gabrielle Bashir SC asked Mr Hadley whether he recalled being accused of assaulting a colleague in the 2GB corridors, which Mr Hadley said CCTV proved never took place. "Fortunately, there was CCTV in corridors and I didn’t come close [to that person]," he said. Mr Hadley told the court he later asked management whether the person who made the accusation would be "disciplined" for making a false complaint. Mr Hadley said he was informed of the accusation by a colleague, who he said was working as a "double agent" for Mr Jones. Hadley took interest in media coverage Mr Hadley has admitted to following the media coverage of Mr Jones's indecent assault trial. He told the court he'd "become more interested in the last few days" but accepted that he had paid some attention to articles written about the hearing throughout the course of the trial. "I didn’t take much notice until I heard from [Jason] Morrison and [another former 2GB colleague]," he said. Shareholder 'had enough of Jones', trial told Mr Hadley said John Singleton, a shareholder of Macquire Media at the time, approached him with the idea of taking over the breakfast slot, saying he'd "had enough of Jones costing him millions" with defamation cases. "I didn’t pursue it, they came to me," he said. The trial heard Mr Hadley was due to take the role in mid-2019 but it never eventuated, and Mr Jones was re-signed for two more years. Mr Hadley rejected multiple suggestions that he was "telling everyone" at 2GB that the breakfast slot was his after he signed the contact. He also denied telling Complainant C about the contract. Details of 'secret' contract revealed Ray Hadley tells the court he signed a contract to replace Alan Jones as the breakfast radio host at 2GB in mid-2019, but only because it would have doubled his salary to $4 million. Mr Hadley said he was approached by management to take the breakfast program and later signed a "secret" contract in late-2018. "They doubled my salary and gave me breakfast money," he said. "I didn’t want to get out of bed at half past one [in the morning] but the money made me do it. "I'll do midnight to dawn for $4 million a year if you want me to." Relationship with alleged victim explored Mr Hadley accepted a suggestion from defence barrister Gabrielle Bashir SC that he already had a "close relationship" with Complainant C before the man later came in regular contact with Mr Jones. Before the cross examination of Mr Hadley begun, he told the prosecution his 2019 conversation with Complainant C, where the man confided in him about his allegations against Mr Jones, had taken place at least a day before he facilitated a phone call with author Peter FitzSimons. The court previously heard that Mr FitzSimons had reached out to Mr Hadley telling him he was "researching" accusations against Mr Jones. Complainant C said he never identified himself to Mr FitzSimons in the phone call and asked for his story not to be made public. Cross-examination begins Ray Hadley has completed his evidence in chief and will now face cross-examination from Alan Joness' defence barrister Gabrielle Bashir SC. Alan Jones watches on from the courtroom Ray Hadley has now resumed his evidence. He was met with another lengthy stare from his former radio colleague Alan Jones as he returned to the court room after a brief judgement. Ray Hadley continues to give evidence We are standing by to bring you live updates from the NSW Local Court, where veteran radio broadcaster Alan Jones is on trial over allegations of indecent assault and sexual touching. Retired 2GB radio host Ray Hadley will return to the witness box today.

The court has previously heard a former colleague of Mr Jones, known as Complainant C, has accused the now-85-year-old of kissing him in a work lift on multiple occasions in 2008.

Complainant C also alleges Mr Jones touched his crotch on a number of occasions.

Mr Jones has been taking notes while Mr Hadley gives evidence. (ABC News: Abubakr Sajid)

The trial was previously told Complainant C confided in Mr Hadley in October 2019.

Mr Jones could be seen staring down Mr Hadley as he returned to the witness box for cross-examination for a second day following a brief legal argument on Wednesday.

Mr Hadley accepted a suggestion by defence barrister Gabrielle Bashir SC that he had a "close relationship" with Complainant C before the alleged victim came in regular contact with Mr Jones.

Mr Hadley on Tuesday told the trial he consoled Complainant C when he "broke down" while discussing Mr Jones's alleged offending.

The former 2GB star first met Mr Jones in the early 1980s, with the trial on Tuesday hearing evidence about an alleged plot for Mr Hadley to take over his counterpart's coveted breakfast slot in 2019.

Mr Hadley's evidence was cut short on Tuesday afternoon to allow legal arguments to be resolved.

Mr Hadley on Tuesday said he asked Complainant C if he had consented to the kissing and touching.

"[Complainant C] broke down and cried. He said, 'No I hated it. I'm not homosexual'," he said.

"[Complainant C said] he felt a sense of guilt that he allowed it to happen and he wished he'd done something about it."

Mr Hadley says Complainant C became emotional during the conversation about Mr Jones. (ABC News: Abubakr Sajid)

Mr Hadley said the man swore him to secrecy, and rejected offers to report the allegations to police, Mr Jones's management or the chair of the radio station.

"[Complainant C said] 'It would ruin me, it would ruin my career … he's too powerful'," he said.

Mr Hadley said the matter was not raised again by either of the men.

The court heard Complainant C later decided to share his allegations with Sydney Morning Herald (SMH) reporter Kate McClymont, who published an article about the claims in December 2023.

Mr Hadley said he acknowledged the reporting in a pre-recorded radio broadcast, and made a statement to police in June 2024.

The trial continues.

World.title: Ferrari's Schumacher-inspired livery, F1 leader to cop penalty in Italy
World.content:
Ferrari will be celebrating the legacy of Michael Schumacher this weekend at its home race, with a special livery dedicated to the seven-time Formula 1 world champion.

This year marks 30 years since Schumacher joined the Scuderia, and 20 years since his final F1 victory in the 2006 Chinese Grand Prix.

Piastri searching for answers as teammate re-enters F1 title picture Oscar Piastri's "disappointing" end to the Dutch Grand Prix leaves the Australian and his McLaren team searching for answers, while his teammate has roared back into the Formula 1 title picture.

With Schumacher at the wheel, Ferrari rose to the top of F1 after years spent without championships.

Ferrari's constructors' championship win in 1999 ended a 16-year wait in the teams' competition, while Schumacher's drivers' championship triumph in 2000 made him the first Ferrari race to become world champion since Jody Scheckter in 1979.

Schumacher won five of his seven drivers' championships with Ferrari, from 2000-2004.

This weekend at the Italian Grand Prix in Monza, a race Schumacher won five times with Ferrari, the Scuderia has a one-off livery which pays tribute to the F1 champion.

Among the features are seven stars on the nose of the car, representing Schumacher's world titles, and drivers Lewis Hamilton — the sport's other seven-time world champion — and Charles Leclerc will wear racing suits that also feature the seven stars and Schumacher's logo.

F1 championship leader to take grid penalty at Monza

Kimi Antonelli has celebrated his 20th birthday as the Formula 1 drivers' championship leader, and heads into his home grand prix with a significant 59-point advantage over his two nearest rivals.

F1 drivers' championship leader Kimi Antonelli is set to start the Italian Grand Prix from the back of the grid. (Reiters: Benoit Tessier)

But the youngest-ever leader of the F1 championship heads into this weekend's race at Monza knowing he has work to do to be near the front of the grid.

Mercedes announced during the previous race weekend in the Netherlands that Antonelli will take an engine penalty this weekend.

F1 teams have an allocation of power unit components they can use in a season. When a driver is fitted with a power unit component that exceeds the allocation, they are handed a penalty at the first event that new part is used.

Mercedes has had multiple power unit issues this year, with Antonelli failing to finish in Barcelona and teammate George Russell suffering issues in Canada and Belgium.

Despite the Italian Grand Prix being Antonelli's home race, Mercedes boss Toto Wolff said now was the right time to do it for the championship leader.

"Our calculations say that that's the best track to take it," Wolff said.

"Obviously, algorithms don't take their nationality into consideration. We're here to fight for a championship and not get the most PR. So yeah, that's what we're going to do."

Monza, known as the Temple of Speed, is expected to be a strong track for Mercedes, which is likely why it is taking the penalty now.

With long straights, there should be plenty of opportunities for Antonelli to pass with his impressive Mercedes power unit.

Monza has been the scene of impressive drives through the field in recent years.

Pierre Gasly won from 10th on the grid driving for AlphaTauri (now Racing Bulls). Max Verstappen won in 2022 after taking a five-place grid penalty, while Lewis Hamilton charged from the last row on the grid to place fifth.

Last year, Isack Hadjar started in the pit lane for Racing Bulls and was able to finish 10th.

ABC Sport will have a live blog of the Formula 1 Italian Grand Prix from 9pm AEST on Sunday, September 6.

World.title: Meet the emerging artists featured in Primavera 2026
World.content:
Who decides what is remembered? What happens to the objects and stories consigned to history's rubbish bin? Can we ever truly understand or recapture the past?

These are some of the questions the artists showcased in this year's Primavera exhibition, which features Australian artists aged 35 or younger, are wrestling with.

Exhibition curator Antares Wells travelled to dozens of studios and galleries in every state and territory to find the most compelling emerging artists, finding many were interested in working with archives, or records of the past.

"When you visit that many artists, five different exhibitions could come out of that," she tells ABC Arts.

"But I identified a preoccupation with what I've called traces; an interest in the relics of the past, picking them up and making something new with them.

"I think it's an eternal theme, but what [the artists in Primavera] are doing with it is distinctive."

Now in it's 34th year, dozens of Australian artists have been highlighted by Primavera. (Supplied: Jessica Maurer)

The eight artists featured this year in Primavera approach the theme from different angles, but there's a through-line of the idea of value; why we discard or overlook things.

Wells says it's an exhibition for the head and the heart.

"It's not a cold, big, bad archive — there's a human heart beating in all of these works, even the ones that seem very sleek and detached," she says.

"I hope [visitors] take away a sense of the intellectual and aesthetic vitality of work in this country, the sheer range and diversity of that work, but also the richness of human stories around us."

Murder at sea and suppressed queer history

Callum McGrath's work, History Piece, examines a queer love triangle which ended in the stabbing murder of 19-year-old stoker John "Jack" Joseph Riley on naval ship HMAS Australia II in 1942. The incident sparked complex and often opaque legal proceedings.

The Naarm/Melbourne based artist has often explored queer history in his work, though this thread of the story was initially suppressed by the authorities dealing with the murder.

"The homosexual element really comes out of a confession that the victim made to the surgeon while he was being treated for stab wounds before he died," McGrath says.

"That [confession] letter was left out of the court proceedings, so that bit was a bit difficult, but I found a copy of it in the archives eventually," McGrath says.

"The fact that the letter was left out of the court hearings on the boat, I think, speaks volumes."

Callum McGrath's History Piece delves into a love story with a grisly ending. (Supplied: Callum McGrath)

McGrath recasts the story as a complex intersection of queer history, power and politics. His multimedia often uses overlapping layers of images and text to produce a work that resists easy interpretation.

"It's accumulative and exhaustive," McGrath says of History Piece.

"Rather than having something concise, the idea was to present the evidence as this accumulation of stuff."

McGrath's magpie approach includes a series of line drawings he did of the key people involved in the case. He created images from original photos using digital software, etched them onto glass with a computer-driven cutting tool and in-filled the etching marks with ink.

McGrath says he liked the allusive properties of creating portraits on glass.

"In my mind, glass is a visual storage device. The [portraits] are meant to be physical objects of history containing data and information. It's a way of engraving history on these objects that could be reused."

Weaving history and family connection together

In Linda Sok's Deities in Temples XXI, a sacred art form almost extinguished by the Khmer Rouge regime is both revived and reinvented.

When the regime seized power in 1975, they set about destroying religious or pre-revolutionary artefacts, including pidans, a traditional form of Cambodian silk weaving that people usually hung from the ceiling of a temple.

Linda Sok delves into her family history via screen printing. (Supplied: Eloise Cato)

Often, the only record of the lost pidans was archival cards stored in the National Museum of Cambodia.

Sok, now based in the USA, found re-creating these lost treasures helped her reconnect her with her family and Cambodian heritage. She shared the archival card descriptions with her family, who then drew what they thought each lost pidan looked like.

"I'd moved to the US and was feeling far away from them," she says.

"I had to overcome their hesitancy, but when they began doing the drawings and sketches, they became more open to it."

Rather than using the intricate traditional weaving technique, which can take years to learn, let alone master, Sok devised her own method.

She would pull a group of threads tight, screen-print the images her family had created onto the threads, and then add painted elements.

"Screen-printing was my way of paying homage to the practice without actually replicating it, and putting my own spin on it as well," she says.

Re-creating the pidans led Sok to reflect on how our record of the past is always fragmented and imperfect.

One of the images her family created featured a tree front and centre despite the official record of that pidan, created by French archivists, not mentioning any trees.

"When I went back to Cambodia, I noticed how prevalent the imagery [of trees] was throughout Buddhist iconography, so it was interesting that [my family] chose to reintroduce it," she says.

"Maybe the archivists had thought the tree wasn't important to include, so it got left out.

"There's no way of telling what exactly the truth of the matter is, but it's an interesting question that I've been thinking about a lot."

Meteorites and 'meteorwrongs'

Sometimes, a member of the public believes they've found a meteorite, an exotic item that has travelled to Earth from outer space.

Then they send the item to their local science museum, only to be told it's just a regular rock or a lump of industrial debris.

These items are sometimes called "meteorwrongs", and they're the focus of Meteorite Enquiries, a gently funny and melancholy work by Boorloo/Perth-based artist Jack Wansbrough.

"They're essentially waste, but there's still all this life and personality in them," Wansbrough says of the objects.

Jack Wansbrough's collection of ‘meteorwrongs’. (Supplied: Jessica Maurer)

Working from an archive cataloguing a museum's correspondence on "meteorwrongs", Wansbrough sought to re-create (or find) substitute objects for each oddity and give these rejected items their moment in the sun.

He then displayed the objects on a low floor bed alongside the archive's yellowing letters and beneath a pair of stained-glass fixtures he made.

Wansbrough spent about six months making and sourcing the objects, combing crystal shops, industrial estates, roadsides and even the car park of a university geology department to find what he was after.

Artist's dazzling terracotta earrings celebrate Indian heritage Monica Rani Rudhar's embellished gold earrings are more than just accessories — they are cultural markers connecting her to family.

"Sometimes, I was looking at photos and a piece I literally found on the ground was almost a perfect match. That was really exciting," Wansbrough says.

"But sometimes, the descriptions are extremely brief, which can make it harder but also easier, in a way. Some letters would just say 'A rock that's been carved', so that gave me an interpretive freedom to carve anything I want."

While the rocks and debris Wansbrough's installation re-creates may not be of scientific interest, each has its own idiosyncratic human story.

"With my work, I'm often pointing away from myself, towards an archive or something external. I find it's an interesting way to work in that you're always looking at this thing in front of you, but also imagining this thing that you can't see."

Primavera 2026: Young Australian Artists runs until September 28 at the Museum of Contemporary Art Australia in Sydney.

World.title: Deadline to save embattled developer Bathla extended for 24 hours
World.content:
Collapsed major Sydney developer Bathla Group appears to have staved off the immediate threat of liquidation, after its administrators extended a self-imposed deadline for $20 million in funding from the group’s private lenders for another 24 hours. Teneo was appointed after Bathla entered voluntary administration last week owing debts of more than $3.3 billion. The administrators had been negotiating with the dozens of private lenders who had propped up the company over years to obtain short-term funding to pay 350 staff and complete almost-finished construction projects. Administrators have extended the deadline to save Bathla for another 24 hours. Brent Lewin It had initially set a deadline of Thursday, the payroll deadline for Bathla’s staff who haven’t been paid for eight weeks. But on Tuesday morning, Stephen Longley, a senior managing director at Teneo, told Nine’s Today program that his administrators would begin wrapping up the company by the end of the day. He warned Bathla’s financial situation was “very dire” and the administrators were running out of hope to find funding to complete the 45 projects under construction. Negotiations to save the developer will now continue until Thursday.



Teneo’s immediate priority remains meeting Thursday’s payroll deadline for Bathla’s 350 staff, who haven’t been paid for eight weeks. Related Article Updated

Bathla collapse Administrators ‘running out of hope’ to finish Bathla projects as deadline for funding push nears The company, which built mainly greenfield housing in Sydney’s north-west and throughout the state, had been in financial peril for months as the quality of its building was interrogated by Building Commission NSW. The NSW government on Tuesday backed its decision to not bail out the company. Treasurer Daniel Mookhey, speaking while in New Delhi on a trade trip on Tuesday afternoon, called on the private lenders to step in to support the administrators, saying it was not fair to ask taxpayers to bail out the companies that “took the risk”. “The first obligation belongs to the private credit firms,” he said. “These are some of the most sophisticated lenders in the Australian economy. They took the risk. The onus is on them to step up and support the administrators.”



Premier Chris Minns, also on the trip, said he was concerned about the risk of contagion across the construction industry as a result of the collapse but stood by the decision not to bail the company out. “I am concerned about it. Like most volume builders, they use a range of contractors as part of their building, so we’re keeping an eye on that,” he said. “[But] they effectively asked for a line of credit from NSW taxpayers, and it’s not my money; it’s NSW taxpayer money. And I wasn’t convinced that that was the best use of taxpayer money, particularly as we didn’t have a detailed or deep understanding as to how Bathla got into these circumstances in the first place, and what the exposure would be for NSW taxpayers if we did tip money in. More to come. Our Breaking News Alert will notify you of significant breaking news when it happens. Get it here.

World.title: Alan Jones trial live updates: Hadley questioned over ‘secret contract’ to take over Jones’ 2GB breakfast radio slot as cross-examination continues
World.content:
Warning: Graphic content

Hello and thank you for reading our live coverage of Alan Jones’ criminal trial in the Downing Centre Local Court in Sydney. I will be bringing you the latest developments today with my colleagues Clare Sibthorpe and Harriet Alexander.

Former 2GB heavyweight Ray Hadley, a long-time colleague of Jones, started giving evidence in the trial on Tuesday. He returns to the witness box today.

Ray Hadley outside the Downing Centre Local Court on Wednesday. Dominic Lorrimer

Jones, 85, is standing trial on 20 counts of indecent assault and two counts of sexual touching without consent spanning six complainants and a 17-year period from 2003 to 2020. He denies the allegations.

Hadley’s evidence relates to a conversation he had with one of the complainants, a man known as “C”, in 2019. Here are the key parts of his testimony so far.

Hadley said complainant “C” told him in 2019 that Jones had “put his hand on my c--- and kissed me” on a number of occasions some years earlier.

“I asked him if he was homosexual, and whether he was consenting to it,” Hadley said. “He broke down and cried and said, ‘no, I hated it. I’m not homosexual’.”

Hadley said he comforted “C” during the conversation and told him it was not his fault. He offered to take the complainant to the police, he said, but “C” had insisted he did not want to do this because Jones was “too powerful”.

Hadley told the court that author and journalist Peter FitzSimons, a journalist at The Sydney Morning Herald, had been investigating allegations against Jones and that he facilitated a phone call between “C” and FitzSimons in 2019.

At this stage the complainant’s identity was kept secret from FitzSimons and the allegations were not reported, the court has heard.

In 2023 the Herald’s chief investigative reporter Kate McClymont spoke to “C”, the court heard, and his allegations were published in an anonymised form. Hadley agreed he discussed the article on air.

Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491.

World.title: Don’t queue, don’t order cocktails: The nine golden rules of British pubs
World.content:
Reviews & adviceUK Opinion Don’t queue, don’t order cocktails: The nine golden rules of British pubs

Will Hawkes Updated September 2, 2026 — 11:37am , first published September 2, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A German couple enters the Coeur de Lion, a delightful but compact pub in Bath. Finding no seats available in the bar – there are only five tables – they head upstairs on the advice of a fellow customer. Halfway up, the same customer shouts after them. “And you need to order at the bar!” A rapid volte-face. Like other drinking cultures, British pubs have their own rules, which visitors should try to follow. iStock Not everyone understands the unwritten rules that govern pubs, even the most basic ones. But there are rules. This isn’t just Anglo-Saxon stiffness: venues around the world, from French bistros to the hawker markets of Singapore, have their own guidelines, their own uncodified way of doing things. British pubs are places to relax, but even relaxation needs rules. Some take it too far, like the Yorkshire pub I visited recently which covered its walls with tatty signs saying: “Mobile, Tablet and Laptop Free Zone!” and “NO SWEARING POLICY”. But rules are vital. These are the key ones (at least as far as I see it): Don’t queue at the bar



Bars are designed for people to wait along, not queue up behind one another. Alamy 



Anyone who uses public transport will have noted the rise of people playing tinny tunes or videos out loud on their phones. This sort of behaviour has started to seep into pubs, and it needs to be quickly stamped out. That doesn’t mean, however, that phones themselves are verboten: if you’re on your own and enjoying a quiet pint, they’re often a godsend. You can read a book on your phone if you’re virtuous, or just send pictures of your pint to jealous pals. British pubs are not the place to order cocktails. iStock Chat to people you don’t know One of the reasons journalists like pubs (not the main one, admittedly) is that it’s the easiest place to have a relaxed conversation with a stranger. You find out all sorts of interesting things. You can take it too far, though: last month, at the Red Lion in Horley, Oxfordshire, I had to restrain myself from interjecting in a conversation about the member of Traffic who had recently died (Dave Mason RIP). It would have meant shouting across the pub, making me look odder than I actually am. Don’t order cocktails



A lot of pubs offer cocktails. I understand why: there’s a good margin on them and pubs need to make money, particularly in this economy. But you still mustn’t order them. The poor sap behind the bar isn’t a cocktail expert (sorry, mixologist), and it will take ages for him to make you a Sex On The Beach. Everyone else at the bar will hate you. The only exception to this rule is at pubs like the Cooper’s Arms in Crowborough, Sussex, where just one cocktail – a negroni, which doesn’t take an age to prepare – is offered. It’s fine to order that. Feel free to share a table with strangers if there’s room (but behave yourself). iStock It’s fine to share tables... Those Germans at the Coeur de Lion may have been bamboozled by the tradition of ordering at the bar, but they come from a country with its own superb beer culture, and its own set of unwritten rules. One of my favourites is how Bavarians like to share tables; they’re not shy about asking people to budge up. This is something we should see more of in British pubs, I think, although it can go too far. I once witnessed a group of old soaks ask to share a table with three unwary students at my local, the Blythe Hill Tavern, before gradually elbowing them out courtesy of their exuberance and, frankly, inebriation. Impressive in its own way, but also a poor show. … but don’t reserve one



A lot of pubs offer table reservations these days, and – like cocktails – you can understand why. I think customers should resist the urge, though. There is nothing more joyless than entering a virtually empty pub and discovering that every table has a little note on it (“Jonty, 8pm”). Spontaneity is key to the pub experience, and by reserving a table you are helping to destroy that. Get your round in Related Article Opinion

UK One of the best things about London is under threat Ben Groundwater Travel writer Young Londoners have, I’m told, started to abandon the tradition of rounds because beer in the capital has become so expensive. I understand and sympathise, but it remains much the most efficient way to do things. It means fewer people at the bar, which is key. I think four people is the optimum number for a round: any more and it becomes unwieldy. Take your glass back to the bar (and definitely don’t take it home)



Does it make you an especially good person if you take empties back to the bar? Yes. You’re making it easier for the pub to run smoothly by helping the staff. By contrast, stealing glasses is a definite no. The reason why Britons drink out of ugly nonic glasses (the tall ones with the bulge that prevents the rim getting scratched or nicked. Nonic = “no nick”) – unlike the Belgians – is that pub theft is endemic. Someone once took a portrait of Margaret Thatcher off the wall at the Red Lion on Parliament Street in London. Can you imagine? It doesn’t bear thinking about. So pop that Cruzcampo “chalice” back on the bar before you get any silly ideas. The Telegraph, London

World.title: Blues prepare for star Cat Holmes to play; Haynes not sighted at training
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Blues prepare for star Cat Holmes to play; Haynes not sighted at training Roy Ward September 2, 2026 — 11:33am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

Carlton will prepare for Geelong star Max Holmes to return for their elimination final at the MCG on Friday night. Holmes hasn’t played since fracturing his ankle in round 19 but is pushing for a return as the Cats try to find a way to beat the Blues who have become one of the form sides of the AFL since Fraser took charge. Blues coach Josh Fraser. Getty Images Fraser was typically calm at his press conference on Wednesday, admitting he would prepare for both scenarios but expected Holmes to play. “Both. I think we have to be prepared for him to play and for him not to be available to play,” Fraser said when asked about the Cats playmaker.



“He’s a proven player who adds a lot to their side and, at this stage, I’m erring on the side of him being available.” While the Blues don’t want to get too caught up with opposition match-ups, Fraser did admit Holmes makes a big difference to Geelong. Cats midfielder Max Holmes. Getty Images “[It’s] significant when you pair him with Bailey Smith and their running capacity they bring and ball-winning ability,” Fraser said. “That poses some real challenge for us, but what we’ve tried to do ... is not tie ourselves in knots around the opposition and continue to focus on what we do well.



“It’s always that balance in being well-prepared for the opposition strengths and making sure you are prepared to bring yours to the table.” One concern for the Blues will be defender Nick Haynes who wasn’t sighted at training on Wednesday morning and still needs to prove his fitness after playing through an ankle issue in the wildcard win over Melbourne. Loading Haynes may still be able to prove his fitness closer to game time, and his experience and poise are important to Carlton’s defence. “It’s fair to say he was a bit sore post game, and he’s probably slowly progressed quite well throughout the week, the early parts of the week,” Fraser said, speaking before training on Wednesday.



“So he’ll need to train again today to prove his fitness, but we’re hopeful on that one.” Fraser was coy about the prospect of forward Will Hayward returning to the side after failing to prove his fitness last game. Blues forward Will Hayward after kicking a goal against Geelong in May. AFL Photos via Getty Images Hayward joined his teammates for training on Wednesday and looked in promising shape, completing some agility drills on his injured ankle during warmups before media were asked to leave the session. “He needs to train and get through training, and we need to then make an assessment on whether he’s fit to perform,” Fraser said.



“So that’s the same approach we’ve taken with all our players this year. But we’re hopeful that he’s in a better place this time around than what he was last week. “He did a power of work to get himself to a point to be considered last week. “Ultimately, we felt like he wasn’t ready, so we’re interested to see what version we get of him today. But I do know that he’s left no stone unturned in trying to be ready to play.” Hayward kicked three goals in the Blues’ win over the Cats round 12 and will give his side a vital dose of finals experience if he can play.



“The way Will plays the position we want him to play is what we will look at,” Fraser said. Related Article Four Points

AFL 2026 This teenager changed Carlton. And he’s not even the Rising Star “And he’s a quality player. He’s added enormously to our playing group, both from what you see on field, but the character he is as well. “So he’s an important part of what we’ve done so far this year, and yeah, if he’s fully fit, then he’ll be a great addition for us.” Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: A 1923 map to extend Melbourne’s tram network could still prove a transport solution
World.content:
NationalVictoriaMelbourne Assembly A 1923 map to extend Melbourne’s tram network could still prove a transport solution Alexander Darling September 2, 2026 — 11:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Melbourne Assembly brings together the people, ideas and conversations shaping the future of our city. See all stories .

Wiam Bou Karram’s morning commute is often a frustrating one, as he tackles one of the city’s busiest highways on the 14-kilometre trip from his home in Moorabbin to work in South Melbourne. “You’ve got three lanes, and they’re usually bumper to bumper,” he says of the daily grind. Wiam Bou Karram in South Road, Moorabbin. Penny Stephens “There are a lot of traffic lights, and a lot of intersections, so you’re stopping every few kilometres.” The Frankston train line is right at his doorstep, but it doesn’t stop anywhere near the street his job is on.



To rub salt into the wound, things could have been totally different – for him and tens of thousands of other Melburnians. A century ago, chief engineer Tom Percival Strickland suggested the Melbourne and Metropolitan Tramways Board significantly widen its network at the same time it was converting its archaic cable tram fleet to electric. In 1923, the routes stretched 201 kilometres across the city from Black Rock to Fawkner, and Box Hill South to Footscray. Strickland had grand plans to more than double that, to 428 kilometres, and while he successfully converted or created 87 kilometres of electric tramways in his time, other tram line extensions were removed entirely from his vision.



The network plateaued at 250 kilometres, and while it’s still the largest urban tram network in the world, carrying 200 million passengers a year, it could have been much larger. Present-day Melburnians viewing the 1923 map of Strickland’s grand ambitions may find themselves mourning lost opportunity. Punt Road, Bell Street, Footscray, Williamstown, Sunshine and Reservoir all could have been strands on the tram network’s spiderweb. Malcolm Rowe, of Melbourne’s Tramway Museum, said when Strickland’s upgrades were jettisoned, parts of Melbourne were condemned to slower commutes. “It would have provided a good basis for the current city to have services where there are major gaps now,” he said, singling out Monash University and Doncaster.



Melbourne’s present-day planners are now asking the same questions Stickland did. Where can we, and should we, put more tram lines? Perhaps unsurprisingly, there’s some overlap with what the chief engineer originally planned. Johnston Street in Collingwood, 1906, before its tram tracks were removed. In 1923, there had been plans to extend this line all the way down Studley Park Road to Kew. Bou Karram could have been gliding to his job on a tram from South Road, Moorabbin, which Strickland envisioned being connected to the rest of the network along with nearby North Road, Bluff Road and Hampton Street. “I would definitely use a tram if it were well-planned, separate from the other lanes of traffic so it doesn’t create new [congestion] problems,” Bou Karram said. “I always prefer to use public transport; it’s more peaceful.”



Shaping the city is a key topic of The Age and the University of Melbourne’s forum, Melbourne Assembly, a three-day event in October bringing together some of the world’s brightest minds in city planning, innovation, education, arts and sport to discuss ideas for the city’s future. Melbourne’s existing tram network shares 180 kilometres of its routes with cars, making each form of travel slower. Alexander Darling In a vote reflecting the type of city our readers value and envision for their future, extending the city’s tram network was the third most popular idea of the readers’ wishlist of big ideas. Strickland’s agenda for Melbourne’s public transport came to a halt for a surprisingly simple reason. “Buses got better,” Rowe explains.



The same year Strickland left his role – 1938 – his boss, Hector Hercules Bell, travelled to Europe for inspiration. Until then, Bell had been continuing the work of converting Melbourne’s cable trams to electric, but he arrived just in time to see the UK ripping up its tramways to replace them with buses. In a cable back to Melbourne, Bell wrote he felt trams were too expensive to justify compared to buses, which had recently undergone “rapid development and improvement”. In the following decades, Melbourne embraced car travel over public transport – the exception being route 86, which now runs from Bundoora to Victoria Harbour, where Bell was forced to put trams back in the ’50s after buses proved unable to handle passenger numbers.



“Drivers were starting to say, ‘We need more access to street space than you’re giving us at the moment, and we want to push the trams aside’,” said Melbourne University urban transport researcher John Stone, who added that it became hard to justify spending on public transport at a time when Melburnians weren’t using it. “The tramways were a big institution, and they didn’t take seriously the threat from cars. They were manoeuvred out of the way by people saying, ‘we need somebody to build this road’, and so we really lost that ability for public transport to compete and for a long time through the ’70s and into the ’80s.” But as traffic increased and costs for car travel increased at pace along with Melbourne’s population, enthusiasm for public transport grew with it. Tram extensions were promised by the Greens and Labor ahead of the 2014 and 2018 elections respectively, but the footprint of Melbourne’s tram network has remained largely the same shape for decades, with notable exceptions in Box Hill, Vermont South and Docklands. This has not gone unnoticed, with Infrastructure Victoria last November urging the government to extend eight tram routes by 2030, to areas where it is planning for thousands more homes.



Related Article Public transport The slowest trams in Melbourne revealed, where it’s almost quicker to walk “These extensions will give developers the confidence to build new homes in these precincts ... support local jobs and create better connected communities,” Infrastructure Victoria chief executive Dr Jonathan Spear said. Among the precincts Infrastructure Victoria said needed connecting was Moorabbin, one of the government’s activity centres which is slated for more than 5000 new homes in buildings up to 12 storeys. Ironically, the proposal closely mirrors what Strickland had planned all those years ago: Route 64 at East Brighton would be extended south to come down the Nepean Highway, past Moorabbin train station and terminate near the new Holmesglen TAFE. Bou Karram said it wouldn’t just be workers like him that would benefit from such a move.



“In this area, there is only one supermarket. For people who live further away from it than me, a tram is definitely a viable option for them to access it,” he said. Related Series

City life Melbourne Assembly “And if they’re struggling to get to the train station, they can use a tram. How would they get there unless they have a car or ride-share?” A government spokesperson did not comment directly on these proposals, but pointed to the recent $1.85 billion investment in G-Class trams and its plans to make tram stops more accessible on certain routes. “We will continue to plan for further improvements to our public transport network as Victoria grows,” they said.



The government announced plans to abolish Infrastructure Victoria late last month, as suggested by a public service review. It is yet to respond to the 30-year infrastructure strategy from November last year, which included tramline extensions. Melbourne Assembly will be held from October 19 to October 21. More information is available on the Melbourne Assembly website, including special offers for Age subscribers

World.title: Italian court gives ‘off-grid’ Australian mother more access to three children
World.content:
WorldEuropeAustralians abroad Italian court gives ‘off-grid’ Australian mother more access to three children David Crowe September 2, 2026 — 11:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: An Italian court has granted an Australian mother a chance to rejoin her three children after they were removed from the family’s rustic home last November over health fears. The decision allows Catherine Birmingham and her British partner, Nathan Trevallion, to gain access to their children in a gradual process under the supervision of social services staff. Nathan Trevallion and Catherine Birmingham with their children. Website: https://catherinelouisebirmingham.com/ But the ruling by the Juvenile Court in L’Aquila, in central Italy east of Rome, will keep the children in a residential care facility until authorities believe it is safe to reunite the family in their own home. Birmingham told the Nine Network earlier this year that the Italian authorities had been wrong to remove the children, declaring she would keep fighting to take them home.



“What I’m fighting is the very, very, very ignorant belief that what we have done to our children was wrong,” Birmingham said. The couple were raising the children, an eight-year-old girl and two six-year-old twin boys, in woods near the town of Palmoli in the central region of Abruzzo. The Italian social services expressed concern at the fact that the off-grid home had no toilet, no electricity and no running water. They also claimed the children were kept isolated and were not being properly homeschooled. The removal of the children made headlines in November as Italian politicians and observers debated whether the “family in the woods” should be allowed to continue their off-grid lifestyle.



On Tuesday, the Juvenile Court ‌approved a staged process under the supervision of social services that could ultimately allow the children to leave residential care. Related Article Exclusive

Foreign relations ‘Empty inside’: The Australian family fighting Italy for their ‘unschooled’ children “The ruling partially revises previous court decisions and sets out ​a gradual reunification process, allowing the children to return home for daytime visits immediately ​and, from October, for weekend overnight stays with their family,” said lawyer Simone Pillon, who acts for the family. The children were taken into care in November after being poisoned by mushrooms, something the parents described as an accident. Birmingham was allowed to stay in the residential care facility, seeing the children for set periods, until a court ruled in March that she should be removed because of tensions with the staff.



In April, the family lost a claim in the Juvenile Court seeking to regain access to the children. The latest decision requires social services to ​assess the children’s reintegration with their parents before any permanent reunification can take place. Pillon said the family planned an ‌appeal to pursue a faster, more complete process to reunite the family. Court documents reported by the Nine Network’s 60 Minutes program in March declared the home was a “dilapidated ruin” without utilities and that there was a lack of essential care for the children, who had no paediatrician and were not attending school. The couple argued, however, that they were practising “parental education” without a curriculum and drawing inspiration from the Steiner system to encourage creativity.



“They know how to sew, they know how to knit, they know how to chop wood, they know how to grow plants from seed,” Birmingham told 60 Minutes. (The Nine Network is the publisher of this masthead.) “They’re learning other life skills that every child that sits there playing with the toys is not learning.” While the home did not have an indoor bathroom, it had an outdoor compost toilet and a tub for washing. “The base philosophy behind it for us is that the children are growing up in this environment where they have freedom with a boundary,” Birmingham told the program in March. Trevallion said: “You wake up in the morning and do whatever you feel like doing. We don’t have to run out the door to take the children to school. It’s just a very relaxed way of waking up, eating breakfast together as a family and continuing through the day.”
