World.title: Yes, Furious is a killer Epstein story but ‘it’s not just him’ …
World.content:
Emmy Rossum shadowed FBI agents for this hit TV show, which just finished its first season. One “horror” stayed with her.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Between the white-hot rage of Beef, the simmering tensions between guests at The White Lotus and Michaela Coel’s eviscerating I May Destroy You, anger is proving a defining theme of this decade’s most acclaimed TV shows. After its caustic first season, Furious might prove the most blistering of them all. Related Article Review What to stream this week: A five-star post-Epstein thriller, plus five more picks Created by Elizabeth Meriwether (The Dropout, New Girl), Furious is a cat-and-mouse thriller about an FBI agent named Alice (Emmy Rossum, Shameless) hunting down a serial killer, Catherine (Lola Petticrew, Say Nothing), a survivor of child trafficking seeking vengeance on the men responsible. Many of them are known to FBI’s sex crimes unit boss Nora (Quincy Tyler Bernstine), whose hands are often tied. All three seek justice in their own way, fuelled by a carcinogenic fury at a judicial system that fails to protect the vulnerable or hold traffickers accountable. The show – loosely inspired by the 1987 film Black Widow – has become a sleeper hit for Disney+, which reports one-day viewership rose 40 per cent by the penultimate episode from July’s premiere. Following the season finale, TV writer Jared Richards speaks with Emmy Rossum (who is also an executive producer) on how she and Meriwether shaped the series’ approach to sexual violence and trauma, what she thinks of the real-world comparisons critics have made to Jeffrey Epstein, plus a teaser of what’s coming for the just-announced second season. Warning: There are spoilers for the season’s full eight episodes below. Loading



Jared Richards: This is a show about sexual violence and its impact, but it doesn’t feature flashbacks to rape or images of grisly crime scenes. There’s an absence of dead women’s bodies. When and how did you and Liz Meriwether decide to not include those images? Emmy Rossum: From the very beginning. It’s also inspired by a film that’s much more interested in the journey of two women who are lonely outcasts getting to know each other – an FBI agent and a serial killer. Very early on, Liz wanted to tell the story of two sides of a coin that were more similar than they were different: a good guy that wasn’t all good, and a bad guy that wasn’t all bad. We were also interested in showing violence that was very female in nature. What does it look like when you can’t always just shoot someone with a gun? When you have to get really close to them with a needle? Or with a curling iron? How do you weaponise a chicken breast? [We tried to play with] things that are traditionally associated with women. Catherine (Lola Petticrew) finds inventive new uses for her curling iron. Disney/Sarah Shatz In terms of flashbacks, the show is not really interested in depicting trauma other than the after-effects: how it’s compartmentalised, how it twists and shapes us over time and how it affects you 25 years later [as with Alice] or 10 years later [as with Catherine]. Alice is also a survivor of abuse. As an actor, was there anything that was difficult to understand about how her trauma emerges? Her [violent] sex life comes to mind as an example. Yeah, that’s certainly what I was scared by. Having a character who’s been a victim of violence, who is seeking out violence in their life, is confusing. Working with psychologists on the role made it make sense.



This is a person who’s become so dissociated from their body that – similar to Catherine, our killer – her superpower is that she’s been able to hold all these secrets and disconnect from herself. That’s what makes her so great at her job; she can work these cases and seemingly not have them permeate her. Lola Petticrew and Emmy Rossum in Furious. Disney/Sarah Shatz When I worked with FBI agents [to prepare for this role], there was this way that they compartmentalised what they were working on – and the way they processed things – where their eyes just weren’t all there. They were with you, but at the same time they were on every exit and every other person in the room and every vulnerability. They were a pressure cooker in a way I found to be totally illuminating. There were certainly things about the character that overlapped with me – certain parts of her pain, her fear, her obsessive tendencies – but also things that were unfamiliar to me. Emmy Rossum stars in Furious. Disney You shadowed FBI agents and underwent drill training for research. What surprised you about that experience? Some agents shared things that had happened to them that made them become an agent. They didn’t think they would get justice for themselves, but it galvanised them to work for others. There was one specific case that I found to be almost one-to-one with Alice that immediately let me wrap my arms around her.



Editor's pick Streaming The best new TV shows to stream in September Many agents really understood that the system didn’t always work. Yet, it’s the only one that we have, and so they have to work within it. Otherwise, we’ll have chaos and vigilantes everywhere. A lot of the time they’re playing a long game. There was one detective that is still waiting to get justice for a child, and sees who they believe to be the perpetrator of this crime at their 7/11 weekly. Just the horror of seeing somebody that you feel has committed a crime that you can’t quite prove at your 7/11 every week. But knowing that one day that kid is going to be old enough to walk in and tell you the story. Or you’re going to get them some other way, for some other crime. It’s having the fortitude to play that long game and to sit with those uncomfortable feelings of frustration for a long time. Nora (Quincy Tyler Bernstine) is often left with her hands tied in the pursuit of justice. Disney/Sarah Shatz You took on so much in this role. How did you deal with the heaviness? I ate a lot of snacks. I got food trucks for the crew. I’m all about having good things to eat and soothing in other ways. And then you’re held up by your crew, right? You’re held up by your other actors, by your camera operators, by your costume team, by Liz, by your directors. You’re not alone out there on the field. I have an amazing family that I come home to at the end of the day, and I eat my kids’ snacks, and I realise that it’s not my story. It’s my job to tell [Alice’s] story that is, unfortunately, similar to a lot of women’s stories – some of whom aren’t even around to tell their stories any more. But it’s my job to channel those things, and then to try to leave them at work.



The final episode is named Hart Island – the New York site for unmarked graves that Alice and Nora visit in the finale to reinter Catherine’s friend Isabel, previously another Jane Doe. What was the importance of that title? It’s a place where people are honoured. But nobody knows who they are, and they’re not claimed. There’s a tenderness, loneliness and a beauty in that, and our story is very much about the women whose stories haven’t been told. Lola Petticrew as Catherine in the Furious finale. Disney/Sarah Shatz Many critics call Furious as a “post-Epstein show”, though he isn’t directly referenced in the show. How do you view that framing? I understand it. We do have a villain in our show [Jay Easton] who has very similar initials, so I get it. I think, unfortunately, it’s not just him. We’ve had 10, 15, 20 mega-predators over the last 20 years in positions of power. And I think there is a lot of rage about that. About the lack of accountability. About the people who have covered it up – and the fact that we know those people’s names off the top of our head and can rattle them all off. Yet we don’t know the women’s names equally well, and some of them aren’t even around to tell their stories. That’s the tragedy. That’s the horror. Furious has just been renewed for a second season. I know you can’t reveal much yet, but when did you and Liz start considering continuing this story?

World.title: Deadline to save embattled developer Bathla extended for 24 hours
World.content:
Collapsed major Sydney developer Bathla Group appears to have staved off the immediate threat of liquidation, after its administrators extended a self-imposed deadline for $20 million in funding from the group’s private lenders for another 24 hours. Teneo was appointed after Bathla entered voluntary administration last week owing debts of more than $3.3 billion. The administrators had been negotiating with the dozens of private lenders who had propped up the company over years to obtain short-term funding to pay 350 staff and complete almost-finished construction projects. Administrators have extended the deadline to save Bathla for another 24 hours. Brent Lewin It had initially set a deadline of Thursday, the payroll deadline for Bathla’s staff who haven’t been paid for eight weeks. But on Tuesday morning, Stephen Longley, a senior managing director at Teneo, told Nine’s Today program that his administrators would begin wrapping up the company by the end of the day. He warned Bathla’s financial situation was “very dire” and the administrators were running out of hope to find funding to complete the 45 projects under construction. Negotiations to save the developer will now continue until Thursday.



Teneo’s immediate priority remains meeting Thursday’s payroll deadline for Bathla’s 350 staff, who haven’t been paid for eight weeks. Related Article Updated

Bathla collapse Administrators ‘running out of hope’ to finish Bathla projects as deadline for funding push nears The company, which built mainly greenfield housing in Sydney’s north-west and throughout the state, had been in financial peril for months as the quality of its building was interrogated by Building Commission NSW. The NSW government on Tuesday backed its decision to not bail out the company. Treasurer Daniel Mookhey, speaking while in New Delhi on a trade trip on Tuesday afternoon, called on the private lenders to step in to support the administrators, saying it was not fair to ask taxpayers to bail out the companies that “took the risk”. “The first obligation belongs to the private credit firms,” he said. “These are some of the most sophisticated lenders in the Australian economy. They took the risk. The onus is on them to step up and support the administrators.”



Premier Chris Minns, also on the trip, said he was concerned about the risk of contagion across the construction industry as a result of the collapse but stood by the decision not to bail the company out. “I am concerned about it. Like most volume builders, they use a range of contractors as part of their building, so we’re keeping an eye on that,” he said. “[But] they effectively asked for a line of credit from NSW taxpayers, and it’s not my money; it’s NSW taxpayer money. And I wasn’t convinced that that was the best use of taxpayer money, particularly as we didn’t have a detailed or deep understanding as to how Bathla got into these circumstances in the first place, and what the exposure would be for NSW taxpayers if we did tip money in. World.title: Alan Jones trial live updates: Hadley questioned over ‘secret contract’ to take over Jones’ 2GB breakfast radio slot as cross-examination continues
World.content:
Warning: Graphic content

Hello and thank you for reading our live coverage of Alan Jones’ criminal trial in the Downing Centre Local Court in Sydney. I will be bringing you the latest developments today with my colleagues Clare Sibthorpe and Harriet Alexander.

Former 2GB heavyweight Ray Hadley, a long-time colleague of Jones, started giving evidence in the trial on Tuesday. He returns to the witness box today.

Ray Hadley outside the Downing Centre Local Court on Wednesday. Dominic Lorrimer

Jones, 85, is standing trial on 20 counts of indecent assault and two counts of sexual touching without consent spanning six complainants and a 17-year period from 2003 to 2020. He denies the allegations.

Hadley’s evidence relates to a conversation he had with one of the complainants, a man known as “C”, in 2019. Here are the key parts of his testimony so far.

Hadley said complainant “C” told him in 2019 that Jones had “put his hand on my c--- and kissed me” on a number of occasions some years earlier.

“I asked him if he was homosexual, and whether he was consenting to it,” Hadley said. “He broke down and cried and said, ‘no, I hated it. I’m not homosexual’.”

Hadley said he comforted “C” during the conversation and told him it was not his fault. He offered to take the complainant to the police, he said, but “C” had insisted he did not want to do this because Jones was “too powerful”.

Hadley told the court that author and journalist Peter FitzSimons, a journalist at The Sydney Morning Herald, had been investigating allegations against Jones and that he facilitated a phone call between “C” and FitzSimons in 2019.

At this stage the complainant’s identity was kept secret from FitzSimons and the allegations were not reported, the court has heard.

In 2023 the Herald’s chief investigative reporter Kate McClymont spoke to “C”, the court heard, and his allegations were published in an anonymised form. Hadley agreed he discussed the article on air.

Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491.

World.title: Don’t queue, don’t order cocktails: The nine golden rules of British pubs
World.content:
Reviews & adviceUK Opinion Don’t queue, don’t order cocktails: The nine golden rules of British pubs

Will Hawkes Updated September 2, 2026 — 11:37am , first published September 2, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A German couple enters the Coeur de Lion, a delightful but compact pub in Bath. Finding no seats available in the bar – there are only five tables – they head upstairs on the advice of a fellow customer. Halfway up, the same customer shouts after them. “And you need to order at the bar!” A rapid volte-face. Like other drinking cultures, British pubs have their own rules, which visitors should try to follow. iStock Not everyone understands the unwritten rules that govern pubs, even the most basic ones. But there are rules. This isn’t just Anglo-Saxon stiffness: venues around the world, from French bistros to the hawker markets of Singapore, have their own guidelines, their own uncodified way of doing things. British pubs are places to relax, but even relaxation needs rules. Some take it too far, like the Yorkshire pub I visited recently which covered its walls with tatty signs saying: “Mobile, Tablet and Laptop Free Zone!” and “NO SWEARING POLICY”. But rules are vital. These are the key ones (at least as far as I see it): Don’t queue at the bar



Bars are designed for people to wait along, not queue up behind one another. Alamy 



Anyone who uses public transport will have noted the rise of people playing tinny tunes or videos out loud on their phones. This sort of behaviour has started to seep into pubs, and it needs to be quickly stamped out. That doesn’t mean, however, that phones themselves are verboten: if you’re on your own and enjoying a quiet pint, they’re often a godsend. You can read a book on your phone if you’re virtuous, or just send pictures of your pint to jealous pals. British pubs are not the place to order cocktails. iStock Chat to people you don’t know One of the reasons journalists like pubs (not the main one, admittedly) is that it’s the easiest place to have a relaxed conversation with a stranger. You find out all sorts of interesting things. You can take it too far, though: last month, at the Red Lion in Horley, Oxfordshire, I had to restrain myself from interjecting in a conversation about the member of Traffic who had recently died (Dave Mason RIP). It would have meant shouting across the pub, making me look odder than I actually am. Don’t order cocktails



A lot of pubs offer cocktails. I understand why: there’s a good margin on them and pubs need to make money, particularly in this economy. But you still mustn’t order them. The poor sap behind the bar isn’t a cocktail expert (sorry, mixologist), and it will take ages for him to make you a Sex On The Beach. Everyone else at the bar will hate you. The only exception to this rule is at pubs like the Cooper’s Arms in Crowborough, Sussex, where just one cocktail – a negroni, which doesn’t take an age to prepare – is offered. It’s fine to order that. Feel free to share a table with strangers if there’s room (but behave yourself). iStock It’s fine to share tables... Those Germans at the Coeur de Lion may have been bamboozled by the tradition of ordering at the bar, but they come from a country with its own superb beer culture, and its own set of unwritten rules. One of my favourites is how Bavarians like to share tables; they’re not shy about asking people to budge up. This is something we should see more of in British pubs, I think, although it can go too far. I once witnessed a group of old soaks ask to share a table with three unwary students at my local, the Blythe Hill Tavern, before gradually elbowing them out courtesy of their exuberance and, frankly, inebriation. Impressive in its own way, but also a poor show. … but don’t reserve one



A lot of pubs offer table reservations these days, and – like cocktails – you can understand why. I think customers should resist the urge, though. There is nothing more joyless than entering a virtually empty pub and discovering that every table has a little note on it (“Jonty, 8pm”). Spontaneity is key to the pub experience, and by reserving a table you are helping to destroy that. Get your round in Related Article Opinion

UK One of the best things about London is under threat Ben Groundwater Travel writer Young Londoners have, I’m told, started to abandon the tradition of rounds because beer in the capital has become so expensive. I understand and sympathise, but it remains much the most efficient way to do things. It means fewer people at the bar, which is key. I think four people is the optimum number for a round: any more and it becomes unwieldy. Take your glass back to the bar (and definitely don’t take it home)



Does it make you an especially good person if you take empties back to the bar? Yes. You’re making it easier for the pub to run smoothly by helping the staff. By contrast, stealing glasses is a definite no. The reason why Britons drink out of ugly nonic glasses (the tall ones with the bulge that prevents the rim getting scratched or nicked. Nonic = “no nick”) – unlike the Belgians – is that pub theft is endemic. Someone once took a portrait of Margaret Thatcher off the wall at the Red Lion on Parliament Street in London. Can you imagine? It doesn’t bear thinking about. So pop that Cruzcampo “chalice” back on the bar before you get any silly ideas. The Telegraph, London

World.title: Blues prepare for star Cat Holmes to play; Haynes not sighted at training
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Blues prepare for star Cat Holmes to play; Haynes not sighted at training Roy Ward September 2, 2026 — 11:33am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

Carlton will prepare for Geelong star Max Holmes to return for their elimination final at the MCG on Friday night. Holmes hasn’t played since fracturing his ankle in round 19 but is pushing for a return as the Cats try to find a way to beat the Blues who have become one of the form sides of the AFL since Fraser took charge. Blues coach Josh Fraser. Getty Images Fraser was typically calm at his press conference on Wednesday, admitting he would prepare for both scenarios but expected Holmes to play. “Both. I think we have to be prepared for him to play and for him not to be available to play,” Fraser said when asked about the Cats playmaker.



“He’s a proven player who adds a lot to their side and, at this stage, I’m erring on the side of him being available.” While the Blues don’t want to get too caught up with opposition match-ups, Fraser did admit Holmes makes a big difference to Geelong. Cats midfielder Max Holmes. Getty Images “[It’s] significant when you pair him with Bailey Smith and their running capacity they bring and ball-winning ability,” Fraser said. “That poses some real challenge for us, but what we’ve tried to do ... is not tie ourselves in knots around the opposition and continue to focus on what we do well.



“It’s always that balance in being well-prepared for the opposition strengths and making sure you are prepared to bring yours to the table.” One concern for the Blues will be defender Nick Haynes who wasn’t sighted at training on Wednesday morning and still needs to prove his fitness after playing through an ankle issue in the wildcard win over Melbourne. Loading Haynes may still be able to prove his fitness closer to game time, and his experience and poise are important to Carlton’s defence. “It’s fair to say he was a bit sore post game, and he’s probably slowly progressed quite well throughout the week, the early parts of the week,” Fraser said, speaking before training on Wednesday.



“So he’ll need to train again today to prove his fitness, but we’re hopeful on that one.” Fraser was coy about the prospect of forward Will Hayward returning to the side after failing to prove his fitness last game. Blues forward Will Hayward after kicking a goal against Geelong in May. AFL Photos via Getty Images Hayward joined his teammates for training on Wednesday and looked in promising shape, completing some agility drills on his injured ankle during warmups before media were asked to leave the session. “He needs to train and get through training, and we need to then make an assessment on whether he’s fit to perform,” Fraser said.



“So that’s the same approach we’ve taken with all our players this year. But we’re hopeful that he’s in a better place this time around than what he was last week. “He did a power of work to get himself to a point to be considered last week. “Ultimately, we felt like he wasn’t ready, so we’re interested to see what version we get of him today. But I do know that he’s left no stone unturned in trying to be ready to play.” Hayward kicked three goals in the Blues’ win over the Cats round 12 and will give his side a vital dose of finals experience if he can play.



“The way Will plays the position we want him to play is what we will look at,” Fraser said. Related Article Four Points

AFL 2026 This teenager changed Carlton. And he’s not even the Rising Star “And he’s a quality player. He’s added enormously to our playing group, both from what you see on field, but the character he is as well. “So he’s an important part of what we’ve done so far this year, and yeah, if he’s fully fit, then he’ll be a great addition for us.” Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

NationalVictoriaMelbourne Assembly A 1923 map to extend Melbourne’s tram network could still prove a transport solution Alexander Darling September 2, 2026 — 11:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Melbourne Assembly brings together the people, ideas and conversations shaping the future of our city. See all stories .

Wiam Bou Karram’s morning commute is often a frustrating one, as he tackles one of the city’s busiest highways on the 14-kilometre trip from his home in Moorabbin to work in South Melbourne. “You’ve got three lanes, and they’re usually bumper to bumper,” he says of the daily grind. Wiam Bou Karram in South Road, Moorabbin. Penny Stephens “There are a lot of traffic lights, and a lot of intersections, so you’re stopping every few kilometres.” The Frankston train line is right at his doorstep, but it doesn’t stop anywhere near the street his job is on.



To rub salt into the wound, things could have been totally different – for him and tens of thousands of other Melburnians. A century ago, chief engineer Tom Percival Strickland suggested the Melbourne and Metropolitan Tramways Board significantly widen its network at the same time it was converting its archaic cable tram fleet to electric. In 1923, the routes stretched 201 kilometres across the city from Black Rock to Fawkner, and Box Hill South to Footscray. Strickland had grand plans to more than double that, to 428 kilometres, and while he successfully converted or created 87 kilometres of electric tramways in his time, other tram line extensions were removed entirely from his vision.



The network plateaued at 250 kilometres, and while it’s still the largest urban tram network in the world, carrying 200 million passengers a year, it could have been much larger. Present-day Melburnians viewing the 1923 map of Strickland’s grand ambitions may find themselves mourning lost opportunity. Punt Road, Bell Street, Footscray, Williamstown, Sunshine and Reservoir all could have been strands on the tram network’s spiderweb. Malcolm Rowe, of Melbourne’s Tramway Museum, said when Strickland’s upgrades were jettisoned, parts of Melbourne were condemned to slower commutes. “It would have provided a good basis for the current city to have services where there are major gaps now,” he said, singling out Monash University and Doncaster.



Melbourne’s present-day planners are now asking the same questions Stickland did. Where can we, and should we, put more tram lines? Perhaps unsurprisingly, there’s some overlap with what the chief engineer originally planned. Johnston Street in Collingwood, 1906, before its tram tracks were removed. In 1923, there had been plans to extend this line all the way down Studley Park Road to Kew. Bou Karram could have been gliding to his job on a tram from South Road, Moorabbin, which Strickland envisioned being connected to the rest of the network along with nearby North Road, Bluff Road and Hampton Street. “I would definitely use a tram if it were well-planned, separate from the other lanes of traffic so it doesn’t create new [congestion] problems,” Bou Karram said. “I always prefer to use public transport; it’s more peaceful.”



Shaping the city is a key topic of The Age and the University of Melbourne’s forum, Melbourne Assembly, a three-day event in October bringing together some of the world’s brightest minds in city planning, innovation, education, arts and sport to discuss ideas for the city’s future. Melbourne’s existing tram network shares 180 kilometres of its routes with cars, making each form of travel slower. Alexander Darling In a vote reflecting the type of city our readers value and envision for their future, extending the city’s tram network was the third most popular idea of the readers’ wishlist of big ideas. Strickland’s agenda for Melbourne’s public transport came to a halt for a surprisingly simple reason. “Buses got better,” Rowe explains.



The same year Strickland left his role – 1938 – his boss, Hector Hercules Bell, travelled to Europe for inspiration. Until then, Bell had been continuing the work of converting Melbourne’s cable trams to electric, but he arrived just in time to see the UK ripping up its tramways to replace them with buses. In a cable back to Melbourne, Bell wrote he felt trams were too expensive to justify compared to buses, which had recently undergone “rapid development and improvement”. In the following decades, Melbourne embraced car travel over public transport – the exception being route 86, which now runs from Bundoora to Victoria Harbour, where Bell was forced to put trams back in the ’50s after buses proved unable to handle passenger numbers.



“Drivers were starting to say, ‘We need more access to street space than you’re giving us at the moment, and we want to push the trams aside’,” said Melbourne University urban transport researcher John Stone, who added that it became hard to justify spending on public transport at a time when Melburnians weren’t using it. “The tramways were a big institution, and they didn’t take seriously the threat from cars. They were manoeuvred out of the way by people saying, ‘we need somebody to build this road’, and so we really lost that ability for public transport to compete and for a long time through the ’70s and into the ’80s.” But as traffic increased and costs for car travel increased at pace along with Melbourne’s population, enthusiasm for public transport grew with it. Tram extensions were promised by the Greens and Labor ahead of the 2014 and 2018 elections respectively, but the footprint of Melbourne’s tram network has remained largely the same shape for decades, with notable exceptions in Box Hill, Vermont South and Docklands. This has not gone unnoticed, with Infrastructure Victoria last November urging the government to extend eight tram routes by 2030, to areas where it is planning for thousands more homes.



Related Article Public transport The slowest trams in Melbourne revealed, where it’s almost quicker to walk “These extensions will give developers the confidence to build new homes in these precincts ... support local jobs and create better connected communities,” Infrastructure Victoria chief executive Dr Jonathan Spear said. Among the precincts Infrastructure Victoria said needed connecting was Moorabbin, one of the government’s activity centres which is slated for more than 5000 new homes in buildings up to 12 storeys. Ironically, the proposal closely mirrors what Strickland had planned all those years ago: Route 64 at East Brighton would be extended south to come down the Nepean Highway, past Moorabbin train station and terminate near the new Holmesglen TAFE. Bou Karram said it wouldn’t just be workers like him that would benefit from such a move.



“In this area, there is only one supermarket. For people who live further away from it than me, a tram is definitely a viable option for them to access it,” he said. Related Series

City life Melbourne Assembly “And if they’re struggling to get to the train station, they can use a tram. How would they get there unless they have a car or ride-share?” A government spokesperson did not comment directly on these proposals, but pointed to the recent $1.85 billion investment in G-Class trams and its plans to make tram stops more accessible on certain routes. “We will continue to plan for further improvements to our public transport network as Victoria grows,” they said.



The government announced plans to abolish Infrastructure Victoria late last month, as suggested by a public service review. It is yet to respond to the 30-year infrastructure strategy from November last year, which included tramline extensions. Melbourne Assembly will be held from October 19 to October 21. More information is available on the Melbourne Assembly website, including special offers for Age subscribers

World.title: Italian court gives ‘off-grid’ Australian mother more access to three children
World.content:
WorldEuropeAustralians abroad Italian court gives ‘off-grid’ Australian mother more access to three children David Crowe September 2, 2026 — 11:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: An Italian court has granted an Australian mother a chance to rejoin her three children after they were removed from the family’s rustic home last November over health fears. The decision allows Catherine Birmingham and her British partner, Nathan Trevallion, to gain access to their children in a gradual process under the supervision of social services staff. Nathan Trevallion and Catherine Birmingham with their children. Website: https://catherinelouisebirmingham.com/ But the ruling by the Juvenile Court in L’Aquila, in central Italy east of Rome, will keep the children in a residential care facility until authorities believe it is safe to reunite the family in their own home. Birmingham told the Nine Network earlier this year that the Italian authorities had been wrong to remove the children, declaring she would keep fighting to take them home.



“What I’m fighting is the very, very, very ignorant belief that what we have done to our children was wrong,” Birmingham said. The couple were raising the children, an eight-year-old girl and two six-year-old twin boys, in woods near the town of Palmoli in the central region of Abruzzo. The Italian social services expressed concern at the fact that the off-grid home had no toilet, no electricity and no running water. They also claimed the children were kept isolated and were not being properly homeschooled. The removal of the children made headlines in November as Italian politicians and observers debated whether the “family in the woods” should be allowed to continue their off-grid lifestyle.



On Tuesday, the Juvenile Court ‌approved a staged process under the supervision of social services that could ultimately allow the children to leave residential care. Related Article Exclusive

Foreign relations ‘Empty inside’: The Australian family fighting Italy for their ‘unschooled’ children “The ruling partially revises previous court decisions and sets out ​a gradual reunification process, allowing the children to return home for daytime visits immediately ​and, from October, for weekend overnight stays with their family,” said lawyer Simone Pillon, who acts for the family. The children were taken into care in November after being poisoned by mushrooms, something the parents described as an accident. Birmingham was allowed to stay in the residential care facility, seeing the children for set periods, until a court ruled in March that she should be removed because of tensions with the staff.



In April, the family lost a claim in the Juvenile Court seeking to regain access to the children. The latest decision requires social services to ​assess the children’s reintegration with their parents before any permanent reunification can take place. Pillon said the family planned an ‌appeal to pursue a faster, more complete process to reunite the family. Court documents reported by the Nine Network’s 60 Minutes program in March declared the home was a “dilapidated ruin” without utilities and that there was a lack of essential care for the children, who had no paediatrician and were not attending school. The couple argued, however, that they were practising “parental education” without a curriculum and drawing inspiration from the Steiner system to encourage creativity.



“They know how to sew, they know how to knit, they know how to chop wood, they know how to grow plants from seed,” Birmingham told 60 Minutes. (The Nine Network is the publisher of this masthead.) “They’re learning other life skills that every child that sits there playing with the toys is not learning.” While the home did not have an indoor bathroom, it had an outdoor compost toilet and a tub for washing. “The base philosophy behind it for us is that the children are growing up in this environment where they have freedom with a boundary,” Birmingham told the program in March. Trevallion said: “You wake up in the morning and do whatever you feel like doing. We don’t have to run out the door to take the children to school. It’s just a very relaxed way of waking up, eating breakfast together as a family and continuing through the day.”



With Reuters Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Yes, Furious is a killer Epstein story but ‘it’s not just him’ …
World.content:
Emmy Rossum shadowed FBI agents for this hit TV show, which just finished its first season. One “horror” stayed with her.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Between the white-hot rage of Beef, the simmering tensions between guests at The White Lotus and Michaela Coel’s eviscerating I May Destroy You, anger is proving a defining theme of this decade’s most acclaimed TV shows. After its caustic first season, Furious might prove the most blistering of them all. Related Article Review What to stream this week: A five-star post-Epstein thriller, plus five more picks Created by Elizabeth Meriwether (The Dropout, New Girl), Furious is a cat-and-mouse thriller about an FBI agent named Alice (Emmy Rossum, Shameless) hunting down a serial killer, Catherine (Lola Petticrew, Say Nothing), a survivor of child trafficking seeking vengeance on the men responsible. Many of them are known to FBI’s sex crimes unit boss Nora (Quincy Tyler Bernstine), whose hands are often tied. All three seek justice in their own way, fuelled by a carcinogenic fury at a judicial system that fails to protect the vulnerable or hold traffickers accountable. The show – loosely inspired by the 1987 film Black Widow – has become a sleeper hit for Disney+, which reports one-day viewership rose 40 per cent by the penultimate episode from July’s premiere. Following the season finale, TV writer Jared Richards speaks with Emmy Rossum (who is also an executive producer) on how she and Meriwether shaped the series’ approach to sexual violence and trauma, what she thinks of the real-world comparisons critics have made to Jeffrey Epstein, plus a teaser of what’s coming for the just-announced second season. Warning: There are spoilers for the season’s full eight episodes below. Loading



Jared Richards: This is a show about sexual violence and its impact, but it doesn’t feature flashbacks to rape or images of grisly crime scenes. There’s an absence of dead women’s bodies. When and how did you and Liz Meriwether decide to not include those images? Emmy Rossum: From the very beginning. It’s also inspired by a film that’s much more interested in the journey of two women who are lonely outcasts getting to know each other – an FBI agent and a serial killer. Very early on, Liz wanted to tell the story of two sides of a coin that were more similar than they were different: a good guy that wasn’t all good, and a bad guy that wasn’t all bad. We were also interested in showing violence that was very female in nature. What does it look like when you can’t always just shoot someone with a gun? When you have to get really close to them with a needle? Or with a curling iron? How do you weaponise a chicken breast? [We tried to play with] things that are traditionally associated with women. Catherine (Lola Petticrew) finds inventive new uses for her curling iron. Disney/Sarah Shatz In terms of flashbacks, the show is not really interested in depicting trauma other than the after-effects: how it’s compartmentalised, how it twists and shapes us over time and how it affects you 25 years later [as with Alice] or 10 years later [as with Catherine]. Alice is also a survivor of abuse. As an actor, was there anything that was difficult to understand about how her trauma emerges? Her [violent] sex life comes to mind as an example. Yeah, that’s certainly what I was scared by. Having a character who’s been a victim of violence, who is seeking out violence in their life, is confusing. Working with psychologists on the role made it make sense.



This is a person who’s become so dissociated from their body that – similar to Catherine, our killer – her superpower is that she’s been able to hold all these secrets and disconnect from herself. That’s what makes her so great at her job; she can work these cases and seemingly not have them permeate her. Lola Petticrew and Emmy Rossum in Furious. Disney/Sarah Shatz When I worked with FBI agents [to prepare for this role], there was this way that they compartmentalised what they were working on – and the way they processed things – where their eyes just weren’t all there. They were with you, but at the same time they were on every exit and every other person in the room and every vulnerability. They were a pressure cooker in a way I found to be totally illuminating. There were certainly things about the character that overlapped with me – certain parts of her pain, her fear, her obsessive tendencies – but also things that were unfamiliar to me. Emmy Rossum stars in Furious. Disney You shadowed FBI agents and underwent drill training for research. What surprised you about that experience? Some agents shared things that had happened to them that made them become an agent. They didn’t think they would get justice for themselves, but it galvanised them to work for others. There was one specific case that I found to be almost one-to-one with Alice that immediately let me wrap my arms around her.



Editor's pick Streaming The best new TV shows to stream in September Many agents really understood that the system didn’t always work. Yet, it’s the only one that we have, and so they have to work within it. Otherwise, we’ll have chaos and vigilantes everywhere. A lot of the time they’re playing a long game. There was one detective that is still waiting to get justice for a child, and sees who they believe to be the perpetrator of this crime at their 7/11 weekly. Just the horror of seeing somebody that you feel has committed a crime that you can’t quite prove at your 7/11 every week. But knowing that one day that kid is going to be old enough to walk in and tell you the story. Or you’re going to get them some other way, for some other crime. It’s having the fortitude to play that long game and to sit with those uncomfortable feelings of frustration for a long time. Nora (Quincy Tyler Bernstine) is often left with her hands tied in the pursuit of justice. Disney/Sarah Shatz You took on so much in this role. How did you deal with the heaviness? I ate a lot of snacks. I got food trucks for the crew. I’m all about having good things to eat and soothing in other ways. And then you’re held up by your crew, right? You’re held up by your other actors, by your camera operators, by your costume team, by Liz, by your directors. You’re not alone out there on the field. I have an amazing family that I come home to at the end of the day, and I eat my kids’ snacks, and I realise that it’s not my story. It’s my job to tell [Alice’s] story that is, unfortunately, similar to a lot of women’s stories – some of whom aren’t even around to tell their stories any more. But it’s my job to channel those things, and then to try to leave them at work.



The final episode is named Hart Island – the New York site for unmarked graves that Alice and Nora visit in the finale to reinter Catherine’s friend Isabel, previously another Jane Doe. What was the importance of that title? It’s a place where people are honoured. But nobody knows who they are, and they’re not claimed. There’s a tenderness, loneliness and a beauty in that, and our story is very much about the women whose stories haven’t been told. Lola Petticrew as Catherine in the Furious finale. Disney/Sarah Shatz Many critics call Furious as a “post-Epstein show”, though he isn’t directly referenced in the show. How do you view that framing? I understand it. We do have a villain in our show [Jay Easton] who has very similar initials, so I get it. I think, unfortunately, it’s not just him. We’ve had 10, 15, 20 mega-predators over the last 20 years in positions of power. And I think there is a lot of rage about that. About the lack of accountability. About the people who have covered it up – and the fact that we know those people’s names off the top of our head and can rattle them all off. Yet we don’t know the women’s names equally well, and some of them aren’t even around to tell their stories. That’s the tragedy. That’s the horror. Furious has just been renewed for a second season. I know you can’t reveal much yet, but when did you and Liz start considering continuing this story?

World.title: Christchurch primary students and staff shelter amid possible gas leak
World.content:
Students and teachers are sheltering at a Christchurch primary school after reports of a possible gas leak.

A staff member from Beckenham Te Kura o Pūroto told RNZ shortly before 1pm the school was waiting for emergency services to arrive but investigations into the leak were underway.

Emergency services were called to the school about 12.35pm.

St John said an ambulance, a rapid response unit and an operations manager are at the school in Sandwich Road at present.

Professional firefighters held an hour-long strike nationwide today between noon and 1pm.

A Fire and Emergency spokesperson said firefighters were alerted to a possible gas leak.

Volunteer firefighters from Sumner and Lyttleton were currently at the school.

World.title: Methanex to effectively close and sell off gas contracts
World.content:
New Zealand's largest gas user Methanex is to effectively close its plant and sell off its gas contracts.

Methanex said a lack of natural gas and a clear pathway to new supplies meant operations in New Zealand were no longer sustainable.

The Canadian-owned company said it had now entered into an agreement to sell all of its New Zealand natural gas contractual entitlements, commencing in the first quarter of next year.

It said it then planned to safely idle and preserve the facility for long-term optionality, should future circumstances support a restart of operations.

The company has in the past been responsible for taking around 30 to 40 percent of all of New Zealand's natural gas production.

ln recent years the country's natural gas production has declined rapidly with little new supply coming on board.

The company, which employs around 200 people, not including contractors and suppliers, said it would work closely with employees, contractors, suppliers, customers, and government stakeholders during the transition period.

Rich Sumner, president and chief executive of Methanex Corporation, said the company had been preparing for this eventuality, given declining gas availability in the country.

Sumner said the company was now focused on supporting its team members during the transition period, and safely operating the plant over the next several months.

New Plymouth Mayor Max Brough said the announcement was disappointing but not unexpected.

"They've got no continuity of supply. They don't have enough gas coming and they're making the best of a bad situation.

"They recognise New Zealand has a gas shortage. This will free it [gas] up for other users, but the price will go up. You need a baseline consumer to keep the price down for others because make no mistake, they've subsidised New Zealand's gas at a retail level and for other users for decades."

He said many people who would lose their jobs as a result of the closure would struggle to find similar work.

"There's no alternative here for those roles.

"They will be heading to where [they can] support their families, and it probably won't be in New Zealand. So that's very disappointing."

But he was optimistic about other gas exploration projects in the city.

"I've rolled out the red carpet and the welcome mat actually, because New Zealand needs gas.

"Whatever your political persuasion is, the reality is, we still need gas to power industry in a lot of places in this country and earn export dollars."

Greens co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick RNZ / REECE BAKER

Ditch LNG import facility - Greens

The Green Party said the closure left the government no reason to push on with its plans to build a liquified natural gas (LNG) import facility.

The government has set out to build the $1 billion terminal, saying it is necessary to shore up energy supply.

"Methanex leaving takes the country's largest gas user out of the market and frees up gas supply through to the end of the decade for electricity generation," said co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick.

"The 'gas shortage' the government has been talking up to try and justify this fossil fuel project is now about to be a great deal smaller."

Swarbrick said if the government did not cancel its plans, it should at least return to the drawing board before signing a deal.

RNZ has approached Energy Minister Simeon Brown for comment.

Meanwhile, Genesis Energy said it had secured additional gas supplies from a third party for the period of March 2027 and 2029.

It has not said who it got it off. It was 11.4 Petajoules (or PJ), about 10 percent of national gas production.

In addition, Genesis said it had exercised its right of first refusal in respect of the Kupe gas supply, securing access to up to 8.6 PJ.

World.title: Thousands expected to attend Koroneihana celebrations this year
World.content:
Thousands will descend on the Waikato settlement of Ngaaruawaahia over the coming days to participate in Koroneihana celebrations.

Tainui waka were the focus of Wednesday's events, a contingent of iwi affiliated to the Waikato region being welcomed.

This year's celebrations will be the second Koroneihana hosted by Te Arikinui Kuini Nga wai hono i te po since the passing of her father Kiingi Tuuheitia Pōtatau Te Wherowhero te tuawhitu in 2024.

Hundreds made their way onto Tuurangawaewae marae on Wednesday morning carrying photos of loved ones they had lost in the past year.

Kawe mate kōrero were shared by the hosts and manuhiri lamenting at the loss of many great leaders of te ao Māori.

Tainui waka welcomed onto Tuurangawaewae Marae. Te Tari o te Kiingitanga

Later on Wednesday afternoon, kapa haka from Te Wharekura o Rakaumanga, Te Wharekura o Kirikiriroa and Te Wharekura o Mangere will perform for manuhiri.

The first national contingent of iwi bringing their kawe mate will be welcomed on Thursday morning at 9am and a second pōwhiri will be held at 1:30pm.

International guests will be welcomed on Friday morning, followed by government representatives at 1:30pm.

Te Arikinui Kuini Nga wai hono i te po will deliver Te Kauwhau a Te Arikinui on Saturday, which is expected to deliver updates on some of the key aspirations outlined last year when she delivered her first address to the nation.

Last year, Te Arikinui delivered an emotional kōrero outlining how much she still missed her late father while making it clear she remained committed to carrying his vision of kotahitanga and sovereignty for Māori forward.

"Anei ra ta taku papa i wawata ai i tumanako ai kia kotahi ai te iwi Māori, tutuki kau ana koutou e te iwi, tutuki kau ana, ka huri noa ake ki te take tuatahi tenei mea te kotahitanga. Koira te kupu mahanga ki taku papa Kiingi Tuheitia. Kiingi o te kotahitanga, me taku whakapono, me ia i konei kua menemene i te kaha o ngai tātou te Māori te tutuki i taua wawata nui,"

"This was the vision my father had for te iwi Māori, and you have achieved this in so many ways, you've demonstrated kotahitanga. This was what my father wanted. He was the King of Kotahitanga, and I believe if he was here with us on Wednesday, he would be smiling proudly at what has been achieved."

She also announced the launch of Te Huinga Taumata Ōhanga ki te Ao (economic summit) and Te Pūtea Haumi Māori, an iwi investment fund aimed at strengthening the economic independence of Māori, and shifting focus away from government funding to independent and innovative approaches to building a brighter future for generations to come.

Te Arikinui Kuini Nga wai hono i te po and the Prince of Wales. Te Tari o te Kiingitanga

"Kei te pirangi te ao ki te mahi tahi me te Māori, ko te kotinga tenei e te whakawhirinaki o tatou ki te kāwanatanga, ko tetahi huarahi pea tenei ki te mana motuhake kua roa roa nei e tumanakotia nei, iwi ora ake ake ake tenei haramai nei."

"The world is eager to work with Māori. Through developing those relationships we will be able to cut ties with the government. This is just one of the many pathways we should consider to achieve the goal of Māori wellbeing and sovereignty for ever more."

World.title: Ellerslie homicide: CCTV cameras painted over at would-be victim's home
World.content:
The would-be victim of an alleged murder plot has described waking up to find the security cameras painted over at her home.

Lok Fung Lorrence Li is on trial in the High Court in Auckland for the murder of Fuk-Fu Joseph Kwok and his wife Mei Han Chong in their home in Ellerslie three years ago.

He's also been charged with conspiring to murder his former landlord.

The landlord, who has name suppression, gave evidence at his trial on Wednesday.

Fuk-Fu Joseph Kwok and Mei Han Chong. Supplied / NZ police

She told the court through an interpreter she rented a single room to Li in March 2023.

Li was a polite tenant, she said.

While there, Li had asked his landlord if his mother could stay in the room with him.

"I said 'the room is very small, and you can find a bigger room'," the landlord said.

Li agreed, and moved out in June.

When his landlord was late to the property change-over, Li began to text her, growing increasingly frustrated.

"The message I can clearly remember said 'if you don't pick up the phone I'll report to the police'," she said.

The texts had made her uneasy, she said.

The change-over continued without anything more, but with Li, the landlord said, was an older man, introduced to her as Li's older brother.

She said his surname was 'Pan'.

The landlord said the two seemed very close.

"The feeling I got at the moment when he said he's the big brother, I felt like he's the one who can protect him," she said.

"He didn't mention he had a brother so I thought he's not his biological brother."

Alleged co-conspirator admits his role

Li's alleged co-conspirator, Shu Man Poon, pleaded guilty to his role in the killings last year.

He is expected to give evidence later in the trial.

The landlord was asked by Li's defence lawyer Paul Dacre KC about her relationship with Li.

"The way he moved out, his text message, his demeanour was so normal," she said.

"Moving house anyway is a tricky thing."

Dacre KC asked the landlord about meeting Li's 'big brother'.

"I asked him 'why are you so kind? So nice?'," the landlord said.

'Pan' told the landlord: "I'm his big brother, his matter is my matter".

"I felt like he was quite protective, and would do anything to protect him."

In the following months, Li asked to return to the rental to look for a suitcase.

The landlord said the small room Li rented had been left empty.

She eventually went to met with Li in late August, but was greeted instead by his 'big brother Pan'.

They searched for the suitcase, with Li arriving later, but could not find it.

Paint spotted

Months later in early November, the landlord woke one morning and found paint on the ground at her home.

She followed it to find her CCTV cameras and sensor lights had been painted over.

The cameras themselves hadn't been recording at the time.

She thought someone had tried to steal a car parked in the drive, the landlord said, cleaning the cameras and turning them back on.

Between 10pm and 11pm that night, the newly restored cameras captured two people wearing caps and masks going past the door.

The camera made a sound and the two spotted the camera, and left.

The camera incident in November happened days before the Kwoks were killed.

The landlord would later recognise the pair as Li and his 'big brother'.

She recognised 'Pan' by his body, and Li by his walk, the landlord said.

World.title: Fewer Kiwis contracting sexually transmitted diseases
World.content:
The number of New Zealanders contracting sexually transmitted diseases has fallen, a newly released report shows.

Syphilis rates have had the biggest drop - about a quarter - and have fallen everywhere except the South Island.

PHF Science analysis on the country's sexually transmitted disease rates in 2025 shows there were drops across all of the three reported diseases - gonorrhoea, chlamydia and syphilis.

Health authorities had been worried about syphilis when it spiked in 2023 but it was now on the decline.

There were 605 cases of infectious syphilis notified last year, a 27 percent drop the previous year, and the lowest rate since 2022, the report said.

The South Island did not improve on the previous year, however its rate of 11 cases per 100,000 was the same as most of the country.

The Northern region - Auckland and Northland, had 13 cases per 100,000.

For gonorrhea, the rate of cases fell by 17 percent last year, with 6306 cases reported.

The Northern region had the highest rate at 1.7 cases per 1000, with the South Island on the lowest at 0.6 per 1000.

Chlamydia rates were down by 13 percent.

The Northern region had the highest rate of five cases per 1000, and the South Island had the lowest at 3.8 per 1000.

PHF's report said the decrease in STIs was likely due to better prevention, testing and management of contacts.

Some at risk people were sometimes prescribed preventative antibiotics.

The report showed New Zealand had had its first recorded case of a super drug resistant strain of gonorrhoea known as XDR neisseria.

The case was linked to overseas and there had been no transmission in New Zealand but it showed the country needed to keep up good surveillance, the report said.

The number of gonorrhoea cases that were antibiotic-resistant to a lesser degree was growing.

World.title: Increased sales see wine group pouring back into business
World.content:
Despite challenges facing the wine industry - declining alcohol consumption and a global glut of grapes - wine company Delegat Group has reported strong sales results for 2026 which it expects to continue.

Key numbers for the year ended June 2026 compared with a year ago:

Reported net profit $39.5m vs $48.8m, down 19 percent

Operating net profit $61.5m vs about $51.3m, up 20 percent

Operating revenue $364.1m vs about $350.1m, up 4 percent

Final dividend 22.0 cents per share, fully imputed

Global case sales 3.3m, up 4 percent

Net debt reduced by $51.8m

The NZX-listed company's operating net profit after tax was 20 percent ahead of last year, at $61.5 million.

However, the net profit after tax of $39.5m was down 19 percent compared to the previous year, largely due to accounting rules which require biological produce like grapes are valued at their market value and a non-cash impairment of Barossa Valley Estate assets.

It saw a writedown of $9m, due to the managed reduction in yields for the 2026 harvest which were down almost 20 percent.

Despite this the 2026 harvest delivered exceptional quality fruit across Marlborough, Hawke's Bay and the Barossa Valley and netted over 38,000 tonnes of grapes.

Delegat Group chief executive Murray Annabell said it had achieved global sales of 3.3 million cases in 2026 - up 4 percent on last year to a diverse market.

"Our focus on growing premium brand demand, strengthening distribution and disciplined management of the business delivered significantly improved sales, profitability, cash flow and balance sheet strength in what remains a challenging trading environment," Annabell said

"We also responded effectively to changes in US tariffs while continuing to invest in our brands, consumer engagement and route to market capabilities."

World.title: Who is responsible? Glaring lack of clarity over Fiji operation to remove street dwellers
World.content:
Authorities in Fiji are offering contradictory accounts of a nationwide effort to remove beggars and street dwellers from public spaces, with questions over warning notices and what support is available for those affected.

The agencies involved have been unable to clearly identify what those services are and who is responsible for providing them, or what happens to people after they are moved from their public places.

The ongoing lack of clarity has raised concerns among civil society organisations that the enforcement effort may be getting ahead of the support systems needed to make it work.

In August, The Fiji Times reported that city rangers were serving warning notices to individuals soliciting alms in public areas. The notices stated that behaviours such as persistent begging or obstructioning footpaths were offences and could lead to "enforcement actions".

The operation has been advertised as a joint effort between the Lautoka City Council, Fiji Police, and the Women, Children and Social Protection Ministry.

RNZ Pacific has repeatedly sought clarification on how the operation works in practice, on what would trigger a warning notice, what happens when someone refuses to leave, what support programmes are offered for street dwellers, and what role each agency plays.

The office of the Minister for Women, Children and Social Protection, Sashi Kiran, declined to comment on the ministry's role in supporting street dwellers or on what programmes being offered to people being moved from public spaces.

The office of Police Commissioner Rusiate Tudravu would only say police were there to "ensure the safety of all parties" and would "use necessary force" if required.

Fiji Police Commissioner Rusiate Tudravu Fiji Police Force

When RNZ Pacific asked what that meant in practice, and what powers police would use if people refused to leave public spaces, no detailed explanations were provided.

RNZ Pacific's specific questions to both the ministry and police remain unanswered.

'No forced relocation'

The Lautoka City Council chairman and acting CEO Ratu Tevita Momoedonu, however, was more forthcoming, and rejected suggestions people were being forcibly removed from streets.

"There is no forced relocation here. We can't force anybody," he said.

He described the initiative as welfare-led, saying street dwellers are being profiled and offered relocation to shelters and rehabilitation services.

"We don't warn people. We profile them, and we call them in meetings, and then we suggest to them the importance or the benefits of being relocated," he added.

When asked about the support programmes being offered by the ministry, Momoedonu said they could not help.

"I can't help you either, because the [Lautoka City] Council, we have our own jurisdictions here. We only help social welfare in profiling," he said.

"The rehabilitation part, the relocation part, it is their (ministry and police) responsibility, not us. If they are not answering to you people, then [they] neither do us," he said.

While Momoedonu denied that warning notices were being used as part of the relocation effort, he did acknowledge that council notices could be issued for breaches of bylaws, and that people involved in criminal activity could be removed.

"If there are bylaws that are violated, then we can issue directives? When there are criminal elements - drinking in public place, taking drugs in public place, disturbing the peace. These are criminal elements."

He said police assist the Lautoka City Council and welfare officers when street dwellers resist engagement, although he commented that police do not "enforce relocations".

A photograph of the Operation Loloma pamphlet Supplied image

In Nadi, Fiji's international gateway, there is a similar operation underway.

A pamphlet from social worker Mohenesh Singh describes "Operation Loloma" as an effort to take beggars off the streets, profile and screen them, and provide "alternative means of livelihood".

"Together, we can create lasting solutions that address the root causes of begging," the pamphlet reads.

"The information collected will see an an individual case plan drawn up for each beggar so that the welfare of the disadvantaged individuals are taken care of by the various networks we have in the country."

RNZ Pacific contacted Singh for comment, asking what street profiling looked like, and what support was offered for street dwellers. He declined to comment about their operation.

FCOSS 'caught by surprise'

Civil society groups which are also involved in working on the issue say they have been left in the dark about the Lautoka initiative.

The Fiji Council of Social Services (FCOSS) executive director Vani Catanasiga said she first learnt about Lautoka City Council's warning notice enforcement when contacted by RNZ Pacific.

"We were caught by surprise, so, I just heard that it was happening in Lautoka," Catanasiga said.

"I was aware about it in Suva, sort of, efforts or clean up ... but I wasn't aware about Lautoka."

Vani Catanasiga says the Fiji Council of Social Services was 'caught by surprise' about the operation. Facebook / Pacific Blue Line

Catanasiga said Fiji's civil sector has repeatedly raised concerns around the lack of co-ordination between Fijian agencies that are working with vulnerable people.

The Lautoka operation, she said, could serve as a "case study" in what happens when co-ordination between involved parties breaks down.

"Unfortunately, in this case, it has to do with a vulnerable group. They're already vulnerable, they're already confused, they're already in need of support, compassion," Catanasiga said.

"When we don't address persistent coordination challenges, it really just does a lot more harm. It exacerbates the harms that they already face."

In this case, Catanasiga said the issue is an absence of communication, and clarity in roles between the different agencies involved.

The additional lack of publicly available detail is concerning for organisations who are meant to be working with vulnerable people, she added.

She described the operations as "optics-led" and said while sympathised with the relevant authorities and people in authority trying to make a difference, the lack of transparency was concerning.

"It's not to penalise those who want to do something about it. It's about [asking], 'okay, have we applied the right processes?'

"Sometimes in our effort to to do this, we miss the more essential work of doing the due diligence. And sometimes we react ... a lot of our approaches are reactionary because it looks bad.

"It's not an excuse to miss the essential steps of safeguarding [and] due diligence that we must apply to our work, particularly around social protection [and] checking on the social safety nets that are supposed to be there."

'Unsustainable'

Catanasiga also suggested authorities were relying on Fiji's long-dormant law on minor offences to justify moving beggars and street dwellers from public places, targeting activities such as begging, loitering and drunk or disorderly behaviour.

"I understand there is a Minor Offences Act that was never operationalised. It was never applied.

"So, I think that they're using that to justify the removal of people from the streets. So begging, all those sorts of activities, loitering, it's covered under that act."

While Catanisaga said she fully supported efforts to move homeless individuals into dignified work and safe housing, the current operations will be unsustainable.

"I'm just concerned about the back end processes that are supposed to be in place, the support system. If not, our efforts to get people off the streets is not going to be sustainable," she said.

Moving forward, Catanasiga said the agencies involved to deal with the issue need to come together to complete the programme they have started.

"We always talk about dignity-centred approaches [to deal with vulnerable people]. This [initiative] is not dignity-centred approaches," she said.

World.title: Sweet results: Mānuka honey company Comvita returns to profit
World.content:
Mānuka honey company Comvita has returned to profit, with higher revenue, stronger cash generation and a sharply improved balance sheet after its recapitalisation.

Key numbers for the year ended June 2026 compared with a year ago:

Net profit $7.7m vs loss of $104.8m

Operating profit $14.0m vs loss of $29.0m

Revenue $213.0m vs $192.4m, up 10.7 percent

Completed $40.5m capital raise and refinancing package

The NZX-listed company reported an almost $105 million loss the year before, prompting it to raise capital with support from F-and-N Ventures, a subsidiary of Singapore-listed consumer group Fraser and Neave.

It came amid challenging times for the company and wider honey sector related to a global glut of honey pushing prices down for producers.

Chief executive Karl Gradon said it was a good result after a reset period.

He said Comvita was entering 2027 with strong foundations to support future growth.

"Our focus now is on continuing to improve operational performance and returns, while pursuing targeted growth opportunities and maintaining financial discipline."

Comvita delivered 765 tonnes of incremental Mānuka honey volume compared with the year before, with Gradon adding the yields and quality had been great.

Chairperson Bridget Coates, said the company stood on firmer ground than it did a year ago.

She said restoring profitability and completing the recapitalisation had "significantly strengthened Comvita's financial position" and created a more stable platform for the future.

"The improvements in revenue, profitability, operating cash flow and debt reflect genuine financial discipline across the business and deliberate actions taken under Comvita's reset programme.

World.title: Bledisloe Cup quadruple-header announced as sevens added to ticket
World.content:
Australia's sevens teams will share the stage in a scheduling first, with the Wallabies and Wallaroos creating a Bledisloe Cup quadruple-header in Sydney.

The Stadium Australia Test against the All Blacks on October 17 already had a support act secured, with the Wallaroos due to host Scotland for the first time in their WXV Global Series clash.

Kick-off times for Bledisloe Cup in Sydney Wallaroos v Scotland, 12pm

Australian sevens men v Fiji, 2:05pm

Australian sevens women v New Zealand, 2.25pm

Wallabies v New Zealand, 3:45pm All times in AEDT

Now two more fixtures will be added to the ticket, with Australia's world champion sevens women to face rivals New Zealand and the men up against two-time Olympic gold medallists Fiji.

"This is an historic moment for Australian rugby, with all four of our Teams In Gold competing on the same pitch, on the same day, on an unmissable occasion," Rugby Australia chief executive Phil Waugh told AAP.

"The day will showcase the very best of rugby with our elite male and female players across the XVs and Sevens formats taking on famous rivals from around the world in an unprecedented line-up of international rugby.

"We look forward to celebrating this extraordinary occasion with our great Australian rugby community and we thank our friends from New Zealand Rugby, Fiji Rugby Union and Scottish Rugby for helping make this day a reality."

The Wallaroos will begin the action before the men's and women's sevens outfits take the field, followed by the Wallabies, who will complete the four-course menu with a late afternoon kick-off at the venue set to host next year's World Cup final.

AAP

World.title: Thea Frodin, Serena Williams's body double in movie, makes US Open debut
World.content:
Making a US Open debut as a teenager is a daunting task, but American Thea Frodin is no stranger to the bright lights.

The 17-year-old played at her home slam for the first time, going down in straight sets to world number two Elena Rybakina 6-3, 6-2.

There were plenty of fans at Grandstand who were there to see Rybakina, this year's Australian Open champion, but Frodin was a mini-celebrity in her own right.

Frodin, from California, was a body double at the age of 12 in the 2021 film King Richard, a movie starring Will Smith about the rise of Serena and Venus Williams with the help of their father, Richard Williams.

Fordin was the body double for actor Demi Singleton, who played Serena in the film, and is now forging her own path at Flushing Meadows.

There was no Hollywood screenwriting for Fordin's debut, with Rybakina never troubled in the win that came after a near three-hour rain delay.

Fordin was not disgraced in the straight-sets defeat. Down 1-5 in the second set, the teenager fired four aces, saving three match points, to extend the match just one extra game.

"She played really well today, and she has great shots," Rybakina said of her teenage opponent.

Fifth seed comes from behind to avoid another US Open boilover

Italian fifth seed Flavio Cobolli has rallied from two sets down to win his first-round match at the US Open, avoiding another early upset on the men's side.

Flavio Cobolli needed more than four hours, and five sets, to make it to the US Open second round. (Getty Images: Julian Finney)

The French Open runner-up beat Francisco Comesana 3-6, 2-6, 6-3, 6-4, 6-4, finishing his match that lasted 4 hours, 12 minutes, not long after some sun had broken through the clouds and allowed play to start on all the outside courts after a morning of rain.

Cobolli made his first career two-set comeback to avoid joining Novak Djokovic (fourth seed) and Arthur Fils (10th seed) among early losers in a men's draw that was already missing top-ranked Jannik Sinner due to injury.

Cobolli said he took a bathroom break after the second set and decided to change everything.

"So I changed all the dress that I started with today and it works," Cobolli said.

"In grand slams it's never done. You have to fight until the last point."

Ninth seed Taylor Fritz, the 2024 runner-up, rolled to a 6-3, 6-2, 6-4 victory over 18-year-old fellow American Darwin Blanch.

Kokkinakis withdraws from US Open before hitting a ball Thanasi Kokkinakis concedes he may have contested his last US Open without even hitting a ball after the cursed star's body failed him once again.

Madison Keys was the only other player to move into the second round early in a tournament where rain threatened to hamper the schedule for a couple of days.

Showers that began Monday night, local time, and could be on and off through the middle of the week delayed play on all the outer courts, allowing action only in Arthur Ashe Stadium and Louis Armstrong Stadium, which have retractable roofs.

Keys, the 22nd seed, beat 19-year-old Alina Korneeva 7-5, 6-4 in the leadoff match in Ashe. The 2017 US Open runner-up was knocked off in the first round last year in Flushing Meadows.

"It's always tough playing someone young and up-and-coming, and they're going after their shots," Keys said.

"And it's so hard to play a first round of a Grand Slam, so nervous and just wanting to do so well. So, really happy I was able to kind of fight through that and win today."

Coco Gauff, the 2023 US Open champion, 17th seed Alex Eala, and men's first seed Alexander Zverev are scheduled to play later on the final night of round one matches.

ABC/AP

World.title: More Aussies march on at US Open, Kokkinakis pulls out with injury
World.content:
Diminutive Dane Sweeny and qualifier Tristan Schoolkate have stormed into the US Open second round to continue Australia's excellent start to the season's final grand slam.

Sweeny was leading the crafty Corentin Moutet 7-6(4), 6-4, 3-0 when the Frenchman retired injured on Tuesday, local time.

Schoolkate then celebrated like Lleyton Hewitt when he finished off American qualifier Nishesh Basavareddy 7-6 (4), 3-6, 6-3, 6-4 in a tick over three hours.

The 25-year-old Sweeny marked his maiden appearance in the US Open main draw with a first-ever victory at an overseas grand slam.

The wildcard next faces either Italian 13th seed Lorenzo Musetti or rising Brit Arthur Fery for an improbable place in the last 32.

Schoolkate is into round two for a second time and will next play Italian fifth seed Fabio Cobolli, the 2026 French Open runner-up.

Sweeny, who only stands 170 centimetres high, and Schoolkate give Australia at least seven players in round two, joining Taylah Preston, Kim Birrell, Maya Joint, Alexei Popyrin and James Duckworth.

Men's sixth seed Alex de Minaur and women's Australian No.1 Daria Kasatkina will try to join the party in their first-round matches later on day three.

Sixth-seeded de Minaur launches his title quest against Italian qualifier Andrea Guerrieri, while Kasatkina is set to face Spain's former world number two Paula Badosa.

Injured Kokkinakis withdraws from US Open before hitting a ball

Thanasi Kokkinakis concedes he may have contested his last US Open without even hitting a ball after the cursed star's body failed him once again.

Kokkinakis formally withdrew from the season's last grand slam after being unable to take the court for his scheduled first-round clash with Spanish wonder boy Rafael Jodar because of an ankle sprain.

Thanasi Kokkinakis has pulled out of the year's final grand slam. (Getty Images: NurPhoto/Robert Szaniszlo)

The Australian suffered his latest injury in Cincinnati two weeks ago and has been racing the clock to be fit for the Open ever since.

He ran out of time and, after a decade battling endless back, shoulder, abdominal, knee and arm injuries, Kokkinakis admits he is losing patience.

"It is a possibility for sure," the 30-year-old told AAP when asked if his US Open career might be over.

"I'm not going to say never. The thing is, I feel like the tennis part, I've still got a lot of good tennis left in me.

"On the limited matches that I've played, I've shown that I'm more than good enough to still compete and then beat some good players.

"But, to be honest, I'm sick of going into tournaments not feeling like I can do it physically and everyone asks me how my body is."

The 30-year-old used — or "wasted" — the fifth of nine injury-protected ranking entries available to him to make the US Open draw.

The one-time Roger Federer slayer now plans on continuing his recovery and trying to be fully fit for the Australian summer.

"I want to go into it being confident in myself and, if I do win, give myself a chance to back up and try and play again," Kokkinakis said.

"That's always the thing. So it's about feeling strong in myself.

"I'll definitely obviously give the next Aussie a crack and see where I'm at after that."

AAP

World.title: Adelaide MotoGP project is more than the track. Here's what's planned in the parklands
World.content:
Headline announcements have a habit of overshadowing, if not totally obscuring, finer details, and the future of the Australian MotoGP has been no exception.

On Sunday, the SA government released its long-awaited plan for the design of a $96 million Adelaide street circuit set to host the race from 2027 — a development that will involve the cutting down of nearly 400 trees to make way for the new track.

The announcement came amid environmental acrimony. The government is currently facing protests and a federal court challenge over its actions in another part of the Adelaide parklands to redevelop the North Adelaide Golf Course.

But the MotoGP project will be about more than the track and the trees — the government is promising what amounts to a sweeping upgrade of the areas around Victoria Park in Adelaide's eastern parklands.

Here's a look at the plan that is currently out for community consultation.

Canopy and habitat

Of all the ramifications of the MotoGP project, the impact on the environment is perhaps the most politically sensitive.

But the government has been keen to spruik what it has described as a "nature-positive outcome" and has promised to plant many more trees than it removes, "meaning a net increase of at least 3,393 trees".

It has also committed to a $15 million environmental spend on "greening, rewilding and revitalising projects to restore habitat and strengthen biodiversity".

Shared-use paths are part of the concept plans. (Supplied: SA government)
