Those projects will include work to reduce pollution entering the River Torrens and to support wildlife such as local butterfly populations.

Asked about how soon the works would be completed, SA Premier Peter Malinauskas spoke of "the next few years".

"We've got a timeline that we want to work within in terms of the release of that funding," he said.

"There'll be capacity constraints about when some projects will be delivered.

"Some of the projects will require a fair bit of design work around the stormwater work that we're doing … to be able to help grow the tree canopy at a faster rate than what otherwise [would be] the case."

Grey-headed flying foxes — which are prone to summer heat stress — will get improved cooling infrastructure and habitat regeneration.

Bat Rescue SA's fundraising coordinator, Judith Bemmer, welcomed the commitment, but also expressed concern about habitat loss as a result of the removal of trees.

"We're worried that there's the potential for starvation of the baby bats, because they won't have some of those trees to fly out to," she said.

"Having said that, the trees close in to the parklands, where their colony is, and the fig trees are all still there.

"We're very hopeful that in the future, as these other trees mature, it will provide both cover and forage for these bats."

Grey-headed flying foxes at Adelaide's Botanic Park. (Supplied: Craig Greer)

Mr Malinauskas said environmental works would also include steps to contribute to platypus rewilding efforts in the Torrens by ecology group Green Adelaide.

"We are putting funding in place to accelerate that work and get it done. There is a bit of work that is required here," he said.

Adelaide Park Lands Association president Mat Monti said that, on their own, tree planting, revegetation and environmental investment were commendable — but that, when coupled with tree removal, they amounted to "greenwashing".

"We don't want them to do it just to excuse the destruction of the eastern parklands for MotoGP," they said.

Fringe benefits

The design for the new street circuit will see MotoGP bikes race along Rundle Road, between Rymill and Rundle parks.

During Adelaide's so-called Mad March festival season, those parks are occupied by Fringe venues Gluttony and The Garden of Unearthly Delights.

Rundle Road — an extension of Rundle Street — will host part of the race. (Supplied: SA government)

The government said the venues stood to gain from the redevelopment works, through upgrades to water, electricity and sewerage infrastructure.

"When Fringe and Gluttony set up down in the East End around Rymill Park, there is often temporary infrastructure they have to bring in at substantial cost," Mr Malinauskas said.

"If we can put some permanent infrastructure in the ground, that makes it easier for them to set up and pack down."

Sport and recreation

The main part of the MotoGP circuit will be in Victoria Park, which currently hosts Adelaide's Supercars races and formerly hosted the F1 Grand Prix.

The heritage grandstand in the park — a hangover from its time as a horseracing venue — will be closer to the race, thanks to a track redesign involving a revised turn-off from Wakefield Road.

The redevelopment could accommodate new playing courts. (Supplied: SA government)

But the government is also promising other works in Victoria Park for community benefit, such as an upgraded soccer field, with lighting, and community space near the grandstand.

It said there would be new running tracks through the eastern parklands, including a 2-kilometre loop in Victoria Park itself.

It also said there would "potentially" be a new skate park and playing courts near Fullarton Road.

"They could be pickleball courts, they could be basketball courts, they could be netball courts," SA Motor Sport Board chief executive Mark Warren told a parliamentary inquiry on Monday.

Mark Warren says the redevelopment will include playing courts and a cycling criterium circuit. (ABC News: Daniel Taylor)

A new water jump will be installed for the Adelaide Equestrian Festival — an annual three-day horse trials event and Olympic qualifier held in the eastern parklands.

"This will give our event a bit of a boost because we won't now have to fund it ourselves, which is great news," board member Karlene Maywald said.

"We're also working closely with the Motor Sport Board and the government to ensure we can deliver our event next April."

Pedal power

Several of the elements of the new design relate to cycling — including plans for the Tour Down Under.

The government said the Victoria Park circuit would be hosting the return of the Tour Down Under classic, a pre-tour street race, from 2028.

The heritage grandstand will be closer to the action because of a track re-design which will also accommodate cycling events, the government says. (Supplied: SA government)

The Motor Sport Board said a new 1.2-kilometre criterium loop would provide space for cycling races and Pedal Prix events.

"That's quite critical because right now the criterium loop that exists has a crossover between park users," Mr Warren said.

"It was important to, in the design, look at how we can have an unobstructed cycling criterium loop, and we believe the current design as it's been put out for consultation will achieve some of that. There's been some discussion already with cycling clubs."

There are also plans for new shared-use paths, and a pedestrian and cyclist refuge on Wakefield Road.

Consultation on the plans is open until September 20.

World.title: Ben Stokes joins Adelaide Strikers for BBL summer
World.content:
Former England cricket captain Ben Stokes will take part in the upcoming Big Bash League season after signing with the Adelaide Strikers, the team has confirmed.

The all-rounder's move had been tipped earlier in the week, but has now been locked in by the Strikers, who said they were looking forward to capitalising on Stokes's "world-class talent" and ability to put in "match-winning performances with both bat and ball".

Stokes retired from international cricket in June, a decision that caused shock waves when it was revealed during a Test match.

His arrival in Adelaide will follow a previous BBL stint, at the Melbourne Renegades in 2015.

"Ben is one of the greatest all-rounders the game has seen, a proven match-winner and a competitor who thrives under pressure," Adelaide head coach Tim Paine said in a statement released by the Strikers.

"We're thrilled to have a player of his ability join our squad."

In the same statement, Stokes said the opportunity to join the Strikers was one he "couldn't pass up".

"Adelaide Oval is an incredible place to play cricket, the Big Bash is a fantastic competition and the Strikers have an exciting group," he said.

"I can't wait to get started, create some special memories with the group and give Strikers fans plenty to cheer about."

Stokes — who made his Test debut in Adelaide in 2013 — will be available for the full BBL summer, the Strikers said.

The hard-hitting, fast-bowling all-rounder captained the England side that was widely expected to challenge Australia for the Ashes in the 2025/26 summer, but was defeated 4-1.

His decision to quit international cricket was revealed shortly before the tea break on day four of the third Test between England and New Zealand at Trent Bridge.

During the series, Stokes made front-page news after being dropped by England for the second Test amid an investigation following a night out with a teammate after the first Test at Lord's.

The 35-year-old is widely recognised as one of the most impactful and talismanic cricketers of the current era, and scored more than 11,000 international runs across T20, ODI and Test formats.

His match-winning performances have included a whirlwind 135 not out against Australia at Headingley in 2019, which steered England to an astonishing one-wicket triumph, and a rearguard 84 not out against New Zealand in the World Cup final the same summer.

His innings of 155 against Australia in a losing cause at Lord's in 2023 occurred in the match made notorious by the controversial run-out of wicketkeeper Jonny Bairstow.

World.title: Beach sprinting was just the start of Damien Cook's NRL story
World.content:
With a bit of luck, they'll tell the old Damien Cook story one more time.

This weekend, the 35-year-old St George Illawarra skipper will play his final NRL match before heading to Super League side Castleford next year.

His farewell will be at Wollongong Showground, the closest ground in the league to the ocean. When the swell's big, you can almost hear the waves crashing on City Beach from the hill.

Maybe it will be when Cook runs out for the 263rd and last time, or perhaps he'll dart out from dummy half to take on the Parramatta defence with a glimpse of the old quickness.

Maybe it'll be the commentators who say it, maybe it'll just be fans in the stands, but someone, somewhere will almost certainly tell somebody else "you know, he used to be a champion beach sprinter."

It's a story nobody seems to tire of telling — Cook himself still hears about it all the time.

"It's the great Dane Gagai's fault. He mentioned it one day when I was doing media — a few people knew about it, but he said it real loud, the journo I was speaking to did a story on it and it got out from there," Cook said.

"It's never stopped; I still get it every day. Commentators say it, I get it in comments, DMs, Instagram stories; if people see a post about a beach sprinter they tag me in it. You have to laugh."

The yarn got its greatest play during Cook's ascent to becoming one of the best hookers in rugby league, which came almost 10 years ago now, and it's worth breaking it out one more time to celebrate the end of an NRL career with an extraordinarily long tail.

It took a while to get going. Cook spent plenty of time as a second-stringer on second-rate teams.

Cook's NRL career took a while to get going. (Getty Images: Brett Hemmings)

He did not make the run on side for an NRL match until he was almost 23 and wasn't a full-time starter at hooker until the year he turned 27.

But after taking the long way, he made up for lost time immediately, and once the beach sprinting tale got used up, we started to tell others.

Cook can't pick his favourite himself. He is overwhelmed by the memories he's made because there are so many.

This late starter has now played the seventh-most matches of any dummy half in the history of the game, so when you ask him about his favourite match there's so much to choose from.

There's the first grade debut back in 2013, of course, which came for St George Illawarra against Wests Tigers at the Sydney Cricket Ground in Heritage Round. The retro jerseys and brown football made it feel like history even while it was happening.

There was the first game at Wollongong a week later. Cook is proud to finish his NRL journey there, given it's where he grew up watching football and where he played his junior grand finals for Helensburgh.

In a nice full-circle moment, his first match there in the top grade came against the Eels, just like his last will.

"The big one that day was when I got under Fuifui Moi Moi — it wasn't me being brave, he was coming straight at me," Cook said.

"I didn't have much of a choice."

Cook is one of the best dummy halves in New South Wales Origin history. (Getty Images)

There's the late-season cameo for Canterbury in 2015, which first made Cook's name and proved he could ride the lightning, and his debut at South Sydney, where he played more than 200 games and spent his most glorious times.

There's his first State of Origin match in front of 90,000 at the MCG in 2018, when he was one of 11 New South Wales debutants alongside players like Nathan Cleary, Tom Trbojevic, Latrell Mitchell and Cameron Murray.

Cook was the best of them that night in a magnificent beginning, and he always seemed to find something extra for the Blues — among dummy halves, only Ben Elias and Danny Buderus have worn the jersey more.

The 2019 decider, when he scored a scorching try right through the heart of the Queensland defence, was perhaps his single greatest highlight in rep football, but playing for Australia against Tonga in Auckland later that season was another special night.

As the Tongan anthem rang out through the night, Cook thought he'd be crushed by the noise.

"All the Tongans were singing their anthem, just this sea of red. I thought 'bloody hell, nobody is going to sing our anthem; we're up against it here'," Cook said.

"But then all the Tongans sang our anthem as well. The sound of it, I'll never forget it."

The pandemic ravaging international football and the eventual emergence of Harry Grant kept Cook to just four Tests, but he did get the special honour of playing one in Wollongong the following season and duly marked it by scoring a try.

It was no barge-over from close range though — it was an intercept that Cook took 70 metres all the way home.

He could have run along Lawrence Hargrave Drive, across the Sea Cliff Bridge, and up the hill all the way back to Helensburgh and the Kiwis wouldn't have caught him.

Cook ran all the way into an Australian jersey. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

Then there's all the club wars as well, because once Cook became one of the best he liked nothing more than testing himself against the top sides.

He says he relished the days where South Sydney had a real shot at being pride of the league again and had it out with the likes of Melbourne, Penrith and the Sydney Roosters with everything to play for and no quarter asked for or given.

All told, when asked to pick a single favourite game, Cook named almost a dozen. He just couldn't leave anything out.

"I know you asked for one, but rugby league has given me so much," Cook said.

"The mates, the moments, the memories, it's why you do it."

Cook himself gave plenty of people similarly glorious memories.

He was fast enough that a dart from dummy half would make the crowd rise, fast enough that he could break into space and round the fullback from anywhere, fast enough that when Wayne Bennett came out favouring the NRL's proposed set restart rules in 2020 some said the wily old coach was doing it just to suit Cook.

But there was more to Cook's game than raw pace. He's a cannier playmaker than some might think — in 2019 he accumulated 18 try assists, more than Grant has ever managed in a single season and equal to Cameron Smith's career high.

Cook was also among the top four players in the league for tackles made in seven of his first eight seasons.

If he gets through 25 tackles on Sunday, which is light work so long as he plays big minutes, he'll pass 10,500 of them for his career, and given the middle of the field is where the giants live, he'll have given up size and weight on just about every one of them.

Cook has never shirked the tough stuff through his long NRL career. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

Somehow, he has gotten through those 10,000 blows without ever being seriously broken — this year marks the 10th season in a row Cook will manage at least 23 games.

That's a point of pride for Cook. Once he got a taste of his dream coming true, it became a prize beyond value.

"It took a while to get there, so once I did I never wanted to let it go. I'm very proud of that because I put a lot of time into recovery and working hard and staying fit and being ready for every pre-season so I can get the most out of it," Cook said.

"I've set high standards for myself, which is why I've been able to play consistently. Even in NSW Cup I tried to do that.

"Touch wood, I haven't had a bad injury since I was at the Dogs when I broke my thumb — the other games that ruin my record were getting rested or COVID protocols, and I wish we could take those off.

"Longevity and consistency are something I'm really proud of."

Both Damien Cook and his club have done it tough in 2026. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

In the end, being there all day every day has taken its toll on Cook. It has slowed him down, and the ravages of age have finally overtaken whatever benefits he gained from his late start.

He has just two try assists and one line break for the season and has spent time on the bench and as 18th man. It feels like this change has come at the right time for him.

The wins have not come as Cook or St George Illawarra would have liked in the two seasons since he joined, but that doesn't mean he won't leave a legacy.

The Dragons have a host of young players who hold the future in their hands, perhaps none more than 23-year-old backrower Hamish Stewart.

Despite recent struggles, Cook's efforts have never wavered. (Getty Images: Brett Hemmings)

"It's me, Gutho [Clint Gutherson] and Cooky in the gym. You see him, day in and day out, and he has the most energy of anyone. He never skips a rep," Stewart said.

"He's been massive for all us young blokes, showing us how to run a team and how a club really works.

"I love how he goes about life off the field as well — I feel like I can go to him about anything."

Stewart has played every game this season and earned plenty of plaudits despite the Red V's struggles.

Along with the Couchman brothers, Dylan Egan and Loko Pasifiki Tonga, Stewart is part of the sun that can break through the clouds and of all those players, his tomorrows may be the brightest.

The Dragons have found wins hard to come by during Cook's time with the club. (AAP: Mark Evans)

If Stewart does go on and makes the most of it, Cook will play a role even if they're not packing down together.

The veteran is the kind of guy who can hold a beaten-down town together, and even if the team hasn't been winning, that doesn't mean Cook hasn't been teaching.

In trying to impart the hard-won wisdom of his rise, Cook is leaving behind something that will last once he's gone. His lessons will remain, like footsteps in the sand.

"You have to make sure you're doing the right things all the time, to lead by example. You have to push right along to the end of the season, even if it's a tough one," Cook said.

"It's easy to tick the boxes when you're winning games, but when you're up against it you still have to push hard every day.

"That's a good value to have, and a lot of the players here have that."

If he's right, that could be the longest tail of all for Cook, who leaves the club in a far better place than he found it.

He has shown these boys how to live, but now they must become men without him.

"He's always got a smile on his face every day. You see him when you walk through the doors and you know you're gonna have a good day," Stewart said.

"That's what I'll miss the most."

Cook's ultimate legacy is the players he leaves behind at St George Illawarra. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

For Cook himself, this is an end but not the end.

He's excited about playing for Castleford next year, to have a new challenge in a new place, to have something to prove again, to do the work and love it and to give it everything he's got, which Cook says is all he's ever done.

He's excited for Sunday, to see family and friends in the crowd and, one last time, to live that dream he would not surrender during the hard times.

There's no beach, but it'll be a fine day to get a sprint in.

"If I told my younger self what would happen over the past 14 or 15 years, I don't think he'd believe me," Cook said.

"Definitely after the season it will [sink in], especially when I'm packing up the house and going through some jerseys. That'll bring back the memories.

"But there's still more to do."

World.title: Is Marnus Labuschagne finally out of luck?
World.content:
For a period of 23 Tests, Marnus Labuschagne was statistically the luckiest batter in Test cricket.

He had more genuine chances dropped or missed than any other batter from his debut up until the end of the 2021/22 Ashes series. He was more often than not able to turn those reprieves into significant scores.

In more recent times, it's been slim pickings. In fact, it's been 23 Tests since his last century, dating back to the fourth Ashes Test at Old Trafford in 2023.

He's been left out of the ODI squad travelling to take on Zimbabwe and South Africa later this month. The right-hander has only missed five of Australia's last 56 ODIs, raising questions about his future in the Test side.

"We're still very much working through what that Test squad looks like, but I can say we separate out those formats," chair of selectors George Bailey told reporters when unveiling the ODI squad.

"He has played some really important one-day cricket for us; at his best that looks a certain way, but the way that squad and team is structuring up there just wasn't space for him."

If you break down Labuschagne's career into the period before his last Test ton and the period since, there is somewhat of a trend: his luck has seemingly run out.

The 2023 Ashes series in England was the last time Marnus Labuschagne made a Test century. (Getty Images: Richard Heathcote)

Looking at only genuine chances missed by opposition teams — dropped catches, missed stumpings, opposition teams not reviewing a decision that would have seen him dismissed, or wickets on a no ball — he was given a reprieve 25 times from 75 innings where he faced at least one ball.

That's a chance every three innings from his Test debut in 2018 to his most recent hundred back in 2023.

Across his first 20 Tests he scored six centuries and 12 fifties, earning him a batting average of 62.15. If, in that time, he had been taken at the first opportunity, that average drops to 46.50.

In the 2019-2021 World Test Championship cycle, Labuschagne played 13 Tests and scored the most runs of any other batter in the world. He finished that period with 1,675 runs at an average of 72.82. Across the 23 innings he was required to bat in, he was afforded 12 chances, or one every 1.92 innings.

When you compare that with Steve Smith in the same period, he was given a reprieve four times, which equates to one every 5.5 innings. Smith was still able to score 1,341 runs in that WTC cycle, which highlights Labuschagne's ability to capitalise when given the opportunity.

In fact, his entire Test career has been based on it.

Labuschagne's luck was a key feature of his game in his early Tests, with his ability to capitalise on opportunities given to him by opposition mistakes. (AP: Rick Rycroft)

Labuschagne made his Test debut in 2018 due to the bans handed down to Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft after the sandpaper incident the last time Australia's Test team toured South Africa.

That put him in the frame for the 2019 Ashes squad and, after a red-hot Smith was hit in the neck by a Jofra Archer bouncer at Lord's, Labuschagne got his next chance as the first concussion substitute in the history of international cricket, courtesy of a rule introduced the month before the series started.

In the next Test in Leeds, Labuschagne was dropped on 14, 42 and 60, and England failed to review an edge that would have been given out when he was on 35. He went on to make 80.

That series, including that fortunate knock of 80 at Headingley, cemented his spot in the side, with Usman Khawaja the unfortunate one to make way when Smith returned, a decision that left Khawaja on the outer for three years.

His ability to turn a reprieve into a significant score was a hallmark of his early Test career. Labuschagne's maiden Test century came against Pakistan at the Gabba in 2019 when he scored an impressive 185 off 279 balls. Pakistan fans might still be ruing the fact he was dropped by Asad Shafiq on 33 that same innings.

Labuschagne made a habit of scoring big runs when given a reprieve by the opposition. (AAP: David Mariuz)

In that WTC cycle alone, if he had been taken at the first opportunity, his batting average would drop to 55.68, which would have had him ranked 11th in the world.

It's not just his luck that's seemingly run out; it's his ability to capitalise on it.

From that first Ashes series to his last Test century, Labuschagne was able to turn missed opportunities into scores of 50 or more on nine occasions, including five hundreds.

Since that last century, he has been afforded only four reprieves, and the most he's added to his total is 18 runs.

Loading...

He was briefly dropped from the side after failing to impress as a makeshift opener in last year's World Test Championship final, missing Australia's tour of the West Indies. But, after only three Tests out of the side, he came back in for the 2025/26 Ashes and has remained in the team since.

When you compare that to the likes of Jake Weatherald, who has been in and out of the Test squad with questions around his form, Labuschagne has not just been given chances by opposition fielders; he's also been given them by the Australian selectors.

With an important series against South Africa on the horizon and his omission from the ODI squad, all eyes now look to see if his luck really has run out.

World.title: Dockers 'know what's on the line' ahead of Hawthorn showdown: Longmuir
World.content:
The Fremantle Dockers may be just three wins from claiming the club's first-ever AFL premiership, but coach Justin Longmuir has dismissed suggestions he will be using that as motivation heading into the finals.

The 2026 version of the Dockers is comfortably the best-performed team in the club's history when it comes to the home-and away season.

Fremantle won 19 of its 23 games to race away with the minor premiership, earning the right to host Hawthorn in a qualifying final at Perth Stadium on Thursday night.

Murphy Reid (left) will return for the Dockers against the Hawks after recovering from a groin knock. (Getty Images: James Wiltshire/AFL Photos )

It has seen excitement build among the Freo faithful, who are hopeful this could be their year, having made just one grand final since the club entered the AFL in the 1995 season, losing to the Hawks in 2013.

But throughout this year's campaign, Longmuir has urged his players to stay in the moment and focus on more immediate tasks, and he insisted thinking about the ultimate goal is not what would get the job done.

'I'm only human': Fremantle star Jackson dreaming of Dockers' maiden flag Luke Jackson has already been to the top of the AFL mountain and now, with Fremantle just three wins from a maiden premiership, the man known as 'Dogga' is desperate to get there again.

"I just don't feel like we need to [lean into it]. If there's someone at the footy club that doesn't see that carrot, well then you're probably in the wrong game, right?" he said.

"All our players know what's on the line, and we just need to make sure that we use whatever motivation that gives us to give it all to your next moment.

"Everyone feels it in different ways … some players will see it as a stimulus and some players will maybe see it as a distraction, and we'll work through that.

"Everyone sees pressure as different things and we've done some work on that, and it's all about staying in the moment.

Hawks forward Nick Watson will be one man the Dockers are keen to keep a close eye on. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Michael Willson)

"The way to win premierships is to win games of footy, and you win games of footy by winning more moments than the opposition.

"We've just got to make sure that we give our best to each moment, and the next moment is the most important one."

Fast start wanted

Much of the talk in the build-up to Thursday's game has focused on the Dockers' home-crowd advantage, after they rode the Wharfie Time rallying cry to come from behind to win their last clash against Hawthorn at Perth Stadium.

But Longmuir is hopeful they will not have to rely on the fans to overcome another slow start.

Fremantle got up in Wharfie Time against the Hawks in round nine, but hope they will not need it this week. (Getty Images: Daniel Carson)

"They're not going to get us over the line if we're not playing good footy, so we've got to give them something to cheer for, and it needs to be from the start," he said.

Key defender Brennan Cox will miss Thursday's match through injury, but Fremantle is set to welcome back the likes of Murphy Reid, Jye Amiss, Heath Chapman and the retiring Sam Switkowski.

Hawthorn is at virtually full strength for the clash, with only two players unavailable on its most recent injury list.

The Hawks enjoyed a comfortable win over West Coast at Perth Stadium in their final game of the home-and-away season.

Tech.title: Google needs Hollywood more than the studios need AI
Tech.content:
Google has reportedly been reaching out to a number of Hollywood’s biggest studios, hoping to strike licensing agreements that would allow it to train its AI models on copyrighted material in exchange for massive piles of cash. In theory, these deals would be a win-win: a huge financial boon to the studios that would also give Google a significant advantage in its race to outpace other AI companies. But while there’s little downside for Google, these deals pose a distinct set of risks to each of the studios that might be thinking about going all-in on AI. Getting into bed with Google this way might benefit Hollywood in the short term, but it could just as easily backfire and leave the public feeling burned by the entertainment industry.

Though Google has not yet been able to get Disney, Warner Bros. Discovery, or Universal to agree to anything officially, the company’s executives have been reaching out to multiple studio representatives with pitches focused on its AI technology, according to unnamed sources speaking to The Los Angeles Times. Google wants permission to train its AI models on the studios’ vast libraries of copyrighted content, and it’s willing to spend hundreds of millions of dollars to get ahold of them. Per The LA Times, Google could pay a studio like Disney / Pixar around $40 million just for the rights to generate outputs featuring a single copyrighted character. That payout could swell well into the billions the more characters Google’s deals encompass, and studios might be able to secure a portion of however much advertising revenue Google makes from AI-generated content featuring that IP on platforms like YouTube.

As expensive as these partnerships would be for Google, they would also be an invaluable tool as the company continues to crystalize its position as one of the most prominent players in the AI game. Gemini being able to spit out Disney-approved images of Darth Vader and Snow White might not seem all that significant on its face, but that’s exactly the sort of thing that could get more ordinary, non tech-obsessed people seeing generative AI in a more positive (if innocuous) light. After years of hearing AI companies boast about their plans to disrupt society and eliminate jobs, public sentiment — especially among young people — about the technology has shifted into the negative. Even with tools like ChatGPT being as popular as they are, the larger AI industry has been so mired in controversy and plagued by concerns about its real world harms that it would now be hard-pressed to put out products that would immediately curry widespread goodwill. Striking deals with film and TV studios would give Google a convenient way to shift the larger narrative about its AI ambitions.

The content developed through these partnerships would presumably look better than the slop currently being churned out by models trained on ill-gotten source data, and having Google’s name and logos slapped all over official AI-generated Disney content would do wonders to legitimize this technology in people’s minds. But even if it didn’t, the partnership would still signal to the public that the entertainment industry sees generative AI as a tool worth embracing. It’s hard to quantify how valuable that framing would be to Google, whose DeepMind arm struck a $75 million investment deal with A24 earlier this summer. But it’s very easy to imagine how taking Google’s AI cash could put studios on a path that ultimately alienates their workers and audiences.

Regardless of whether a studio were to incorporate AI tools into their production workflows or simply feature user-generated AI content on their platforms (which was Disney and OpenAI’s plan before their partnership collapsed), striking a licensing agreement with Google would be a watershed moment.

Lionsgate, a notable studio but not a major player, struck a licensing deal with Runway in 2024. So far, nothing concrete has come out of that partnership, but the companies say they’re working on a plan to release AI-generated shorts. Once any one of the big legacy studios hop on to the AI bandwagon and manage to actually make something they can show the world, more production houses have a reason to follow suit. AI’s potential to speed production timelines up while keeping costs down is one of the main things that has kept studios interested in utilizing the technology. Shareholders would absolutely love it if production houses could put out more movies while spending less money, but doing that by using AI tools would almost certainly put a significant portion of the entertainment workforce out of jobs.

What may be keeping Disney and other studios from rushing to take Google up on its offers is the way that people have reacted to seeing AI used in the production of films like Spider-Man: Brand New Day. Fans were dismayed to find AI-generated images in Brand New Day’s official artbook, and the negative reaction might have been even more intense had people known about the technology’s use before the film hit theaters. It’s impossible to know for sure whether awareness about AI’s presence in Brand New Day’s production would have kept it from making $2 billion at the box office. But it stands to reason that none of the studios is eager to be the first to learn what happens when they release a project that’s presented as being the product of Google’s AI tools.

Though Google has everything to gain from Hollywood embracing AI, the studios have to be mindful of how endorsing this technology could leave them out on a limb. And as much as Google might be presenting its products as the solution to all of the entertainment industry’s issues, the AI industry needs Hollywood more than Hollywood needs more slop.

Tech.title: Anthropic launches Claude Fable 5.1 and says it’s up to 45 percent cheaper for agentic work
Tech.content:
is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Anthropic says its newest AI models, Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1, address criticisms from customers about price, data retention, and overzealous safeguards. The company claims Claude Fable 5.1 offers stronger performance than Fable 5, but costs around 25 percent less typically and up to 45 percent less for complex agentic tasks, thanks to reduced pricing on cached data that was already processed and stored.

Along with the announcement, a slew of early impressions popped up, including from Every CEO Dan Shipper, who claims, “It’s the strongest coding model we’ve used, but now it’s fast, token-efficient, and crucially actually speaks like a normal person.”

Box CEO Aaron Levie is another early access believer, saying that his company’s agent with Fable 5.1 picked up on subtleties and ambiguities in data that Fable 5 missed in the same test. Meanwhile, Lisan al Gaib points out that on benchmarks, Mythos 5.1 with low reasoning scores the same as its predecessor set to Max reasoning.

Fable 5.1 also has “more precise safeguards” that Anthropic says are less likely to block basic biology questions than Fable 5, but Mythos 5.1 has the same biology restrictions as the previous model. Anthropic also explained its progress on data retention, saying that Enterprise Frontier Safeguards offer “complete privacy” by storing data on the customer’s cloud servers instead of its own, and will start rolling out later this fall.

Anthropic says it’s “now allowing Fable 5.1 to be used for identifying software vulnerabilities,” but it will still redirect some cybersecurity tasks to Opus models, like “penetration testing, exploit generation, and binary-based vulnerability scanning.” Claude Fable 5.1 is now available on all platforms, while Mythos 5.1 is available to Project Glasswing participants only.

Tech.title: Apple Maps follows Google in renaming Lake Ontario
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Apple Maps has officially changed the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America, as reported earlier by Bloomberg. The company joins Google in re-labeling the Great Lake following an executive order signed by President Donald Trump in the midst of a trade dispute with Canada.

The Canadian version of Apple Maps still shows “Lake Ontario” when panning over the area, while international versions of the app show both names, according to Bloomberg. Google updated its map shortly after the name change went live in the US Geographic Names Information System (GNIS), but Apple waited a bit longer.

Best Buy is celebrating Labor Day all week long with big deals, including a deep discount on the Lenovo Yoga 7i 2-in-1, taking its original $1,1199.99 price down to $749.99.
